#10297. Architectural Choices in China's Open-Source AI Ecosystem: Building Beyond DeepSeek

This is the second blog in a three-part series on China's open source community's historical advancements since January 2025's "DeepSeek Moment." The first blog is available here, and the third blog is available here.

In this second piece we turn our focus from models to the architectural and hardware choices Chinese companies have made as openness becomes the norm.

For AI researchers and developers contributing to and relying on the open source ecosystem and for policymakers understanding the rapidly changing environment, architectural preferences, modality diversification, license permissiveness, small model popularity, and growing adoption of Chinese hardware point to leadership strategies across a multitude of paths. DeepSeek R1's own characteristics inspired overlap and competition, and contributed to heavier focus on domestic hardware in China.

In the past year, leading models from the Chinese community had almost unanimously moved toward Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, including Kimi K2, MiniMax M2, and Qwen3. R1 itself was an MoE model, it also proved a crucial point: strong reasoning could be open, reproducible, and engineered in practice. Under China's real-world constraints, maintaining high capability while controlling cost, and ensuring models could be trained, deployed, and widely adopted, MoE emerged as a natural solution.

MoE is like a controllable compute distribution system; under a single capability framework, compute resources are allocated across requests and deployment environments by dynamically activating different numbers of experts according to task complexity and value. More importantly, it does not require every inference to consume the full set of resources, nor does it assume that all deployment environments share identical hardware conditions.

The overall direction of Chinese open-source models in 2025 was clear: not necessarily the strongest possible performance, but ability to operate sustainably, deploy flexibly, and evolve continuously, achieving the best cost performance balance.

Starting in February 2025, open-source activity was no longer focused only on text models. It quickly expanded into multimodal and agent-based directions: Any-to-Any models, text-to-image, image-to-video, text-to-video, TTS, 3D, and agents all progressed in parallel. What the community pushed forward was not just model weights, but a full set of engineering assets, including inference deployment, datasets and evaluation, toolchains, workflows, and edge-to-cloud coordination. The parallel emergence of video generation tools, 3D components, distillation datasets, and agent frameworks pointed to something larger than isolated breakthroughs---it pointed to reusable system-level capabilities.

The competition to lead similar to DeepSeek in a non-text modality heated up. StepFun's released high performance multimodal models, excelling in audio, video, and image generation and processing or editing. Their latest speech-to-speech model Step-Audio-R1.1 boasts state-of-the-art performance, beating proprietary models.  Tencent also reflected this shift through open-source work in video and 3D. Its Hunyuan Video models and projects such as Hunyuan 3D reflect growing competition beyond text-centric models.

Models in the 0.5B--30B range were easier to run locally, fine-tune, and integrate into business systems and agent workflows. For example: Among the Qwen series, Qwen 1.5-0.5B has the most derivative models. In environments with limited compute or strict compliance requirements, these models were far better suited for long-term operation. At the same time, leading players often used large MoE models in the 100B--700B range as capability ceilings or "teacher models," then distilled those capabilities down into many smaller models. This created a clear structure: a few very large models at the top, and many practical models underneath. The growing share of small models in monthly summaries reflected real usage needs in the community.

https://huggingface.co/spaces/cfahlgren1/hub-model-tree-stats

After R1, Apache 2.0 became close to the default choice for open models from the Chinese community. More permissive licenses lowered the friction around using, modifying, and deploying models in production, making it much easier for companies to move open models into real systems. Familiarity with standard licenses, such as Apache 2.0 and MIT, similarly eased usage; prescriptive and tailored licenses add friction through unfamiliarity and new legal barriers, contributing to the decline seen in the graph below.

Based on the releases of all organizations shown in Chinese Open Source Heatmap

In 2025, model releases increasingly aligned with inference frameworks, quantization formats, serving engines, and edge runtimes. A prominent goal was no longer just to make weights downloadable, but to ensure that models could run directly on target domestic hardware---and run reliably and efficiently. This change was most visible on the inference side. For example, With DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, both Huawei Ascend and Cambricon chips achieved day-zero support, not as cloud demos, but as reproducible inference pipelines released alongside the weights, enabling developers to validate real-world performance directly.

At the same time, training-side signals began to appear. Ant Group's Ling open models use optimized training on domestic AI chips to achieve near NVIDIA H800 performance, cutting the cost of training 1 trillion tokens by about 20%. Baidu's open Qianfan-VL models clearly documented that the model was trained on a cluster of more than 5,000 Baidu Kunlun P800 accelerators, their flagship AI chip, with details on parallelization and efficiency. At the beginning of 2026, Zhipu's GLM-Image and China Telecom's latest open model - TeleChat3, were both announced as being trained entirely on domestic chips. These disclosures showed that domestic computers were no longer limited to inference, but had started to enter key stages of the training pipeline.

On the serving and infrastructure side, engineering capabilities are being systematically open-sourced. Moonshot AI released its serving system: Mooncake, and explicitly supported features such as prefill/decoding separation. By open-sourcing production-grade experience, these efforts significantly raised the baseline for deployment and operations across the community, making it easier to run models reliably at scale. This direction was echoed across the ecosystem. Baidu's FastDeploy 2.0 emphasized extreme quantization and cluster-level optimization to reduce inference costs under tight compute budgets. Alibaba's Qwen ecosystem pursued full-stack integration, tightly aligning models, inference frameworks, quantization strategies, and cloud deployment workflows to minimize friction from development to production. Still, reports of compute constraints in China threaten expansion; Zhipu AI is reportedly restricting usage amid a computing crunch.

When models, tools, and engineering are delivered together, the ecosystem no longer grows by adding projects, but by structurally differentiating on a shared foundation-and beginning to evolve on its own. How China will respond to U.S. hardware sales and export controls as NVIDIA sells H200s continues to be an open question. Read more about the shifting global compute landscape here.

The "DeepSeek Moment" of January 2025 did more than trigger a wave of new open models. It forced a deeper reconsideration of how AI systems should be built when open source is no longer optional but foundational and why those underlying choices now carry strategic weight.

Chinese companies are no longer optimizing isolated models. Instead, they are pursuing distinct architectural paths aimed at building full ecosystems suited to an open-source world. In an increasingly commoditized model landscape, these decisions signal a clear shift in competition from model performance to system design.

Our next blog will go deeper into organizational wins and share some of what we expect to see in 2026.

What China has made open-source has never been a single model weight, but the entire AI ecosystem.

I would love to hear your views on China's system design.

Really interesting anniversary post! It’s inspiring to see how the DeepSeek R1 release helped expand the global open-source AI ecosystem, lowering barriers and sparking new innovation over the past year.

Insightful analysis of architectural innovations in the open-source AI ecosystem! Understanding these different architectural approaches is crucial for making informed design decisions. When documenting our own system architectures and evaluating different approaches, I've found InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) incredibly valuable—it turns plain English system descriptions into architecture diagrams that you can iterate on through conversation. Makes it much easier to communicate architectural trade-offs and maintain living documentation.

One point that strikes me is that Chinese open source seems to have internalized something that the West still treats as secondary: when models become commodities, the real differentiator becomes systemic operability. It's not about "the best weight," but about who delivers a complete system—from training to inference—that works under real cost, hardware, and compliance constraints. This completely changes the axis of competition.

#10296. Screwed up at work? Here’s how to learn from your mistake without overcorrecting

Part of what separates great leaders and employees from merely good ones is the ability to learn effectively from mistakes. Often, we talk about learning from mistakes as if most people don’t. But while we can always point to a few people who seem blissfully unchanged by their errors, a more dangerous trend is the continuous attempt to fight the last war—which ultimately leads to ineffective learning.

That is, we focus too hard on the most recent failure. Our biggest concern becomes avoiding the mistake or bad outcome that happened last. As a result, we forget the many other lessons we have learned. That tendency to make significant changes based on the most recent mistake can lead our behavior to veer wildly and lead to other mistakes down the line.

Here are three things you can do to avoid changing too much as the result of an error.

1. Focus on the smallest fix posible

When you make a mistake at work, and particularly when it’s a big one, it tends to dominate your thinking. The consequences may still be felt across the organization, and you’re embarrassed. You may even imagine that everyone you see is thinking about what you did wrong.

Because this recent error is at the forefront of your mind, you are likely to emphasize avoiding that same mistake in the next thing you work on. Unfortunately, when you do that, this error is going to be overrepresented in the planning you do for whatever project you’re working on next. You may become so focused on that problem that you miss other potential difficulties. You may even change routines that have served you well in the past just to avoid the same mistake again.

Instead, when you develop an idea about how to correct your mistake, think intentionally about the smallest thing you can change. If you purposefully underemphasize the change you want to make, that will provide a counterweight to the attention you’re paying to that recent mistake. It will help dampen the tendency to overreact.

2. Think about what works

If you’re a reasonably conscientious person, you probably don’t make mistakes all the time and, in fact, are probably successful at most of what you do. However, it’s likely you find the errors you do make to be embarrassing and unacceptable.

You certainly don’t want to make the same mistake twice. But instituting a correction needs to be done in the context of the many things that you do well.

It is certainly important to do some kind of after-action report to determine what went wrong that led to your mistake. But after you figure out what went wrong, make sure that you also think about what goes right most of the time. Understand how your current way of working leads to good outcomes most of the time.

The aim is to ensure that when you make a correction, the changes you make preserve as much of what typically leads to good outcomes as possible and focus just on those things that are most likely to lead to the mistake you made.

3. Track your learning

We live in a limited window of the present. That is, it is hard to remember all of the things that you do that have become habits and how those influence the effectiveness of your work. You might be able to remember your work style from a few weeks ago, but the way you did your work last year or the year before that may feel like a mystery. It can be even harder to remember what aspects of work you struggled with.

It can be helpful to keep a diary of the way you work, your struggles, and the biggest mistake you can remember from a given time period. Every three months, put a half hour on your calendar to update your journal. Write about the three key projects you’re doing at that moment. Think about the changes you have made to your work routines over the past few months. Write about what aspects of work are going well and which feel like a struggle.

When you make a mistake at work, go back over that journal and read about the evolution of your work over time. Reading your journal has several benefits when you’re dealing with a new mistake you have just made. It reminds you of ways you have struggled in the past that are no longer a problem. It may remind you of changes you made in the past that you are no longer keeping up and should return to. It can also give you a sense of the many ways you have improved your workflow over the years.

All of these elements can be helpful when correcting a mistake. When you are no longer struggling with things that caused you fits in the past, it helps you to be aware that the habits you developed are largely successful. You may also realize that your current mistake reflects that past changes have fallen by the wayside and need to be reinstated. Recognizing the many ways you have adapted your work over the years can also help you to avoid undoing past changes in the zeal to avoid a current mistake. All of these can help you to right-size the correction you are making now.

#10295. Motorola Signature 27 delivery dates slip ahead of launch as it expands to more regions

Motorola and Best Buy websites are now showing an early December shipping date, despite at least one customer already receiving tracking info.

Tons of excitement surrounds Motorola’s upcoming release of the Signature 27, and now retail websites are showing that new preorders won’t be arriving until early December. The original announcement in early November proclaimed a November 19 release date, but Motorola tells 9to5Google:

We’re excited by the strong consumer response of the new motorola signature 27, with demand exceeding our initial expectations. As a result, some orders may experience updated shipping timelines. Our teams are working to meet demand and get devices to customers as quickly as possible.

Motorola and Best Buy websites are still showing “Pre-order” buttons, so while you can order one right now, December 8 and December 11 are the current ship dates. Motorola also just announced that the Motorola Signature 27 will be officially available in India starting December 9 (via GSMArena), further complicating the supply chain.

Despite this, one Redditor who preordered says they received a tracking number for the Signature 27 and the free Motorola Watch Ultra preorder, and it’s scheduled to arrive on November 25. The Motorola Signature 27 has been available in Europe since November 16, so it’s clear demand is quite high for Motorola’s biggest premium launch in a long time.

The Motorola Signature 27 is the most premium phone Motorola has possibly ever launched in North America. The company has shied away from releasing flagship phones here for years, although Motorola’s Razr line of foldable phones often blends premium specs with more mid-range ones. The excitement for the Signature 27 is completely understandable in this case, especially now that Motorola is offering the full seven-year software update treatment that Samsung and Google do.

#10293. We Got Claude to Build CUDA Kernels and teach open models!

The best thing about agent skills is upskilling your agents on hard problems. There are two ways to look at that:

This blog post walks through the process of using a new tool, upskill, to generate and evaluate agent skills with large models and use them with smaller models. We will benchmark upskill on the task of writing CUDA kernels for diffusers models, but the process is generally useful for cutting costs, or using smaller models on hard and domain-specific problems.

In case you missed it, agent skills are taking the coding agent game by storm. In fact, they’re a straightforward concept to define model context as files, like instructions as markdown and code as scripts. The file format makes them easy to generate, share, and review. In short, they’re a practical medium to share capabilities across models and tools, and they're most useful in specific domains or hard problems. Not stuff the model can do well anyway.

This post showcases this process by using Claude to generate a Skill file that can be used by open source models for a complex and specialized task: write CUDA kernels. We first tried a simple skill based on existing documentation, and we found that it improved performance for some others, but not all. In fact, it could even degrade performance or increase token usage for some models. Check out the plot below to see the performance of the model with and without the basic skill.

Now, let's walk through how you can use upskill to upskill your agents on hard problems, and measure performance.

First, we use Claude Code to build a kernel interactively and export the trace. We worked through the process by instructing, validating, and adding documentation links. This somewhat naive process is important to reveal the models' initial challenges. In fact, you can iterate on this multiple times, by trying to solve the task with draft versions of the skill, and experimenting with smaller models. Each time, you can instruct the agent to improve the skill and test it on the smaller model.

Here's an example of the skill that we created and have been using to build kernels. We started from this agent trace where the agent was able to build a kernel, but not without some help.

Once the teacher model has performed the task, we need them to make a skill. There are a number of effective ways to do this.

In most cases, the first 2 options result in functional skills. However, the performance of an agent with the skill is unknown. That’s where upskill is useful, because it will also generate test cases for your skill based on the trace. It then compares the results under both scenarios: using the trace, or applying the skill. We see below that the original model (Claude Opus) met the same performance with and without the skill. This means the skill captured the task for this model. Great!

Finally, we need to transfer our newly created skill to the tool or model we intend to use. Most tools like codex, cursor, and opencode have settled on a consistent format for skills, which is a directory at {agent}/skills/{skill_name}/SKILL.md , so we just need to copy the skill directory to this location.

With upskill we can pass a skill and a set of models to the eval command and upskill will run the test cases on those models with and without the skill to compare performance. We can see here that the skill increases accuracy on some open models, but not on all.

In this case, we might want to iterate further on the gpt-oss skills by regenerating the skill. We can do upskill generate --from {skill}.

There is more to agent skills than model performance. Often agents can reach a given accuracy with or without a skill, they just need to consume more tokens to get there. For recurring tasks, we want to optimize agents to use less tokens to achieve the same accuracy. The results below reveal another dimension to the skill. Some models are significantly reducing their performance token usage, whilst others are using more tokens with the skill. For example, with moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Thinking the skill is clearly effective in terms of accuracy and token usage. However, for Claude Opus 4.5 there is no clear performance increase and an increase in token usage, so you would not want to use this skill with Claude Opus 4.5.

tldr; try out and evaluate models with the skills you create. Use upskill eval or a similar tool to evaluate the models performance with and without skills.

That’s the high level end to end of upskilling your coding agents on hard problems. Try out upskill now like this:

We have a high level understanding of how we can upskill an agent. Let’s now look at the use case we solved for writing CUDA kernels.

We didn’t just want to write kernel code, but understand the full kernel-builder workflow: project structure, build.toml configuration, architecture-specific optimizations, and PyTorch bindings. This tutorial shows how upskill creates validated skills that actually work.

The kernel-builder-cuda-kernels skill teaches Claude everything it needs to know about CUDA development: which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings.

With this skill, you can tell Claude things like:

And Claude will create the complete project structure, CUDA implementation, and build configuration—following the exact conventions that kernel-builder expects.

This isn't about generating boilerplate. The skill encodes domain expertise: H100 uses compute capability 9.0, shared memory should be aligned to 128 bytes, async memory copies require __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900. Knowledge that would take hours to gather from documentation gets packaged into ~500 tokens that load on demand.

That's it. Upskill uses Anthropic Claude Opus-4.5 model by default but also supports OpenAI and local models via OpenAI-compatible endpoints as generators. We want to use the more expensive and higher quality models to generate skills, and the smaller ones to use them. Think robin hood.

Let's walk through generating a skill that teaches agents how to build CUDA kernels with HuggingFace's kernels library.

Above we used upskill, but it could in fact be any agent or chat tool and an exported trace.

Also, we could start from an existing skill and add to it:

upskill loads the existing skill, applies your improvements, and re-evaluates to ensure the changes help.

upskill creates a skill, generates test cases, evaluates performance, and refines based on failures:

The baseline shows how the model performs without any skill. The "with skill" result shows performance after the skill is injected into context. A 35% improvement means the skill is working.

The skill is saved as a directory following the Agent Skills specification:

The important test is: does this skill help local or cheaper models to build kernels?

A 45% improvement on "unsloth/GLM-4.7-Flash-GGUF:Q4_0" means the skill successfully transfers domain knowledge from a capable model to a faster, cheaper one. Skills that work on weaker models will definitely work on stronger ones.

This is the core value proposition: use expensive models to create skills, then deploy those skills with cheap or local models.

upskill uses a teacher-student approach to evaluate models where the teacher model generates test cases for the student model to be evaluated on.

If you pass an existing skill to upskill eval, it will generate test cases for the skill and evaluate the model on them. Test cases are simple input/output pairs that verify the agent understands the task:

We can also test how a skill performs across different models:

This helps you find the cost-performance sweet spot: maybe Haiku with the skill is good enough for your use case, saving significant API costs.

We've shown that upskill can create validated skills that transfer domain expertise from powerful models to cheaper ones. The kernel-builder skill is just one example of what's possible.

The approach works for any specialized task where you'd otherwise write detailed prompts repeatedly. Skills are portable across Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other tools that support the Agent Skills specification.

#10291. Sizing GPU Memory for a RAG Service: KV Cache, Context and Concurrency

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) app is usually drawn as a language model plus a vector database. When it goes live, the part that fails first is rarely the retrieval. It is GPU memory on the generation model, because a model that loads fine for one request can run out of memory when several users send long questions at once.

This article shows how to estimate that limit before you deploy, with a short script you can run, and then covers what else in the pipeline can slow responses down.

Serving a model takes more than its weights. The GPU also holds:

the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with the length of every active request

memory used by the inference runtime itself

SitePoint's guide to running a local LLM on 10GB of VRAM makes the same point for a single desktop GPU: the usable budget is the total VRAM minus overhead, and the KV cache grows with the context window, so the real model budget is smaller than the number on the box.

For a RAG service, the KV cache matters even more. Retrieved passages are pasted into the prompt, so every request carries a long context, and every concurrent request holds its own cache.

The cache size per token depends on the model's architecture: two tensors (keys and values) for every layer, for every KV head. This script turns those numbers into a rough limit on concurrent requests:

def kv_bytes_per_token(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, dtype_bytes=2):

# Keys and values, for every layer, for one token.

return 2 *layers *kv_heads *head_dim *dtype_bytes

def max_concurrent(vram_gb, weights_gb, ctx_tokens, per_token, reserve_gb=2.0):

budget = (vram_gb - weights_gb - reserve_gb) * GIB

return int(budget // (ctx_tokens * per_token))

per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(32, 8, 128)

print(per_token // 1024, "KiB per token")

n = max_concurrent(24, 16, ctx, per_token)

print(ctx, "tokens ->", n, "concurrent requests")

For a 24 GB GPU holding about 16 GB of fp16 weights with 2 GB kept in reserve, it prints:

The numbers are estimates. Real runtimes add their own overhead, and the architecture values come from the model's configuration file, so read them from the model you actually use. The pattern is what matters: doubling the context length halves the number of requests that fit. A RAG prompt that stuffs in ten retrieved chunks costs real capacity.

Serving runtimes do not simply crash when the cache is full. The vLLM documentation on optimization and tuning explains that when KV cache space is insufficient for all batched requests, the engine preempts some of them and recomputes them later, which can hurt end-to-end latency. Its suggested remedies include giving the cache more memory, reducing the number of concurrent sequences or batched tokens, or sharding the model across GPUs.

So the symptom of undersizing is often not an error. It is slow, uneven responses under load. Test with realistic prompt lengths and several simultaneous users, not a single request.

Embedding and ingestion have a different profile from generation. Embedding is often lighter than serving a large language model, and some teams run it on CPU. Document parsing, chunking and tokenization also run on CPU, so a fast GPU cannot make up for a slow CPU upstream. SitePoint's tutorial on a local RAG system for private documents walks through chunking, embeddings, vector storage and reranking, and is a good map of which stages run where.

RAM: vector indexes, document loaders and caches all live in system memory, so large collections need more of it.

Storage: model files, indexes, logs and backups add up. Fast storage shortens model loading and re-indexing.

Network: if the vector database, application server and model server sit in different places, latency adds to every request.

Two layouts are common. A single instance runs everything and is simplest for prototypes and internal tools. Separated services put ingestion and retrieval on smaller machines and keep the GPU for generation, which scales better as traffic grows.

Memory estimates only hold if the GPU memory is really yours. On a shared or time-sliced GPU, other workloads can take memory and compute away from your service, which makes capacity hard to plan. Hosting providers describe this in different terms, such as passthrough, vGPU, MIG and time-slicing. For a view of how one GPU hosting provider explains those allocation methods, GPU Mart's GPU virtualization guide compares them. It is a hosting company's page, so confirm any provider's claims about isolation and performance with your own load test.

Whatever provider you choose, ask these questions:

Is the physical GPU assigned to you exclusively, or partitioned or time-sliced?

Do you have root access to install your own drivers, CUDA libraries and containers?

Which minimum commitments, regions and support terms apply?

A small stack can run as a handful of containers: an API service for request handling and prompt assembly, an ingestion worker, a vector database and a model server. Keeping them separate lets you monitor each one's memory and CPU use and move the heavy one to bigger hardware without rewriting the rest.

For a service that stays up all month, a fixed monthly term is easier to forecast than hourly capacity. Hourly capacity suits testing quantization settings or processing a one-off document batch.

Is GPU memory always the bottleneck for RAG?

Not always. Generation usually hits memory first, but slow parsing, a small CPU or a distant vector database can dominate response time.

Does quantization solve the memory problem?

It shrinks the weights, but the KV cache still grows with context length and concurrency. Test with your real prompt sizes.

It depends on volume. Small workloads can run on CPU, while a large ingestion job may benefit from a GPU for a limited time.

Size a RAG service for the worst realistic moment, not the single-request demo. Estimate the KV cache from the model's architecture, remember that long retrieved contexts reduce how many requests fit, watch for preemption under load, keep CPU, RAM, storage and network in the plan, and find out whether the GPU is exclusive or shared. The script above is small, but it turns a vague worry about memory into numbers you can check.

#10288. Introducing Daggr: Chain apps programmatically, inspect visually

TL;DR: Daggr is a new, open-source Python library for building AI workflows that connect Gradio apps, ML models, and custom functions. It automatically generates a visual canvas where you can inspect intermediate outputs, rerun individual steps, and manage state for complex pipelines, all in a few lines of Python code!

If you've built AI applications that combine multiple models or processing steps, you know the pain: chaining API calls, debugging pipelines, and losing track of intermediate results. When something goes wrong in step 5 of a 10-step workflow, you often have to re-run everything just to see what happened.

Most developers either build fragile scripts that are hard to debug or turn to heavy orchestration platforms designed for production pipelines—not rapid experimentation.

We've been working on Daggr to solve problems we kept running into when building AI demos and workflows:

Visualize your code flow: Unlike node-based GUI editors, where you drag and connect nodes visually, Daggr takes a code-first approach. You define workflows in Python, and a visual canvas is generated automatically. This means you get the best of both worlds: version-controllable code and visual inspection of intermediate outputs.

Inspect and Rerun Any Step: The visual canvas isn't just for show. You can inspect the output of any node, modify inputs, and rerun individual steps without executing the entire pipeline. This is invaluable when you're debugging a 10-step workflow and only step 7 is misbehaving. You can even provide “backup nodes” – replacing one model or Space with another – to build resilient workflows.

First-Class Gradio Integration: Since Daggr is built by the Gradio team, it works seamlessly with Gradio Spaces. Point to any public (or private) Space and you can use it as a node in your workflow. No adapters, no wrappers—just reference the Space name and API endpoint.

State Persistence: Daggr automatically saves your workflow state, input values, cached results, canvas position—so you can pick up where you left off. Use "sheets" to maintain multiple workspaces within the same app.

Install daggr with pip or uv, it just requires Python 3.10 or higher:

In this example, the Space returns both original image and the edited image, so we return only the edited image.

That's it. Run this script and you get a visual canvas served on port 7860 launched automatically, as well as a shareable live link, showing both nodes connected, with inputs you can modify and outputs you can inspect at each step.

GradioNode calls a Gradio Space API endpoint or locally served Gradio app. Passing run_locally=True, Daggr automatically clones the Space, creates an isolated virtual environment, and launches the app. If local execution fails, it gracefully falls back to the remote API.

Let’s write the first step, which is the background remover. We will clone and run this Space locally. This Space runs on CPU, and takes ~13 seconds to run. You can swap with this app if you have an NVIDIA GPU.

We can now pass in the function to initialize the FnNode.

Daggr is in beta and intentionally lightweight. APIs may change between versions, and while we persist workflow state locally, data loss is possible during updates. If you have feature requests or find bugs, please open an issue here. We’re looking forward to your feedback! Share your daggr workflows on socials with Gradio for a chance to be featured. This is a great point. We'd like to support them, but are thinking about the right API because we'd also like programmatic inspection / API usage, which requires some level of determinism. If you have any suggestions, please feel free to open an issue here: https://github.com/gradio-app/daggr

Do you have any issues running Daggr in a jupyter notebook? It should be supported, but if run into issues, please feel free to open an issue here: https://github.com/gradio-app/daggr

The visual inspection capability for chained apps is brilliant! Being able to see the flow programmatically while maintaining visibility is so important for debugging and understanding system behavior. Speaking of visualizing system flows, I've been using InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) for documenting our application architectures—it generates diagrams from plain English descriptions and lets you refine through conversation. It's been a great complement to tools like Daggr for communicating the overall system design to the broader team.

This is a solid approach to pipeline transparency. Working with Funnelsflex deployments, we often see a friction point between rigid UI funnel builders and the flexibility of raw Python scripts. Daggr seems to bridge that gap by keeping the logic in the code where it belongs, while providing the visual state persistence that’s usually missing in standard Gradio chains.

The ability to rerun individual nodes without triggering the entire inference stack is a huge win for debugging complex flexible workflows. I’m curious to see how it handles state management when scaling to high-concurrency environments, but for rapid prototyping and 'inspectable' AI apps, it’s a very clean implementation.https://funnelsflex.io/

#10286. Beijing’s AI ambitions are under threat as models may fall behind by up to nine months versus competitors — Chinese AI labs are under heavy fire from export controls, maturing chip stacks and a distillation crackdown

This week, several reports have detailed how closing GPU rental loopholes across Asia may have had an impact on the development of Chinese AI models. In September, Mozilla estimated that open-weight AI models were three to six months behind the frontier. Since then, developments in the AI industry and export control rules could mean that Chinese AI models, many of which are typically open-weight, might fall even further behind Western counterparts, by up to nine months.

Zhipu AI, the developer of the GLM series of models, has allegedly pushed its release calendar back as a result of reduced access to advanced AI accelerators, Reuters said. It's an open secret that data centers located in Asia have been renting compute capacity to Chinese entities for some time. In light of the recent Nvidia scandal involving Jensen Huang and Megaspeed, the U.S. Department of Commerce has since tightened its rules over how data centers lend their compute capacity to Chinese entities. This has created an environment where there is, in fact, an excess of compute capacity available in the region, Bloomberg reported.

These curbs have a knock-on effect on how companies train their AI models, with Nvidia's AI accelerators being the most coveted; not having access to them stifles the development of AI in the region. However, this isn't entirely true across the industry. DeepSeek is attempting to wean itself off foreign silicon and instead adopting Huawei's Ascend AI chips, and porting its libraries away from CUDA and onto the open-source CANN. However, this hasn't stopped Chinese AI labs from facing another issue: tightened security against the distillation of AI models.

Distillation is a practice wherein the way a model thinks can be extracted and then learned from. It is largely believed to be the method in which Chinese AI labs have made great leaps in intelligence over the past several years, though several of China's leading labs refute that claim. The Western frontier has become more obtuse: Anthropic in October detailed how it's leveled up its own defences against distillation attacks, and the obfuscation of an AI model's chain of thought adds another hurdle. According to The Information, this is an issue that DeepSeek is now reportedly reckoning with. If distillation curbs the development of Chinese AI models even further, the gap between Eastern and Western frontier intelligence grows from three to six months to an estimated nine months.

If you look at Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index, which ranks AI models across a wide range of benchmarks and scores them in numerical order, Anthropic currently has the leading public AI model: Claude Fable 5.2, at a total of 65 points. Meanwhile, the leading Chinese AI model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, sits at 47. Between the two contenders are practically every Western frontier lab: OpenAI, Google, and Meta are all outgunning Chinese competitors, which were, just a few short months ago, competing at the frontier across many tasks.

It's important to mention that Artificial Analysis also changed its methodology over recent weeks, with China's AI models falling slightly further behind in added benchmarks, such as the Omniscience score, which tracks how often an AI is likely to hallucinate. This is paired with a jump in capability among the Western labs: Right now, it's on the Chinese AI labs' shoulders to respond in kind, and if current releases are anything to go by, they are falling short of expectations, especially in domains such as cybersecurity. An Epoch AI report characterized the difference in capabilities between GLM 5.3 and Claude Opus 5.5 as a six-to-seven-month gap in intelligence. With the release of newer models like Claude Fable 5.2, it's likely that gap has only widened, and the same story is likely to play out over the next few months across additional domains.

With additional safeguards against distillation and powerful compute resources becoming more difficult to find, this poses a difficult question for the Chinese labs: How can they keep up the pace and stay competitive while the odds are stacked against them?

China still holds the overall top spot in the open-weight arena with Kimi K3.1 Pro, though Western companies are bringing more performant models out as the months pass. China's second tier of open-weight models, which can often be run locally, e.g Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-27B (20 on AA), is facing competition from the American-made Thinking Machines Labs' Inkling 2 Mini (20 on AA), which was recently released. With the release of the larger (closed-weight and API only) Qwen 4 model seemingly not landing quite as well with users, it remains to be seen whether Alibaba can maintain the advantage of time, as Inkling 2 Mini was released just this week, while Qwen 3.8-27B has been out for several months.

With devices like the RTX Spark, AMD's AI Halo, and more, users are increasingly getting their own choice of running an open-weight AI, and for all intents and purposes, that usually means using a Chinese model to get the most intelligence out of your machine. However, recent developments show that smaller Western labs are also beginning to bridge that gap.

This is yet another arena in which Chinese and Western labs will want to wrest control from one another. Notably, Google has not released another series of Gemma models following Gemma 4 back in April. If a fifth generation of Google's Gemma models arrives, they'd likely be close cousins to the Gemini Neon, Carbon, Argon, and Hydrogen family, though that remains speculation until Google confirms anything official.

Against the backdrop of export controls and tightening restrictions on AI distillation, Chinese AI labs are in a tough spot, and all eyes are on frontier labs like Moonshot AI, Zhipu, Deepseek, Alibaba, and Xiaomi to see if they can scale the intelligence wall that their Western counterparts currently present. More compute for training resources may be an answer, but for comparison's sake, Huawei's upcoming Ascend 950DT accelerator offers 2 PFLOPS of FP4 compute and 1 PFLOPS of FP8, while an Nvidia Rubin R200 offers 50 PFLOPS in inference and 35 PFLOPS in dense workloads. In memory capacity and bandwidth, the Ascend 950DT can offer 144GB of HiZQ 2.0 with 4 TB/s of bandwidth across a 2 TB/s interconnect. Rubin, on the other hand, offers 288GB of HBM4, with bandwidth ranging from 19.2-22 TB/s, across an NvLink interconnect at 2.6 TB/s.

If China's AI ambitions are to compete with the West, its silicon needs to either scale so the country can produce more chips to outgun a Western AI deployment with sheer numbers, or it needs to develop more advanced accelerators, while also managing the CANN software stack. The chips are figuratively, and literally, stacked heavily against China. As the race to develop Artificial Intelligence marches on, the Department of Commerce's latest measures have undoubtedly made it incredibly difficult for the country to compete.

#10285. Nothing Ear (note) is yet another AI recorder, but with earbuds inside

Set to launch on December 8, Nothing has confirmed its mysterious AI product will be called “Ear (note),” and it’s an AI recorder with earbuds inside.

Update 11/25: Nothing has shared another image of Ear (note), showing how the case opens and the earbuds inside. The company adds that the audio quality matches Nothing’s “best in-ear audio experience,” explaining:

Ear (note) is a new approach to personal productivity, making it easy to transcribe, summarise and act on in-person conversations, calls, online meetings and thoughts – without requiring an additional device or new behaviours. At the same time, Ear (note) doesn’t compromise on audio, combining Hi-Res Audio and high-quality audio capture with AI that works in the background.

Introducing a new form factor, this is also the most evolved version of Nothing’s transparent design language. Built around an aluminium case with squared edges and a cool metallic finish, Ear (note) introduces machined metal and brutalist forms into Nothing’s transparent design language. Clear windows are inspired by the contours of topographic maps, revealing depth and dimensionality within the case. The TALK button and a new RECORD button draw on the controls on a retro Walkman, both positioned to be easy to reach and to provide tactile feedback when activated.

Speaking to Bloomberg, Nothing has confirmed that its new AI product is “Ear (note).” This builds on a pair of earbuds by turning the charging case into an AI-powered recorder.

The case has a “Talk” button, like Ear (3), which can be used to record your own voice, where a record button enables the ability to “record and transcribe conversations.” Ear (3a)’s ability to record audio from the earbuds will also carry over to Ear (note), giving the product the ability to record both conversations in person and over the phone.

Nothing is entering a crowded market here with products from Plaud, Amazon, and countless others already offering AI recording/transcribing products, but building in earbuds is indeed a unique selling point.

Nothing Ear (note) is launching on December 8, though pricing is unclear. Pei’s comments suggest a subscription will be used in some capacity.

#10284. From Script to Screen: A Developer's Workflow for Long-Form AI Video

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Generating a single AI video clip is easy now. You send a prompt and get a few seconds of footage back. The trouble starts when the goal is three, five, or ten minutes of video where the same character looks the same in every scene, the style does not drift, and the captions line up with the picture.

Most guides stop at the clip. This one covers the part after it, treating a video as a small build pipeline: a storyboard that is data, prompts generated from that data, clips normalised and stitched with ffmpeg, and captions derived from the same source. If you want to wire a generation model into your own application first, SitePoint's guide to integrating generative video APIs into web applications covers the request and webhook side. If the finished video is headed to a YouTube channel, how to get a YouTube API key and use the Data API is a good starting point for the publishing side. Everything between those two is below.

Long-form AI video fails at the seams between clips, not inside them. Plan for continuity before you generate anything.

A storyboard stored as JSON can be validated, versioned, diffed, and turned into prompts by code, which a pile of loose prompts cannot.

Repeat the full character description in every prompt. Models do not remember the previous clip.

Clips from different generations rarely share resolution, frame rate, or codec settings. Normalise them before joining.

Captions are cheapest when generated from the script and measured clip durations, not transcribed afterwards.

Current video models generate short clips, commonly a handful of seconds each. A longer video is therefore many clips, and every clip is an independent generation. The model has no memory of what the character wore in the previous one.

That produces three kinds of failure. The character drifts, so hair, clothing, or proportions change between scenes. The style drifts, so lighting and colour grade shift from cut to cut. And the technical specs drift, so one clip is 24 frames per second at one resolution and the next is something else. Each of these is fixable, but only if the project is organised so the fixes can be applied consistently.

Start with a structured storyboard instead of a document full of prompts. One file holds the style, a "character bible", and an ordered list of scenes.

"style": "soft watercolor picture book illustration, warm evening light, 16:9",

"mira": "a nine year old girl with short curly black hair, a yellow raincoat and red rubber boots",

"lantern": "a small round paper lantern with a gentle orange glow and a tiny smiling face"

"setting": "a narrow cobblestone street in light rain",

"action": "walks slowly past closed shops, looking up at the sky",

"camera": "slow push in from a medium shot",

"narration": "It had rained all afternoon, and the street was quiet."

"action": "finds the lantern glowing on a wooden crate and kneels beside it",

"narration": "Then she noticed something glowing under the awning."

Because it is data, a script can check it before you spend any generation credits. Two checks pay for themselves quickly: every character named in a scene must exist in the bible, and no scene may be longer than the clip limit of the model you use.

const known = new Set(Object.keys(board.characters));

errors.push${scene.id}: unknown character "${name}");

${scene.id}: ${scene.duration}s is over the ${MAX_CLIP_SECONDS}s clip limit, split it into shots

Treat MAX_CLIP_SECONDS as a setting. Limits differ between models and change over time, so check the one you are using rather than trusting the number in this example.

Never write the per-scene prompt by hand. Generate it, so the style line and the character descriptions are identical every time.

The character description appears word for word in every scene that includes that character. This is the single most effective consistency tactic that needs no special tooling. Changing a detail, say the colour of the boots, becomes one edit in the bible instead of a search through twenty prompts, and the diff shows exactly what changed between versions.

Put the style line first and keep it identical across all scenes.

Describe one action per clip. Two sequential actions in one prompt often produce a blend of both.

Keep camera directions simple. A single move per clip is more reliable than a combination.

Avoid naming real people, brands, or existing characters in prompts. Beyond the rights issue, it makes results harder to reproduce.

Clips from separate generations often disagree on resolution, frame rate, pixel format, or codec parameters. Joining them directly can produce stutters, green frames, or an outright error. Convert every clip to one agreed format first.

-vf "scale=1280:720:force_original_aspect_ratio=decrease,pad=1280:720:(ow-iw)/2:(oh-ih)/2,fps=24,format=yuv420p" \

-an -c:v libx264 -crf 18 "norm/$(basename "$f")"

The filter scales each clip to fit a 1280 by 720 frame, adds padding if the aspect ratio differs, sets 24 frames per second, and forces a widely compatible pixel format. The -an flag drops any audio the model generated, since narration will be added as one track later. Name clips with zero padded numbers such as s01.mp4 and s02.mp4, so a shell glob sorts them in story order.

Once every file shares the same parameters, the concat demuxer can join them without re-encoding:

for f in norm/*.mp4; do echo "file '$PWD/$f'"; done > list.txt

ffmpeg -y -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy stitched.mp4

Hard cuts are the safe default. Crossfades are possible with ffmpeg's xfade filter, but they require careful offset arithmetic and a re-encode, so add them only when a cut genuinely looks wrong.

Captions are easiest when they come from the script, not from a speech recognition pass over the finished video. The storyboard already holds the narration text and each scene's length, so an SRT file is a few lines of code. Use measured durations rather than planned ones, because a generated clip is often a little shorter or longer than requested.

const { execFileSync } = require('node:child_process');

const ms = Math.round(totalSeconds * 1000);

const h = String(Math.floor(ms / 3600000)).padStart(2, '0');

const m = String(Math.floor((ms % 3600000) / 60000)).padStart(2, '0');

const s = String(Math.floor((ms % 60000) / 1000)).padStart(2, '0');

const rest = String(ms % 1000).padStart(3, '0');

const end = cursor + scene.duration; // set from measureSeconds() after generation

${blocks.length + 1}\n${toTimestamp(start)} --> ${toTimestamp(end)}\n${scene.narration}\n

Update each scene's duration from measureSeconds on the normalised clip before calling buildSrt. If a narration line is long, split it across two caption blocks so it stays readable. Then combine picture, voiceover, and captions in one final step:

ffmpeg -y -i stitched.mp4 -i narration.mp3 -i captions.srt \

-c:v copy -c:a aac -c:s mov_text -shortest final.mp4

Soft captions like these can be switched off by the viewer and read by assistive technology, which is better than burning text into the picture. Keep the .srt file as well, since most platforms accept it as a separate upload.

Everything above is a good fit when you need repeatability: many videos from templates, versioned storyboards, automated publishing, or tight control over the model. The price is that you own the glue code, the ffmpeg settings, and the failures.

For one off projects, or when the people making the video are not developers, a managed platform is often the more sensible choice. Tools such as magiclight.ai bundle story to video generation, character handling, voice, and an editor in one interface, and advertise videos of up to 50 minutes. Check the specifics yourself, because claims like that are marketing, and results depend on your content. One point matters for developers in particular: if you need to automate generation from your own code, confirm that the platform you pick offers an API or export route before you build a workflow around it. A tool with a good editor and no programmatic access suits a different job than the pipeline in this article.

A short manual pass catches what automation does not. Watch the whole video once at normal speed, looking only at continuity. Read the captions against the audio. Check that no real person's likeness, brand mark, or protected character slipped into the footage. Finally, check the disclosure rules of the platform you publish on, since many now ask creators to label realistic synthetic media, and the rules change.

The model is only one component of a long-form AI video. The reliability comes from the structure around it: a validated storyboard, prompts generated from it, clips forced into one format, and captions derived from measured data. Each of those is ordinary software engineering, and none of it depends on which generation model you choose, so the pipeline survives when the model changes.

Start with a two minute video and four or five scenes. Fix the seams there before scaling up, because every continuity problem you find at that size is one you will not have to hunt for in a ten minute project.
