#10271. How Developers Can Detect Fake Payment Gateways and Build Secure Checkout Integrations

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Online payments are an essential part of modern web applications. E-commerce platforms, subscription services, and online marketplaces all depend on payment gateways to process transactions and manage customer orders.

However, integrating a payment gateway involves more than adding a payment button or displaying a checkout form. Developers must ensure that payment requests are sent to legitimate providers, transaction information is validated correctly, and payment confirmations cannot be manipulated.

Fake payment gateways introduce another challenge. They can imitate legitimate payment interfaces, use copied checkout templates, and redirect customers to fraudulent websites. Even when a checkout page looks professional, its underlying implementation may not be trustworthy.

For developers, understanding these risks is important when designing payment workflows. This article explores common payment integration vulnerabilities and practical techniques for building secure checkout systems using JavaScript and Node.js.

A payment gateway connects an application with a payment processing service. It handles transaction requests and communicates payment results to the merchant's application.

A typical checkout process involves several components:

A frontend checkout interface where customers review their orders.

A backend application that creates payment requests.

A payment provider that processes transactions.

A webhook endpoint that receives payment notifications.

A database that stores order and transaction information.

Attackers can target different parts of this process.

For example, a fraudulent website may copy the appearance of a legitimate checkout page while sending submitted information to an unauthorized server. Another approach involves manipulating payment requests or creating fake confirmation pages that make an unsuccessful transaction appear complete.

These techniques are also relevant to marketplace fraud. An eBay scam can involve fraudulent payment requests and misleading transaction links, illustrating why developers need to consider payment security beyond the appearance of a checkout page.

The important distinction is that a legitimate-looking interface does not establish that the payment request is reaching an authorized provider.

One of the first steps in reviewing a payment integration is checking where the application sends its payment requests.

Developers should inspect network requests using browser developer tools. The Network tab can reveal which domains receive requests when a customer opens the checkout page or submits a payment form.

Look for unexpected requests, unfamiliar domains, and scripts loaded from sources that are not part of the approved integration.

For example, a checkout application might load a payment script like this:

The URL above is illustrative, not an actual payment provider.

Developers should compare the script URL and integration method with the provider's official documentation rather than trusting a URL simply because it appears familiar.

Reviewing external JavaScript dependencies.

Checking whether payment forms submit data to approved endpoints.

Confirming that HTTPS is used throughout the payment process.

Reviewing changes to payment-related scripts during development.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) can also restrict which domains are allowed to load scripts and receive certain types of requests.

These example domains must be replaced with the actual domains documented by the selected payment provider.

A carefully configured policy can reduce the risk of unauthorized scripts and unexpected form submissions.

A common mistake in payment development is trusting values submitted directly from the browser.

Consider an application where the frontend sends an order ID and payment amount to the backend.

An attacker could modify the amount before submitting the request. If the backend accepts that value without checking the original order, the application may create a payment session for an incorrect amount.

The safer approach is to retrieve the order from the database and calculate the amount on the server.

Here, payment Gateway create Checkout Session() represents a provider-specific server-side SDK method.

The important part is that the backend retrieves the amount from its own database rather than accepting a price supplied by the customer.

Developers should also validate product IDs, quantities, discounts, currency, and order ownership before creating a payment session.

This prevents frontend manipulation from directly determining the final transaction amount.

Developers should avoid building payment processing around unverified scripts, copied templates, or unknown third-party services.

Instead, use official APIs and SDKs provided by established payment processors.

A hosted checkout integration is one common option. The merchant's backend creates a payment session through the provider's API, and the customer is redirected to the provider's hosted checkout page.

This approach can reduce the amount of sensitive card information handled by the merchant's application.

However, developers still need to configure the integration correctly.

Store secret API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager.

Never expose private credentials in frontend JavaScript.

Use the provider's official SDK where available.

Validate checkout session creation on the backend.

Restrict success and cancellation URLs to approved destinations.

Use HTTPS for application and payment communication.

Developers should also understand the difference between public and secret API credentials. Public keys may be designed for browser use, while secret keys must remain on the server.

The OWASP Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration Cheat Sheet provides additional guidance on securing payment requests, validating transaction details, and handling payment callbacks.

Payment providers often use webhooks to notify applications when transactions are completed, failed, or refunded.

However, webhook endpoints are publicly accessible URLs in many integrations. Without proper verification, an attacker may send a fabricated HTTP request that looks like a successful payment notification.

Developers should verify webhook signatures using the payment provider's official SDK.

Consider this simplified Node.js example:

The verify Webhook() method represents the signature verification functionality of a payment provider's SDK. It is not a universal Node.js method.

The example also assumes that the provider's event contains the relevant order and transaction details. Developers should follow the provider's actual event schema and retrieve the authoritative payment status when required.

The application should never mark an order as paid simply because a customer has reached a success URL.

Instead, payment confirmation should depend on an authenticated provider notification or a server-side verification request.

Another important issue in payment development is duplicate processing.

Imagine a customer clicks the payment button twice because the first request takes too long. The application may create two payment sessions or attempt to charge the customer more than once.

Network interruptions and automatic retries can create similar situations.

Idempotency helps prevent these problems by ensuring that repeated requests with the same idempotency key do not create duplicate operations.

A simplified example using Node.js might look like this:

The example uses a provider-specific idempotency option. Actual SDK syntax and key requirements vary between providers.

In a production application, developers should also store payment attempts in the database and enforce appropriate uniqueness constraints.

This helps maintain consistent transaction records even when requests are repeated or interrupted.

A payment integration should be tested beyond the normal successful checkout process.

Most established payment providers offer sandbox environments that allow developers to simulate transactions without charging real customers.

These environments are useful for testing different transaction scenarios.

Developers should also test whether the application handles provider downtime correctly.

For example, if the payment provider becomes temporarily unavailable, the application should not mark an order as completed or assume that the transaction succeeded.

Automated integration tests can help verify these scenarios before deployment. Monitoring payment failures, unexpected status changes, and repeated webhook errors can also help developers identify problems after release.

Security does not end when a payment integration goes live.

Developers should implement monitoring to identify unusual transaction patterns and unexpected changes in payment behavior.

Recording payment attempts and transaction IDs.

Monitoring webhook signature verification failures.

Detecting repeated requests for the same order.

Alerting on unexpected order status changes.

However, logging must be implemented carefully.

Applications should never store card verification codes or expose secret API keys in application logs. Sensitive information should be excluded from debugging output, and access to transaction records should be restricted.

Developers should also follow the payment provider's security requirements and applicable PCI DSS obligations when handling payment data.

Detecting fake payment gateways and building secure checkout integrations requires more than checking whether a payment page looks legitimate.

Developers need to examine the complete transaction flow, validate payment information on the server, use official payment APIs, verify webhook signatures, and prevent duplicate transactions.

JavaScript and Node.js provide useful tools for implementing these security controls, but the reliability of a payment system ultimately depends on how its frontend, backend, database, and payment provider communicate.

A well-designed checkout integration should verify every important transaction before fulfilling an order. By following these development practices, teams can build payment systems that are easier to maintain, more reliable, and better protected against common payment manipulation techniques.

#10268. WhatsApp officially adds scheduled messages, and the rollout is scheduled too

It’s about time. WhatsApp announced today that it is finally adding support for scheduled messages in its app.

A staple of many other messaging apps, WhatsApp is adding scheduled messages to its app. This gives users the ability to write a message but schedule sending it to another user or group chat at a later time.

Scheduled messages on WhatsApp can be sent up to 14 days after you draft them in both 1:1 chats and group chats. You can schedule through a long-press on the send button, with a menu popping up to let you pick the future time when the message will be sent. You can also see scheduled messages before they’re sent to cancel sending or edit the message.

WhatsApp notes that these messages are sent even if your phone’s battery is dead or if the device is off, and everything is still end-to-end encrypted. It works with text, photos, and videos, but apparently not with voice notes.

That said, the rollout is also scheduled out. WhatsApp says the feature will start showing up for users “over the coming weeks” globally, so you might be waiting a bit longer for this long overdue release.

#10267. Community Evals: Because we're done trusting black-box leaderboards over the community

TL;DR: Benchmark datasets on Hugging Face can now host leaderboards. Models store their own eval scores. Everything links together. The community can submit results via PR. Verified badges prove that the results can be reproduced.

Let's be real about where we are with evals in 2026. MMLU is saturated above 91%. GSM8K hit 94%+. HumanEval is conquered. Yet some models that ace benchmarks still can't reliably browse the web, write production code, or handle multi-step tasks without hallucinating, based on usage reports. There is a clear gap between benchmark scores and real-world performance.

Furthermore, there is another gap within reported benchmark scores. Multiple sources report different results. From Model Cards, to papers, to evaluation platforms, there is no alignment in reported scores. The result is that the community lacks a single source of truth.

Decentralized and transparent evaluation reporting.

We are going to take evaluations on the Hugging Face Hub in a new direction by decentralizing reporting and allowing the entire community to openly report scores for benchmarks. At first, we will start with a shortlist of 4 benchmarks and over time we’ll expand to the most relevant benchmarks.

For Benchmarks: Dataset repos can now register as benchmarks (MMLU-Pro, GPQA, HLE are already live). They automatically aggregate reported results from across the Hub and display leaderboards in the dataset card. The benchmark defines the eval spec via eval.yaml, based on the Inspect AI format, so anyone can reproduce it. The reported results need to align with the task definition.

For Models: Eval scores live in .eval_results/*.yaml in the model repo. They appear on the model card and are fed into benchmark datasets. Both the model author’s results and open pull requests for results will be aggregated. Model authors will be able to close score PR and hide results.

For the Community: Any user can submit evaluation results for any model via a PR. Results get shown as "community", without waiting for model authors to merge or close. The community can link to sources like a paper, Model Card, third-party evaluation platform, or inspect eval logs. The community can discuss scores like any PR. Since the Hub is Git based, there is a history of when evals were added, when changes were made, etc. The sources look like below.

To learn more about evaluation results, check out the docs.

Decentralizing evaluation will expose scores that already exist across the community in sources like model cards and papers. By exposing these scores, the community can build on top of them to aggregate, track, and understand scores across the field. Also, all scores will be exposed via Hub APIs, making it easy to aggregate and build curated leaderboards, dashboards, etc.

Community evals do not replace benchmarks so leaderboards and closed evals with published results are still crucial. However, we believe it's important to contribute to the field with open eval results based on reproducible eval specs.

This won't solve benchmark saturation or close the benchmark-reality gap. Nor will it stop training on test sets. But it makes the game visible by exposing what is evaluated, how, when, and by whom.

Mostly, we hope to make the Hub an active place to build and share reproducible benchmarks. Particularly focusing on new tasks and domains that challenge SOTA models more.

Read the docs: To learn more about evaluation results, check out the docs.

Add eval results: Publish the evals you conducted as YAML files in .eval_results/ on any model repo.

Check out the scores on the benchmark dataset.

Register a new benchmark: Add eval.yaml to your dataset repo and contact us to be included in the shortlist.

The feature is in beta. We're building in the open. Feedback welcome.

Great initiative, aggregating multiple signals is the way to go!

Although such a measure has not solved the problems encountered in the current evaluation, at least it is indeed a very good measure in terms of decentralization and mobilizing the power of the community for co-construction.

Will there be the integration with existing huggingface lighteval?

hi @naufalso ! Lighteval now suport inspect-ai as a backend, so everything supported by inspect is integrrated in lighteval 🔥

This is a very important and timely initiative. It’s easy to get lost in the sea of leaderboards, each with its own format and reporting style. The Inspect AI log format brings much‑needed standardization, and having Hugging Face host evaluation logs is a real game changer. One reason many valuable benchmarks fade away is that original contributors often lack the resources to continuously maintain leaderboards. The Community Evals initiative has tremendous potential to address this gap, and I truly appreciate the effort behind it.

That gives it the ability to offer you real network choice when you sign up for a new plan (we’ll explain more later), and keeps your costs low. Really low.

But you’re reading this on 9to5Google, so how does it impact you as an Android user? That’s a great question.

RedPocket is offering $150 rebates on Android devices like the Pixel 11, Galaxy S26, Galaxy Z Flip 7, Moto G Play, and more. (You can also get $100 rebates for iPhones if you’re into that sort of thing.)

These offers run from November 9 through the 30th at redpocket.com, so don’t wait too long to save big.

It’s OK if you haven’t heard of RedPocket Mobile, because it has been quietly working for 20 years to improve the way people use their phones. Founded in 2006, the company works with all three major US carriers — AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon — and because it doesn’t own any of its towers, it can pass along significant savings to its customers. Here’s what the company says on its website:

RedPocket was built for price-conscious consumers who want real value and freedom from rigid, high-cost contracts. As a no-contract carrier, we’ve stayed focused on making reliable, transparent, and flexible phone service for everyone. Our plans are designed to fit real lifestyles, whether you’re a heavy data user, a frequent traveler, or just looking to cut your monthly bill.

One thing to note about all of these plans: the annual prices are paid upfront, not billed monthly. Promotional pricing applies to the first year, and after that, annual plans renew at $110 for Essentials, $220 for Plus, and $330 for Premium.

#10263. Introducing SyGra Studio

SyGra 2.0.0 introduces Studio, an interactive environment that turns synthetic data generation into a transparent, visual craft. Instead of juggling YAML files and terminals, you compose flows directly on the canvas, preview datasets before committing, tune prompts with inline variable hints, and watch executions stream live—all from a single pane. Under the hood it’s the same platform, so everything you do visually generates the corresponding SyGra compatible graph config and task executor scripts.

Let’s walk through this experience step by step.

Open Studio, click Create Flow, and Start/End nodes appear automatically. Before adding anything else:

Once validated, Studio keeps the configuration in sync and pipes those variables throughout the flow—no manual wiring or guesswork.

Drag the blocks you need from the palette. For a story-generation pipeline:

Studio’s detail panel keeps everything in context—model parameters, prompt editor, tool configuration, pre/post-process code, and even multi-LLM settings if you want parallel generations. Typing { inside a prompt surfaces every available state variable instantly.

Open the Code Panel to inspect the exact YAML/JSON Studio is generating. This is the same artifact written to tasks/examples/, so what you see is what gets committed.

After the run, download outputs, compare against prior executions, get metadata of latency and usage details.

SyGra Studio can also execute existing workflow in the tasks. For example, in the tasks/examples/glaive_code_assistant/ workflow — it ingests the glaiveai/glaive-code-assistant-v2 dataset, drafts answers, critiques them, and loops until the critique returns “NO MORE FEEDBACK.”

SyGra Studio turns synthetic data workflows into a visual, user friendly experience. Configure once, build with confidence, run with full observability, generate the data without ever leaving the canvas.

SyGra Studio looks like a powerful platform for synthetic data generation workflows! For teams working with complex data pipelines like this, clear system documentation is essential. I've been using InfraSketch (https://www.infrasketch.net/) to document our ML infrastructure—you describe your system architecture in plain English and it generates diagrams that you can refine conversationally. It's been really helpful for onboarding new team members and creating design docs that actually stay current with our evolving architecture.

SyGra Studio is a legit unlock: visual graph workflows that remove the pain of hand-editing YAML. Good work!

#10261. How to Test Android Apps on Windows: A Practical Guide to Emulators and APK Testing

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Most Android bugs are not exotic. They are a button hidden behind a keyboard, a screen that breaks on a smaller display, a permission prompt nobody tested, or an install that fails on an older version of the system. You can catch many of these problems without owning a single test phone, as long as you set up your Windows PC properly and test with a plan.

This guide covers how to prepare Windows, how to choose and configure an emulator, how to install and verify APK files with Android Debug Bridge (ADB), what a good test session checks, and where virtual devices stop being trustworthy. It includes a small Python helper that explains install failures and reads launch times from ADB output, with tests. Tool versions and menu names change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

● Emulators find the large, repeatable problems fast. Use them for functional checks, layouts and install testing, and confirm hardware behavior on real devices.

● Prepare Windows first. Enable hardware virtualization and the Windows Hypervisor Platform, and check the result with the emulator’s own acceleration check.

● Match the virtual device to real users. Test the oldest and newest Android versions you support, a small screen and a modest memory profile.

● Learn ADB. It makes installs, data resets and evidence capture scriptable and repeatable.

● Do not trust emulator performance numbers. Your PC is usually faster than your users’ phones.

Testing on a desktop gives you speed and control that physical phones rarely match. A fresh install takes seconds. You can wipe app data, change the screen size, switch the Android version and try again without hunting for a charger. When a tester finds a bug, they can record the screen, copy the log and attach both to a report from the same machine.

It also opens testing to people who are not developers. Product managers, support staff, designers and content reviewers can open a build, follow a script and report what they see with a full-size screen, a keyboard and a mouse. That alone shortens the feedback loop on most teams.

The tradeoff is realism, which this guide returns to later. For now, the point is that an emulator is the fastest way to find the large, obvious, repeatable problems, which is exactly what you want to clear out before involving real devices.

There are two broad families of tools, and they suit different work.

The first is the official Android Emulator that comes with Android Studio. It simulates hardware in detail, supports a wide range of device profiles and connects directly to debugging and profiling tools. It is the right choice when you are tracing a crash, profiling memory or testing against a specific system image. It is also heavier to install and configure.

The second family is general-purpose emulators built for speed and convenience. A good android emulator such as LDPlayer installs quickly, runs on ordinary hardware, can open several instances side by side, and makes it easy to drop in an APK, map keyboard controls and record the screen. Other examples include BlueStacks and Genymotion, the latter aimed at developers and test automation. Many of these tools are designed first for gaming or for general app use, so check whether they expose the Android versions, system images and debugging features your testing needs.

Many teams use both: the official tools for debugging, and a lighter emulator for broad functional testing. When you compare options, ask a few practical questions:

Preparing Windows Before You Install Anything

Ten minutes of preparation prevents most early frustration.

Turn on hardware virtualization. Emulators run dramatically faster when virtualization is enabled in your BIOS or UEFI. The setting is usually called Intel Virtualization Technology (VT-x) or SVM Mode on AMD systems. If your emulator feels slow for no clear reason, check this first.

Enable the Windows Hypervisor Platform. The Android documentation recommends the Windows Hypervisor Platform (WHPX) for Windows acceleration, and notes that you can turn it on under “Turn Windows features on or off”, then restart. Its older Android Emulator hypervisor driver is being phased out, so check the current emulator acceleration guide for your setup. Also note that a hardware-accelerated emulator cannot run inside another virtual machine.

Verify it. The emulator includes a check that reports whether acceleration is usable:

Update your graphics drivers. Android interfaces rely on graphics acceleration. Outdated drivers cause black screens, flickering and random crashes that testers wrongly blame on the app.

Check memory and storage. As a rule of thumb, 8 GB of RAM is workable for a single virtual device and 16 GB is more comfortable for several. Leave several gigabytes of free disk space, because every virtual device stores its own system image and data.

Close heavy background programs. Browsers with dozens of tabs and other virtual machines compete for the same resources and make performance results misleading.

The default configuration is rarely the one your audience uses. Spend a few minutes matching it to reality.

Pick a screen size and density similar to a popular mid-range phone rather than a very large display, because layout problems tend to appear on smaller screens first. Assign a sensible number of CPU cores and memory, enough to be smooth but not so much that you hide performance problems your users on modest phones will feel.

Choose the Android version carefully. If your app supports several versions, test at least the oldest and the newest. Behavior changes significantly between releases, especially around permissions, notifications, background activity and gesture navigation. For example, Android 13 (API level 33) introduced a runtime notification permission, so a flow that works on an older version can silently differ on a newer one.

With the Android Emulator, you can list and start saved devices from the command line, which helps when you keep several profiles:

Finally, confirm the network works by loading a web page in the virtual browser. A surprising number of reported app bugs turn out to be a virtual device with no connection.

An APK is the package file Android uses to install an app. Installing one on a virtual device is easy, but doing it carefully makes your results more reliable.

Use trusted files only. Take builds from your own team, your continuous integration system or the developer’s official release page. An APK from a random download site can be modified or carry malware, and testing it proves nothing about the real product.

Install it. Most emulators accept a dragged APK file or have an install option. If you use the command line, Android Debug Bridge (ADB) installs a package with a single command and is the better route when you want to automate repeated installs. These are the commands you will use most:

adb devices                          # confirm the emulator is connected

adb install -r app-debug.apk         # install, replacing an existing copy

adb shell pm clear com.example.app   # wipe app data for a fresh start

adb shell am start -W -n com.example.app/.MainActivity   # launch and print timing

adb logcat -d > session.log          # save the log for a bug report

adb exec-out screencap -p > shot.png # take a screenshot

Know the common install failures. If the install fails, the message usually explains why. A package built for a newer Android version than your device runs is rejected, a build compiled only for a different processor architecture may not install or may crash on launch, and an update signed with a different key than the installed version is refused, in which case you uninstall the old version first. The helper below turns raw ADB output into a one-line explanation and also reads the launch time that am start -W prints:

"""Small helpers for reading adb output during APK testing."""

"INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK": "The app needs a newer Android version than this device runs.",

"INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS": "The app has no native code for this device's CPU architecture.",

"INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE": "Signed with a different key than the installed copy. Uninstall first.",

"INSTALL_FAILED_VERSION_DOWNGRADE": "The installed copy has a higher version code. Uninstall first.",

"INSTALL_FAILED_INSUFFICIENT_STORAGE": "The virtual device is out of storage. Wipe data or enlarge the disk.",

def explain_install_failure(output: str) -> str:

"""Turn raw adb install output into a one-line explanation."""

m = re.search(r"(INSTALL_[A-Z_]+)", output)

return "Unknown failure. Read the full adb message."

return f"{code}: " + INSTALL_HINTS.get(code, "No hint recorded for this code.")

"""Read TotalTime from adb shell am start -W output, or None if the launch failed."""

m = re.search(r"TotalTime:\s*(\d+)", output)

The tests feed it realistic ADB output, including a successful install, three common failures, an unknown code, a successful launch and a failed one:

from adbtools import explain_install_failure, launch_time_ms

assert explain_install_failure("Performing Streamed Install\nSuccess") == "Installed."

older = "adb: failed to install app.apk: Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_OLDER_SDK]"

assert "newer Android" in explain_install_failure(older)

abi = "Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_NO_MATCHING_ABIS: Failed to extract native libraries, res=-113]"

assert "architecture" in explain_install_failure(abi)

sig = "Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE: Package com.example signatures do not match]"

assert "Uninstall first" in explain_install_failure(sig)

assert explain_install_failure("Failure [INSTALL_FAILED_SOMETHING_NEW]").endswith("No hint recorded for this code.")

assert explain_install_failure("error: device offline").startswith("Unknown failure")

good = "Starting: Intent { cmp=com.example/.MainActivity }\nStatus: ok\nActivity: com.example/.MainActivity\nTotalTime: 523\nWaitTime: 530\nComplete"

assert launch_time_ms("Error type 3\nError: Activity class does not exist.") is None

Understand split packages. Many modern apps ship as bundles made of several files instead of one APK. If you are given a bundle format, you may need a tool that installs all the parts together, or a universal APK generated for testing.

Test the right build. Debug builds and release builds do not always behave the same. Release builds often apply code shrinking and optimization that can break features that worked in debug. Before sign-off, run your main flows on a release build, not only the one developers use daily.

Wandering through an app and tapping things will find some problems. A structured pass finds far more. Work through these areas on each build.

Capture evidence as you go. A short screen recording with the exact steps, plus the saved log, is worth far more to a developer than a paragraph of description.

A very common mistake is testing everything on one virtual device and assuming the result applies everywhere. Android is a fragmented platform, and your audience is spread across many versions, screen sizes and memory limits.

Create a small set of profiles and rotate through them. A low-memory profile reveals how the app behaves on budget hardware. A small screen exposes cramped layouts. An older Android version shows compatibility gaps. A different language and region setting reveals text-length problems, date and number formatting issues and right-to-left layout errors.

Because tools such as the Android Emulator and several third-party emulators let you keep multiple saved devices, you can keep these profiles ready and compare behavior across them. This is where testing on Windows becomes efficient, turning a long list of devices you would have to buy into a handful of saved configurations.

Being honest about the limits protects you from false confidence.

● Hardware features. Camera quality, fingerprint sensors, Bluetooth accessories, NFC, precise GPS behavior and motion sensors are hard to reproduce faithfully. You can simulate basic values, but real hardware behaves differently.

● Real performance. Speed on an emulator depends on your PC. A strong computer can make an app feel faster than it will on a typical phone, so never use emulator results as proof of smooth performance for users.

● Manufacturer customizations. Phone makers modify Android with their own battery management, notification handling and interface layers. An app can work on a clean system and fail on one brand’s modified version, particularly around background tasks and push notifications.

● Real networks. A home network is stable. Mobile networks have weak signal, handoffs between towers and restrictions that an emulator will not recreate.

● Apps that block virtual devices. Some apps, particularly in banking, security and competitive gaming, detect virtual environments and refuse to run. That is a deliberate choice by the developer, and testers should respect it instead of attempting to bypass it.

The sensible approach is to let emulators handle the broad middle of your testing, then confirm anything involving hardware, payments or notifications on a few real devices before release. The script above also only interprets a handful of ADB messages, so it is a convenience for triage, not a replacement for reading the full output.

If you want something simple to adopt, use this sequence on every build.

Start with a clean virtual device matching a common phone.

Install the new build and run a quick smoke test, a fast pass over the main features to confirm nothing is fundamentally broken.

Test the specific areas that changed in this version in more depth.

Repeat the most important flows on a second profile with a different Android version and screen size.

Log every problem with exact steps, the build number, the device profile and a screenshot or recording.

Before release, verify camera, location, notifications and payments on at least one physical phone.

Write this down as a short checklist and share it. Consistent steps make results comparable between testers and between builds, which is how you notice regressions instead of rediscovering the same bugs.

Do I need Android Studio to test an APK on Windows? Not necessarily. Many emulators accept an APK directly, and ADB can be installed on its own as part of the Android platform tools. Android Studio becomes useful when you need to debug or profile.

Why is my emulator slow? The usual causes are virtualization or the Windows Hypervisor Platform being off, outdated graphics drivers, too little memory and heavy background programs. Run the acceleration check first.

Can an emulator replace a real test phone? No. It covers the broad middle of testing, but hardware, true performance, manufacturer behavior and real networks need a few physical devices.

Is it safe to install APKs from the internet? Only from trusted sources, such as your own team, your build system or an official release page. Files from random sites can be modified or carry malware.

Testing Android apps on Windows is practical, affordable and flexible when you treat the emulator as a tool with a clear purpose. It gives you fast installs, repeatable conditions and easy access to many device profiles, which makes it well suited to functional checks, layout reviews and APK testing. It does not replace real hardware for sensors, true performance and manufacturer-specific behavior, so keep a few physical devices for the final confirmation.

Prepare your PC, choose a tool that fits your workflow, configure devices that resemble real users, follow a consistent checklist and vary your environments. Do that consistently and you will catch most problems long before they reach your users.

Tenebrae Lux is a gag that has inspired some larger conversations about the gap between indie games and big-budget blockbusters.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One of the most intriguing games of the year is called Tenebrae Lux. It’s a moody, black-and-white title with obtuse puzzles and a main character that constantly narrates to himself with dramatic language. Its credits attribute pretty much everything to a developer named Johannes Zuch. It’s generated a lot of discussion for seemingly mocking games like Jonathan Blow’s The Witness or The Chinese Room’s Dear Esther. It’s also a game that only exists inside of Grand Theft Auto VI.

Developer Rockstar Games has stuffed a lot of satirical media inside of GTA VI, including TV shows you can watch, books you can read, and radio shows you can listen to. It’s all in service of making the world feel like a funhouse-mirror version of our current reality — Ted Lasso star Jason Sudeikis plays a right-wing radio host, for example. There are more games you can play inside GTA VI in addition to Tenebrae Lux, including a zombie-themed roguelike. But Tenebrae Lux, which you have to see as part of GTA VI’s main story, is the one that has struck a chord, including with indie developers like Sam Barlow and Robert Yang.

“I have to admit it’s kind of funny for the biggest blockbuster game of all time to go after arthouse indie,” Yang tells The Verge, noting that it’s “like a fighter jet getting obsessed with an ant, petty in a funny way.” (Given that GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day, the gulf between Rockstar and indie game studios that are struggling to get by is vast.)

But Yang suggested that Rockstar developers are probably well versed in the types of games they’re lampooning in GTA VI. “I don’t think gamers understand how much indie experimental stuff any decent AAA dev plays,” Yang said, pointing out that Rockstar’s environmental artists and level designers “all probably love Dear Esther,” the influential first-person game that helped popularize the “walking sim” concept when it launched in 2012.

“I was mostly taken with what it meant that the millions of people playing the game were having to sit down and play through an extended gag about indie games,” Barlow tells The Verge. “That made me feel like we were part of larger culture.” He added that he hopes some of these players might “seek out what these arty indie games might be.”

Rockstar is self-aware enough to use its video games to poke fun at the medium itself. As part of a long conversation between protagonist Jason Duval and his friend Cal Hampton before they start playing Tenebrae Lux, Cal hypes the game by saying that none of it is “just sitting around waiting for people to finish talking.” Initially, you only play Tenebrae Lux for a few minutes, which is enough time to get stumped on the initial puzzles, before the game cuts back to Jason being bored. “Got anything else, a little less, uh… y’know?” he asks. They play the zombie game, titled Street Trash 3 Dezombifier, right after. (You can go back and play the entirety of Tenebrae Lux later if you want.)

Barlow said that the cut “felt very true to the character and story. I gather there is more to the game, but it felt natural to me to hit a wall with the pretentious puzzle design and then move on!”

Yang also pointed out that from a design perspective, GTA VI has more in common with Tenebrae Lux than Street Trash 3 Dezombifier. GTA VI is “basically a walking sim where you walk around Florida and listen to people talk,” Yang said. “What’s the difference? Well, just like a billion dollars I guess.”

#10259. Transformers.js v4: Now Available on NPM!

We're excited to announce that Transformers.js v4 is now available on NPM! After a year of development (we started in March 2025 🤯), we're finally ready for you to use it.

The biggest change is undoubtedly the adoption of a new WebGPU Runtime, completely rewritten in C++. We've worked closely with the ONNX Runtime team to thoroughly test this runtime across our ~200 supported model architectures, as well as many new v4-exclusive architectures.

In addition to better operator support (for performance, accuracy, and coverage), this new WebGPU runtime allows the same transformers.js code to be used across a wide variety of JavaScript environments, including browsers, server-side runtimes, and desktop applications. That's right, you can now run WebGPU-accelerated models directly in Node, Bun, and Deno!

We've proven that it's possible to run state-of-the-art AI models 100% locally in the browser, and now we're focused on performance: making these models run as fast as possible, even in resource-constrained environments. This required completely rethinking our export strategy, especially for large language models. We achieve this by re-implementing new models operation by operation, leveraging specialized ONNX Runtime Contrib Operators like com.microsoft.GroupQueryAttention, com.microsoft.MatMulNBits, or com.microsoft.QMoE to maximize performance.

For example, adopting the com.microsoft.MultiHeadAttention operator, we were able to achieve a ~4x speedup for BERT-based embedding models.

Developing a new major version gave us the opportunity to invest in the codebase and tackle long-overdue refactoring efforts.

Until now, the GitHub repository served as our npm package. This worked well as long as the repository only exposed a single library. However, looking to the future, we saw the need for various sub-packages that depend heavily on the Transformers.js core while addressing different use cases, like library-specific implementations, or smaller utilities that most users don't need but are essential for some.

That's why we converted the repository to a monorepo using pnpm workspaces. This allows us to ship smaller packages that depend on @huggingface/transformers without the overhead of maintaining separate repositories.

Another major refactoring effort targeted the ever-growing models.js file. In v3, all available models were defined in a single file spanning over 8,000 lines, becoming increasingly difficult to maintain. For v4, we split this into smaller, focused modules with a clear distinction between utility functions, core logic, and model-specific implementations. This new structure improves readability and makes it much easier to add new models. Developers can now focus on model-specific logic without navigating through thousands of lines of unrelated code.

In v3, many Transformers.js example projects lived directly in the main repository. For v4, we've moved them to a dedicated repository, allowing us to maintain a cleaner codebase focused on the core library. This also makes it easier for users to find and contribute to examples without sifting through the main repository.

We updated the Prettier configuration and reformatted all files in the repository. This ensures consistent formatting throughout the codebase, with all future PRs automatically following the same style. No more debates about formatting... Prettier handles it all, keeping the code clean and readable for everyone.

Thanks to our new export strategy and ONNX Runtime's expanding support for custom operators, we've been able to add many new models and architectures to Transformers.js v4. These include popular models like GPT-OSS, Chatterbox, GraniteMoeHybrid, LFM2-MoE, HunYuanDenseV1, Apertus, Olmo3, FalconH1, and Youtu-LLM. Many of these required us to implement support for advanced architectural patterns, including Mamba (state-space models), Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and Mixture of Experts (MoE). Perhaps most importantly, these models are all compatible with WebGPU, allowing users to run them directly in the browser or server-side JavaScript environments with hardware acceleration. We've released several Transformers.js v4 demos so far... and we'll continue to release more!

We've migrated our build system from Webpack to esbuild, and the results have been incredible. Build times dropped from 2 seconds to just 200 milliseconds, a 10x improvement that makes development iteration significantly faster. Speed isn't the only benefit, though: bundle sizes also decreased by an average of 10% across all builds. The most notable improvement is in transformers.web.js, our default export, which is now 53% smaller, meaning faster downloads and quicker startup times for users.

Version 4 also adds new library features that make it easier to build robust, production-ready applications.

The new ModelRegistry API is designed for production workflows. It provides explicit visibility into pipeline assets before loading anything: list required files with get_pipeline_files, inspect per-file metadata with get_file_metadata (quite useful to calculate total download size), check cache status with is_pipeline_cached, and clear cached artifacts with clear_pipeline_cache. You can also query available precision types for a model with get_available_dtypes. Based on this new API, progress_callback now includes a progress_total event, making it easy to render end-to-end loading progress without manually aggregating per-file updates.

We also added new environment controls for model loading. env.useWasmCache enables caching of WASM runtime files (when cache storage is available), allowing applications to work fully offline after the initial load.

env.fetch lets you provide a custom fetch implementation for use cases such as authenticated model access, custom headers, and abortable requests.

Finally, logging is easier to manage in real-world deployments. ONNX Runtime WebGPU warnings are now hidden by default, and you can set explicit verbosity levels for both Transformers.js and ONNX Runtime. This update, also driven by community feedback, keeps console output focused on actionable signals rather than low-value noise.

A frequent request from users was to extract the tokenization logic into a separate library, and with v4, that's exactly what we've done. @huggingface/tokenizers is a complete refactor of the tokenization logic, designed to work seamlessly across browsers and server-side runtimes. At just 8.8kB (gzipped) with zero dependencies, it's incredibly lightweight while remaining fully type-safe.

This separation keeps the core of Transformers.js focused and lean while offering a versatile, standalone tool that any WebML project can use independently.

We've made several quality-of-life improvements across the library. The type system has been enhanced with dynamic pipeline types that adapt based on inputs, providing better developer experience and type safety.

Additionally, we've added support for larger models exceeding 8B parameters. In our tests, we've been able to run GPT-OSS 20B (q4f16) at ~60 tokens per second on an M4 Pro Max.

We want to extend our heartfelt thanks to everyone who contributed to this major release, especially the ONNX Runtime team for their incredible work on the new WebGPU runtime and their support throughout development, as well as all external contributors and early testers.

#10258. Hello Weather is the best Apple Weather app on Android

While Pixel Weather serves my needs quite well, I’ve been looking for a way to check Apple Weather (previously Dark Sky) forecast data on Android, and I’ve finally found it with Hello Weather by Electric Dream Machine.

Hello Weather started out on iOS before coming to Android a few years ago. On Apple devices, the app got a big redesign last year, and it just came to Android last month with a promise that updates will roll out to both platforms at the same time going forward.

The app has a four-tab layout with the bottom bar aligning with the latest Material 3 Expressive height, avoiding a common pitfall. One small customization is being able to turn on/off tab names.

Locations shows a list of all your saved cities, while Forecast is the main view. The current condition with a large icon — five different sets are available — appears first. Be sure to enable the stats row so you can see cards like Wind, Cloud Cover, and UV Index without having to tap for the bottom sheet. When open, you get the following stats presented as a grid: Today (temperature range), Precipitation, Wind, Humidity, UV Index, Cloud Cover, Visibility, Pressure, Air Quality, Pollen, Daylight, and Moon Phase.

The Hourly Forecast section is a scrollable carousel, with the Bonus Info toggle in Settings adding another stat. “Automatic” will intelligently select “relevant info for you.” You can tap to browse the hourly breakdown in a sheet view.

Finally, there’s the Daily Forecast section that gives you an eight-day overview via a temperature-range layout, which is my favorite way to visualize this information. Again, this can be tapped to get a bottom sheet explorer.

I've lost count on how many weather apps on Android I've tried out over the years but since the Pixel Weather app became a thing I've tried far fewer and the few I have tried while many have been prettier to look at, I've always ended up coming back to the stock PW app. It never hurts to have options though and this one looks like a good one. Thanks for the mention, I hadn't heard of it before.

The Radar tab is up next, with Google Maps powering this view. From the three-dot overflow menu, you can customize the Animation Speed, Map Layers, Style, and Options.

Settings is where you can make all the aforementioned customizations, including changing which Forecast Data source you’re using. The usual players are here, like The Weather Channel and AccuWeather. I also like the stylized in-app changelog.

In Notifications, you can have a persistent silent alert appear. There’s also the ability to receive Morning and Evening Reports, along with Precipitation and Severe Alerts. This is joined by a trio of homescreen widgets.

Getting a gaming laptop this Black Friday doesn't have to be a hassle. Getting a gaming laptop is pretty tough — different systems can tout similar specs, but in reality, their performance can vary wildly. This is down to different power ratings across mobile GPUs, which can muddy the waters when you're looking on storefronts. It's often obfuscated in listings or omitted entirely.

So we're here to cut through the noise and nonsense to bring you our picks of the best deals we've found thus far. We also have our Black Friday Gaming Laptop Deals Live Blog in action, so check that out if you want more options.

The Asus ROG Strix G16 comes with a 16-inch screen, with an 1900 x 1200 pixel resolution, a 16:10 aspect ratio, and refresh and response rates of 165Hz and 3ms, respectively. Hardware inside this gaming laptop includes Nvidia's GeForce RTX 5070 Ti laptop GPU, an AMD Ryzen 9 8940HX processor, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 1TB SSD for storage.

This Asus ROG Strix G16 gaming laptop offers a solid price-to-performance ratio and comes with AMD's Ryzen 9 8940HX CPU, sporting 16 cores and 32 threads. Packing in the gaming punch is the included RTX 5070 Ti 12GB, with GDDR7 memory and a total graphics power of 115W; this is the full-fat variant of the chip, and dynamic boost can also see this rise to up to 140W. When paired with a relatively modest screen resolution and display, it certainly bodes well for getting solid performance from modern titles. And you should be able to saturate the display's refresh rate when turning on features like Multi Frame Generation in single-player titles.

One thing to keep in mind here is that the laptop does sacrifice display quality, and its CPU isn't on the latest Zen 5 architecture; it's based on AMD's Zen 4 Dragon Range refresh chips. But it's still mighty fast and should suit both gaming and productivity workloads.

Get a 16-inch gaming laptop with Intel Core Ultra 7 255HX, RTX 5070 Ti with 12GB of VRAM, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and a 512GB SSD.

Coming in slightly cheaper than the above Asus ROG Strix system, this MSI Vector 16 HX AI laptop from Newegg offers much of the same specifications: right down to the TGP of the GPU. MSI's 5070 Ti mobile chip carries the same 115W TGP, in addition to the screen resolution. It also moves CPUs to Intel's 20-core, 20-thread Core Ultra 7 255HX, which is a newer architecture compared to the ROG Strix G16's Dragon Range offering. However, you get a lower screen refresh rate at 144Hz and half the storage included. It does trade blows effectively with the Asus model in many respects, though, including offering dual Thunderbolt 5 ports and a 2.5GbE port over the ROG Strix's 1GbE port. With the sizes of modern games, though, it's tough to outright tell you to run out and purchase a system with only 512 GB of storage, so this system remains our alternative pick for most people.

The MSI Crosshair sports a 16-inch, 240Hz display with a 2560 x 1600 resolution that's powered by an 115W max TGP Nvidia RTX 5060 graphics with 8GB of GDDR7 VRAM. Other specs include an AMD Ryzen 7 8840HX processor, 16GB of memory, and a 1TB SSD.

Sporting 1TB of NVMe storage and 16GB of DDR5 RAM, this more entry-level system can offer solid computing power while staying within a limited budget. Something that prospective buyers should watch out for is the display's resolution: you get a 16:10, 2560 x 1600 screen resolution and 240Hz refresh rate on this system, meaning that the laptop will likely struggle in modern titles, especially at high settings. Turning on upscaling tech like DLSS might help smooth things over somewhat, but given that you'll be doing things other than gaming on this laptop, it makes for a comfortable everyday system that offers a sharp display.

Lenovo's Legion 5i sports a 15.3-inch, 3K display that's powered by an Intel Core 7 245HX processor, an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060 graphics card, and 16GB of RAM. For storage, there's a 512GB SSD.

With that said, you get 1TB of storage here, which is slightly disappointing, but given how NAND pricing is going, it's par for the course right now.

In real-world terms, your framerates will undoubtedly be slower, and saturating its 16-inch, 2560 x 1600 display will be a lot more difficult. However, that neutered power limit also puts it in contention with the RTX 5070 Ti-based systems we've listed, but with more VRAM. If that 4GB difference matters to you, and you are willing to pay the difference, then this deal offers a solid amount of silicon for your cash.

It's still an incredible laptop by all rights, however HP's option edges things out on value, and spec-wise.

#10255. OpenEnv in Practice: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents in Real-World Environments

AI agents often perform impressively in controlled research settings, yet struggle when deployed in real-world systems where they must reason across multiple steps, interact with real tools and APIs, operate under partial information, and recover from errors in stateful, permissioned environments—highlighting a persistent gap between research success and production reliability.

OpenEnv is an open-source framework from Meta and Hugging Face designed to address this challenge by standardizing how agents interact with real environments. As part of this collaboration, Turing contributed a production-grade calendar management environment to study tool-using agents under realistic constraints such as access control, temporal reasoning, and multi-agent coordination.

In this post, we explore how OpenEnv works in practice, why calendars serve as a powerful benchmark for real-world agent evaluation, and what our findings reveal about the current limitations of tool-using agents.

OpenEnv is a framework for evaluating AI agents against real systems rather than simulations. It provides a standardized way to connect agents to real tools and workflows while preserving the structure needed for consistent and reliable evaluation.

OpenEnv uses a gym-oriented API (reset, step, action, observations) like OpenAI's Gymnasium. Also, OpenEnv uses a standard MCP tool call interface to connect to envs which provides a consistent interface across domains and simulation to production environments.

The environments maintain state across multiple actions—enabling long-horizon reasoning—and can connect directly to real APIs and tools such as browsers, code repositories, or calendars. This shifts evaluation from "Can this work in a controlled demo?" to "Can this operate reliably in the real world?"

Calendar systems are deceptively complex. While scheduling a meeting seems simple, real-world calendar management requires agents to reason over time, permissions, multiple users, and incomplete information—often across several dependent steps. These properties make calendars a powerful testbed for evaluating tool-using agents outside controlled simulations.

To ground OpenEnv in this kind of realistic, demanding use case, Turing built a production-grade calendar management environment referred to as the Calendar Gym. Rather than simulating scheduling in the abstract, it exposes agents to the same constraints they would face in real calendar systems: Access Control Lists across users and calendars, limited visibility into other users' state, and multi-step workflows where actions must be chained in the correct order. Agents interact with a rich set of calendar operations—from listing calendars to modifying events and permissions—and must handle failed actions, incorrect assumptions, and missing permissions. Each session runs in an isolated environment, enabling reliable comparisons across runs.

Below is a code example of how to use the Calendar Gym. We explore the environment, discover available tools, list calendars, create an event, and print the result.

Below is an excerpt of what the Calendar Gym returns when you call ListToolsAction. Each entry includes the tool name plus an input schema (what arguments the tool accepts).

Evaluating agents in the Calendar Gym revealed consistent patterns which were common across multiple domains. While agents often perform well on individual game like actions, reliability breaks down as tasks become longer, more ambiguous, and more constrained.

Multi-step reasoning is the primary bottleneck. Agents struggle to correctly chain actions across longer workflows, suggesting that benchmarks need to test sustained reasoning over multiple dependent steps—not just single tool calls.

Ambiguity significantly degrades performance. Agents achieved close to 90% success on tasks with explicit calendar identifiers, but success dropped to roughly 40% when the same tasks were phrased using natural language descriptions. Building stronger lookup and validation into agent loops—rather than relying on the LLM to resolve references unaided—appears essential.

Correct tool choice isn't enough. Across failed interactions, more than half of errors stemmed from malformed tool arguments or incorrect ordering, even when the right tool was selected. Reliable agent behavior depends as much on execution quality and structured feedback as on tool selection—environment design matters.

These challenges are not unique to scheduling and calendars. They reflect broader limitations that emerge whenever agents operate in changing systems over long periods of time, and they point toward evaluation frameworks that test permissions, partial observability, and multi-step workflows together.

OpenEnv provides a foundation for testing agents under realistic conditions, and the Calendar Gym demonstrates how seemingly simple domains can surface deep challenges in reasoning, ambiguity resolution, and tool use. By evaluating agents where failure is measurable and constraints are real, we gain clearer insight into what it takes to build agents that operate reliably in production.

For a deeper dive into the Calendar Gym's design, benchmarking methodology, and quantitative results, explore the full technical article on Turing's site. To explore a clone of the Calendar Gym, visit the Calendar Gym space.

In practice, tool integrations rarely fail in dramatic ways; they fail in small, predictable ones. When wiring up MCP tools to real APIs (like calendar operations), we encountered a handful of recurring issues.

Below are three common failure modes we’ve seen in production, along with representative error payloads and mitigation strategies. These examples illustrate not just what can go wrong, but how structured errors can help agents recover gracefully.

The agent calls a valid tool (e.g. events_insert), but the arguments do not match the declared JSON schema.

We can mitigate this by providing one canonical example of a correct 'events_insert' call in your prompt. Return structured validation errors so the model can repair and retry instead of failing silently.

The tool call is syntactically correct, but the API rejects it due to insufficient permissions.

We can mitigate this by clearly documenting the required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call. Clearly document required OAuth scopes. Return structured, actionable remediation steps so the agent can guide the user instead of retrying the same failing call.

The event is rejected by the API, or it is created at an unexpected time.

We can mitigate this by standardizing on RFC3339 with explicit timezone offsets (e.g. 2026-02-11T09:30:00-05:00). Include at least one correct datetime example in your documentation to anchor model behavior and reduce repair retries.

Game modding communities are racing to get Grand Theft Auto VI running on PC, but one big effort has been taken down by Take-Two today. Leonida, a fan project by 15-year-old “NotRexed,” has vanished after a DMCA takedown notice from GTA VI publisher Take-Two.

Leonida was designed to translate a leaked GTA VI Xbox build to run natively on Windows. Cyberleek, the leaker who posted multiple GTA VI gameplay videos over the summer, published a full Xbox build of the game earlier this week. The leak has kicked recompilation efforts up a notch, as modders race to reverse-engineer the game’s code and rebuild it into native PC code.

Some have managed to get the game to boot on PC, but recompiling the full game won’t be easy — even with help from AI tools like Claude. Take-Two is trying to slow this progress, and its IP enforcement team targeted the main GitHub repository for Leonida and more than 2,900 forks of it, claiming that it “infringes upon Take-Two’s copyrighted works and facilitates copyright infringement of Rockstar Games title, Grand Theft Auto VI.”

PortWatch VI is tracking the efforts to recompile, emulate, or port the leaked Xbox build over to PC. At the time of publishing, the VIctory project and forks of it are leading the way. People are also trying to use XCL, a compatibility layer that runs Xbox Series X games on a Windows PC, to get GTA VI running.

At this point, it seems like Take-Two might not be able to avoid the inevitable here. The clock started ticking down to the release of the PC version last week, and if recent reports are true, we might see it in a few months. If GTA VI is close to being officially ready for PC, we could hear about a release before modders manage to get the game running on PC unofficially.

#10252. What to Check Before Adding a Tripo Model to a Website

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A 3D model can look convincing in a still image and still be awkward on a website. The real questions appear when someone rotates it, loads it on a typical connection, or views it on a narrow phone screen. AI generators have made the first draft of a model cheap, which shifts the work toward the part developers and designers already know: budgets, testing and fallbacks.

This article walks through a web-readiness review for an AI-generated model, using an openwork ceramic vessel generated from a single reference image with Tripo as the worked example. The checks apply equally to output from other generators. It includes a small Node.js script that audits a GLB file against a size budget, and the markup for a lightweight viewer with a static fallback. The model shown is one candidate, so it cannot prove browser speed, mobile behavior, hidden geometry or export compatibility. Those are checks to run on your own asset.

Traditional 3D work involves modeling, polygon layout, materials, scale and export. AI generation can shorten the blank-workspace stage. A beginner may discover the category through a search such as AI 3D model generator free, but an initial candidate is useful only if it survives review.

For this vessel, start with the negative space, meaning the openings between the ribs. A flattering front view can hide a blocked cavity, a thin wall, or two surfaces passing through each other. Generation moves the bottleneck from making a first shape to deciding whether that shape is usable.

Image-to-3D tools use a visual reference to create a model candidate, while text-to-3D routes start from a written prompt. Tripo offers both, and other hosted options include Meshy, Rodin by Hyper3D and 3D AI Studio, all of which list GLB among their export formats, while open-source models such as TripoSR and Stable Fast 3D let you run generation yourself. Features, pricing, licensing and output quality differ and change often, so check each vendor’s current documentation. The image route suits this example because the folds, uneven rim and openings already exist in the source.

Whichever tool you use, it can provide a candidate for inspection. It cannot decide whether the source is licensed, whether the unseen rear structure is believable, or whether the exported asset suits a particular viewer. Those judgments belong to the person publishing the page.

Give the object one job. In a portfolio, this vessel might show how its shell and openings relate. That is narrower than calling it printable, manufacturable or dimensionally accurate. Note what must remain recognizable, and provide a still image if the interactive view fails.

Use an image you own or have permission to reuse. Busy backgrounds can distract an image-based workflow, so isolate the object when possible. One photograph also leaves the back and underside unknown. Treat those areas as review risks, not as details confirmed by the source.

After generation, rotate beyond the familiar front. Check the rear, top, underside and sides. Trace each large opening. Look for merged ribs, intersecting surfaces or an unstable base. A wireframe view, when available, can expose crowded geometry. A single front-facing candidate cannot answer these hidden-angle questions, so check them on your own model.

Record the download size, polygon count and texture dimensions. Polygons are the small flat faces that form the shape, and web viewers draw them as triangles. This matters because generator defaults are often tuned for quality, not for the web. In the generation screenshot for this vessel, the viewer reports roughly 1.95 million faces and the settings show 4K texture quality. That is a fine starting point for inspection but a heavy asset for a phone on a mobile connection. Curved ribs may need many triangles, but the count should still fit your page budget.

glTF is the open format most web viewers expect, and GLB is its single-file form that can bundle geometry, textures and materials. The format does not guarantee good performance, so measure the package. The script below reads a GLB with the open-source glTF Transform library, counts triangles, lists texture sizes, and compares them with a budget. The budget values are placeholders; set your own from your target devices.

Run it with node audit.mjs model.glb after installing @gltf-transform/core. It exits with a non-zero status when the asset is over budget, so you can run it in CI. A short test builds two GLBs with known triangle counts, one small and one with 200,000 triangles, and checks that the first passes and the second fails with the right message:

When an asset fails, glTF Transform also has a command line. gltf-transform inspect model.glb reports what is inside a file, and gltf-transform optimize input.glb output.glb --compress draco --texture-compress webp applies geometry and texture compression. Compression and mesh simplification can introduce artifacts, especially around thin ribs and openings, so reopen the result and re-check the angles from Gate 3 instead of accepting a smaller file blindly. Also check that your viewer supports the compression you choose.

Load the asset in the intended viewer at desktop and phone widths. Check framing, touch rotation, keyboard access, scrolling and a slower connection. The Google-backed model-viewer web component is one low-code option, and libraries such as three.js give you more control at the cost of more code. The markup below shows the pieces that matter for a first release: a poster image that loads first, lazy loading so the heavy file waits until needed, a text alternative, and visible controls.

The alt text, a poster and touch-action="pan-y" (so a vertical swipe still scrolls the page on a phone) address the common failures. Check the current model-viewer documentation for attribute names and the recommended script include, since they can change between versions. Also consider the WCAG guidance on non-text content: provide a useful description, and offer instructions plus a static image for people who cannot operate the viewer.

A single front-facing candidate is enough to discuss the method, not to certify a finished web asset. Call it a prototype until the exported file passes the checks required by its actual destination.

The same review pattern can be adapted to an architectural ornament, exhibition object, packaging concept or game prop, but each destination adds its own geometry, scale and delivery requirements. A portfolio may accept an inferred rear surface if that limitation is clear. A sales page, printable file or measured product needs stronger references and technical validation.

The audit script counts triangles, texture sizes and file size only. It does not detect self-intersections, thin walls, flipped normals or licensing problems, and passing it does not make an asset good. The budget numbers are illustrative, and real limits depend on your audience’s devices and connections. Tool features and terms change, so verify them with the vendor before you rely on them, and treat any speed or quality claims on vendor pages as the vendor’s own.

Inspect the angle you would normally crop out. Confirm input rights, measure the download, and test touch, keyboard and a slow connection. Reread the surrounding copy, because claims of fabrication accuracy or production readiness need supporting evidence. For this vessel, “exploratory web model” is an honest label, and more demanding claims require better references and a specialist review.

Decide what visitors should learn or do before adding a 3D viewer. A modest prototype with a useful fallback can beat a dramatic asset that loads slowly or hides limitations.

Do I need to code to create a model with an AI generator? No code is required to generate an initial model candidate in Tripo or similar tools. Publishing it interactively is separate work and usually involves a viewer, hosting, responsive testing and enough HTML or JavaScript knowledge to diagnose problems.

When should I use image-to-3D instead of text-to-3D? Use image-to-3D when a rights-cleared visual should guide the form, and text-to-3D when the idea begins as words. Do not treat the two routes as interchangeable evidence.

Is a generated model ready to publish as soon as it exports? No. Inspect the shape from several angles, measure the delivery package, test the intended viewer and prepare a fallback. Higher-stakes uses may also need specialist geometry, scale, material and rights review.

How can a beginner keep web 3D manageable? Give one object one clear job. Set a file-size target, test desktop and phone widths, keep interaction simple, and retain a still image for readers who cannot load or operate the viewer.

#10251. ‘Old’ Galaxy phones are a better deal; here’s what you should buy

Old is a label, and saying last year’s Galaxy flagships from Samsung are dated or worthless is disingenuous. You can get a killer deal on a phone a generation or two old.

Beyond that, it still has a flagship SoC in the Snapdragon 8 Elite – the same 3nm foundation as the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. It also takes on much of the same design, so if you like the rounded corners of the Galaxy S26 Ultra, you’ll be missing out on almost nothing by choosing the Galaxy S25 Ultra for a better deal.

Right now, a 1TB model Galaxy S25 Ultra can be had for $780 on Amazon. It’s a “renewed” model, but that’s an excellent choice over a used device, since Samsung isn’t making them anymore. That’s down from the original $1,659 price tag when it launched. It’s also a good bit cheaper than the best deal you can get on an S26 Ultra – $1,049 for 256GB model from Samsung.

You can get a slightly better deal on something like the Galaxy S24 Ultra, though it might not have the same upsides as the S25 Ultra. There are a couple of reasons for that.

First, it’s already in its second year of a seven-year update policy. In effect, you’re only getting five years of updates. Second, it doesn’t have the newest design language, if that’s something important to you.

On the flip side, you might prefer the boxier look Samsung used to run by on its devices.

The Galaxy S24 Ultra deal on Amazon that sits it at $591 right now also applies to the 512GB model, unlike the deal for a 1TB variant above. Still, it’s a solid deal for a phone that really isn’t that old, and it’s close to what the mid-range Galaxy A57 sells for, new.

It’ll still handle everyday tasks with next to no issues, and that makes it a great gift – possibly overkill for a first phone, to be frank.

The Galaxy S25 Plus is closer to a “first phone” than an Ultra model would be. It has excellent specs, but it only misses out on some of the raw power Samsung’s flagships have and an S Pen.

During Black Friday deal week on Amazon, it looks like an unlocked Galaxy S25 Plus goes for $683. It’s higher than the previous year’s Ultra, but it isn’t as expensive as the renewed Galaxy S25 Ultra. It has the same design language as Samsung’s new phones, and it still has six of the seven years left in its update lifetime.

It certainly beats paying over $900 for the new one, even with a deal.

This is also a good opportunity to get a foldable, if you’ve been eyeing the Galaxy Z Fold lineup. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 series is fantastic, and it blows other devices out of the water. But it’s pricey.

Instead of paying $1,499 for a Galaxy Z Fold 8 right now, even though that’s a great deal, you can get a 512GB Galaxy Z Fold 7 for $867 on Amazon. It’ll be sold under Amazon’s “Renewed” program, so it’ll be covered under some type of warranty.

Doing that is also a great way to get set up for a trade-in deal when the next set of Galaxy Z Fold 9 devices roll out.

Fun fact: Samsung is selling a refurbished Galaxy Z Fold 7 for the exact same price as the Galaxy Z Fold 8 while the new one is on sale. Obviously, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the better choice on Samsung’s website.

If you’re absolutely set on getting a Galaxy phone that came out in the last year, Samsung’s deals are better than anywhere else. When Samsung runs deals like it has right now, that’s the best time to buy a device. In any other case, it can be a hard bargain.

The Galaxy S26 Ultra is always a good choice, but it’s going to be $999 without a trade-in. That said, trade-in values are boosted right now. You can get $600 for something like your Galaxy S24 Ultra, but you can’t stack discounts. Trading a Galaxy S24 Ultra in brings the Galaxy S26 Ultra down to $799. Still a good deal.

Samsung’s devices offer the latest Android updates and features, even if they’re a couple of years old. Some of the Galaxy phones we knew as the “best” last year are affordable options right now.
