When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

There's more to gaming than having the latest $7,000 GPU. Black Friday is a great time to pick up some new gaming peripherals, which will significantly improve your gaming experience at a fraction of the cost of, well, $7,000.

Some of our favorite gaming mice are currently on sale — both the current generation and the last generation, and, let's face it: a lot of last-gen gaming mice are very, very similar to the current generation. So now is the time to pick up a gaming mouse or two, as there's almost certainly something on sale that will work for you, whether you're looking for an ultra-lightweight, stripped-down mouse for competitive eSports, or a multi-functional, multi-button mouse for MMOs (and some productivity on the side).

If the allure of the DeathAdder V4 Pro's upgraded sensor and significantly improved battery life are calling your name, great news — this mouse is also currently on sale for just $137.74 at Amazon — or $129.99, if you don't mind the Niko-branded version. The DeathAdder V4 Pro features Razer's Focus Pro 45K Gen-2 optical sensor, which has a maximum resolution of 45,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 900 IPS, and can handle up to 85G's of force. It weighs just 56g and has the same shape and size as its predecessor.

This mouse sports Razer's Focus Pro 45K Gen-2 sensor and gets up to 150 hours of battery life. It comes with an 8,000 Hz polling dongle and features a silver, black, and white pattern associated with esports competitor NiKo, but the regular versions of the mouse are also on sale.

The DeathAdder V4 Pro features Razer's Gen-4 optical switches, which are rated for 100 million clicks and feel and sound different than the switches in the DeathAdder V3 Pro — they're lighter and have a slightly higher, more hollow-sounding click, but they feel great. The notched optical scroll wheel also feels lighter, and I found it felt more accurate and precise than the DeathAdder V3 Pro's scroll wheel despite having freer movement.

Read our full review of the DeathAdder V4 Pro here.

The Basilisk V3 Pro is basically the last generation of the Basilisk lineup. The Basilisk V3 Pro isn't as performance-focused as is the DeathAdder V3 Pro — this ergonomically-contoured wireless gaming mouse also features Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 30,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS, and can handle up to 70G's of force. It has 11 programmable buttons and 13 zones of bright, customizable RGB lighting, and it weighs 3.95 ounces (112g).

Razer's flagship wireless Basilisk V3 Pro features Razer's Focus Pro 30K optical sensor, Gen-3 optical mouse switches, and 13 zones of bright RGB underglow lighting. It gets up to 110 hours of battery life and is compatible with Razer's HyperPolling Wireless Dongle and Mouse Dock Pro.

Like the DeathAdder V3 Pro, this mouse also works with Razer's HyperPolling Wireless Dongle (sold separately) to get up to an 8,000 Hz wireless polling rate; it's also compatible with Razer's Mouse Dock Pro (sold separately), which integrates the HyperPolling Wireless Dongle and also allows for wireless charging (and also features 8 zones of customizable RGB lighting, because why not).

Read our full review of the Basilisk V3 Pro here.

If you're looking for something ultra-light, well, it's in the name: the Logitech G Pro X Superlight 2 is a pseudo-ambidextrous ultra-lightweight mouse weighing just 2.12 ounces (60g) and designed for those who need speed above all else. And it's currently on sale at Logitech's website for $74.99 — nearly 60% off its retail price of $179.99.

Logitech's ultralight 60g wireless mouse features a pseudo-ambidextrous symmetrical shape and sports the brand's Hero 2 optical sensor and Lightforce hybrid optical/mechanical switches.

The Pro X Superlight 2 features Logitech's Hero 2 optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 32,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 500 IPS, and can handle up to 40G's of force. It has five programmable buttons; its primary buttons feature Logitech's Lightforce hybrid optical/mechanical switches, which can actuate both optically (for the lowest latency) and mechanically (for saving power).

Read our full review of the Pro X Superlight 2 here.

Logitech's G502 X Plus is still one of our favorite mice — both for its comfortable, ergonomic right-handed shape and its pretty, bright RGB light strip. Not to mention its comfortable button layout and top-of-the-line sensor, which has been improved through a firmware update to Logitech's Hero 44K, with a maximum resolution of 44,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 678 IPS, and up to 40 G's of acceleration.

This versatile, ergonomic gaming mouse features Logitech's Hero 44K optical sensor and gets up to 130 hours of battery life with the lighting turned off.

The G502 X Plus has 13 programmable controls and features a handful of extra buttons — an adjustable DPI shift / trigger button, as well as two button on the side of the left mouse button. It comes with a dual-mode tilt wheel that switches between frictionless free-spin and precise, notched scrolling at the click of a switch, and feels great. It also comes in four colors now, including the recently-introduced black/purple and white/mint colorways, and all four colors are currently on sale.

Read our full Logitech G502 X Plus review here.

Maybe ultralight and stripped-down gaming mice aren't your thing. If you're looking for a mouse with all the buttons, Corsair's Scimitar Elite SE Wireless is a good option, and it's currently on sale for almost 50% off at Best Buy — you can pick it up for just $69.99, which is 46% off its original MSRP of $139.99.

This MMO / MOBA-focused mouse features 16 programmable buttons, 12 of which are on its customizable, movable side panel. It also sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS, and can handle up to 50G's of force.

The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless features 16 programmable buttons, 12 of which are on its movable side panel — you can move the side panel forward or backward, depending on your hand size and what's most comfortable for you. It sports Corsair's Marksman S 33K optical sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 33,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 750 IPS, and can handle up to 50G's of force. It weighs 4.02 ounces (114g), but let's face it — if you're looking for a mouse with 16 programmable buttons, weight is not your top priority. The Scimitar Elite SE Wireless also features a pretty solid battery life of 150 hours over its 2.4GHz wireless connection, which means you'll only have to charge it every couple of weeks (and that's if you're a serious gamer).

Read our full review of the Scimitar Elite SE Wireless here.

If you're looking for something modular and potentially customizable, HyperX's Pulsefire Saga Pro is a wireless gaming mouse with a couple of modular options in the box, plus the ability to print your own pieces. This lightweight gaming mouse also features five programmable buttons and up to a 4,000 Hz wireless polling rate, and it's currently on sale at Best Buy for $79.99 — $40 off its MSRP of $119.99.

This ultra-lightweight wireless mouse is modular and comes with 2 humps, 2 sets of primary buttons, and 2 sets of side buttons. It features up to a 4,000 Hz wireless polling rate and HyperX's 26K sensor.

The Pulsefire Saga Pro sports HyperX's 26K sensor, which has a maximum sensitivity of 26,000 DPI and a maximum speed of 650 IPS, and can handle up to 50G's of force. This is the same sensor we've seen in HyperX's mice for a couple of years now — it's a solid sensor in terms of speed and accuracy, but it might not be for you if you're looking for the latest and greatest.

However, if you're just looking for lightweight modularity, the Pulsefire Saga Pro is where it's at: this mouse comes with two mouse humps, two sets of primary mouse buttons, and two sets of side buttons, and it implements its modularity well — everything fits together nicely and feels sturdy, and we had no issues with creaking or parts moving around in our testing. All configurations will give you a weight of 2.54 ounces (72g).

#10249. Custom Kernels for All from Codex and Claude

tl;dr: We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end.

Writing CUDA kernels is hard. Writing CUDA kernels that correctly integrate with transformers and diffusers is harder. There are architecture-specific memory access patterns, vectorization strategies, warp shuffle reductions, and a dozen integration pitfalls that trip up even experienced developers. It is exactly the kind of specialized, high-stakes problem where agent skills shine.

We gave coding agents the domain knowledge they need, like which GPU architecture to target, how to structure a kernel-builder project, when to use shared memory versus registers, and how to write PyTorch bindings. The agents did the rest. If you have used the LLM training skill or read We Got Claude to Teach Open Models, the pattern will feel familiar: package domain expertise into a skill, point the agent at a problem, and let it work.

The Kernel Hub solved the distribution of custom hardware kernels. You can load pre-compiled kernels from the Hub with a single get_kernel call. No builds, no flags. However, someone still needs to write the kernels. That is the gap this skill fills.

CUDA kernel development has a brutal surface area:

This is domain knowledge that gets lost in documentation tabs and Stack Overflow answers. An agent skill packages it into context that loads on demand.

First, let's show how to use the skill right away, then we'll dive into the details of how we benchmarked the kernels.

The skill ships with the kernels library. Install it into your coding agent with a single command:

This drops the skill into .claude/skills/cuda-kernels/ where Claude Code and Cursor pick it up automatically. For other agents:

Or, you can go for something more open-ended:

The agent can read the skill, select the right architecture parameters, generate the CUDA source, write the PyTorch bindings, set up build.toml, and create a benchmark script.

If you're working on more complex kernels, or architecture-specific optimizations, that aren't covered in the skill, then the skill supplies the fundamental building blocks and patterns to get you started. We are also open to contributions on the skill itself.

The skill is roughly 550 tokens of structured guidance plus reference scripts, GPU optimization guides, troubleshooting docs, and complete working examples. Agentic coding tools like Codex and Claude can read this and produce a working kernel project.

When an agent loads this, it gets everything it needs to go from "write me an RMSNorm kernel" to a buildable, benchmarkable project. It will grep and glob the skill to find the relevant files and directories. So it's important to structure the skill in a way that is easy to find.

The agent is instructed to generate kernels that conform to the templates in references/kernel-templates.md and produce a complete kernel project:

The agent built RMSNorm, RoPE 3D, GEGLU, and AdaLN kernels for LTX-Video, a video generation pipeline from diffusers. The full example is at examples/ltx_video/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to check out the generated kernel, got to this example

First, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline. This is the main speedup in the optimized pipeline.

Average speedup: 1.88x and a bandwidth efficiency: 34.7% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Next, we compare the end-to-end video generation performance of the optimized kernels against the baseline (no compile) and the torch.compile baseline.

RMSNorm accounts for ~5% of total compute in LTX-Video. The remaining time is spent in attention, linear projections, and VAE decode. The 6% end-to-end speedup from a single kernel type is consistent with that profile.

The agent built an RMSNorm kernel for Qwen3-8B, a large language model from transformers with 65 RMSNorm modules across 32 layers. The full example is at examples/qwen3_8b/. We optimized the RMSNorm kernel for H100. Both benchmarks were run on H100 80GB HBM3 at precision BFloat16.

If you want to explore the kernel, check it out here.

Once again, we compare the isolated RMSNorm kernel performance against the PyTorch baseline.

Average speedup: 1.94x and a bandwidth efficiency: 22.3% of H100 theoretical (3,350 GB/s)

Speedup scales with sequence length: 1.58x at 128 tokens, 2.47x at 8192 tokens. For long-context inference, the custom kernel roughly halves RMSNorm latency.

The agent gives you a working kernel. The Kernel Hub lets you share it so anyone can load it without compilation. Here is the full path from agent output to published kernel.

The agent produces a project that already follows the kernel-builder layout:

The build.toml tells kernel-builder what to build. The agent generates this for you, including the correct cuda-capabilities for your target GPU:

Kernel Hub kernels must support all recent PyTorch and CUDA configurations. The kernel-builder Nix flake handles this automatically. Copy the example flake.nix into your project and run:

This builds the kernel for every required PyTorch/CUDA variant and places the results in build/. For faster builds, enable the HuggingFace Nix cache:

Create a model repo on the Hub and upload the built kernel:

Once published, anyone can use your kernel with zero compilation:

get_kernel detects the user's Python, PyTorch, and CUDA versions and downloads the matching pre-compiled binary. No builds, no flags, typically ready in seconds.

The skill and the Hub are complementary. The skill handles development. The Hub handles distribution. Build a kernel with the skill, validate it with the benchmark scripts, publish it to the Hub, and it becomes a one-liner for everyone else.

We built an agent skill that teaches coding agents how to write production CUDA kernels. Then we pointed Claude and Codex at two real targets: a diffusers pipeline and a transformers model. The agents produced working kernels for both, with correct PyTorch bindings and benchmarks, end to end. We benchmarked the kernels and found that the optimized kernels can provide a speedup in both isolated and end-to-end performance.

Installation with pip install kernels works, but the command has no skills option:

The kernels repo has kernels-builder and the kernels library.

This is the reason why doing a pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/kernels.git would not work.

Question: Is the baseline in section Isolated RMSNorm benchmark (Pytorch baseline) using torch.compile() or not? Custom kernels should be ideally beating torch.compiled code.

#10248. Why GTA VI’s version of Florida feels so real

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Virtual city expert Emma Fraser explains what makes Rockstar’s latest open world work.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

There are plenty of reasons why Grand Theft Auto VI is so popular: the 13 years of anticipation, the relatable lead characters and romantic storyline, the sheer level of depth. But another major factor is the sense of place. The GTA series is unmatched when it comes to re-creating the feeling of a bustling, real-world city, and GTA VI’s fictional rendition of Florida is the studio’s most lifelike setting yet. It has functioning buses and trains, plentiful buildings you can go into and explore, residents you can chat with, and huge areas where you can interact with wildlife far away from the bright lights of the Miami-like Vice City. For Emma Fraser, an assistant professor at UC Berkeley who studies urban ruins and virtual cities, the sense of realism has created a unique sensation while playing.

“There’s something about this particular game that is really discombobulating and distracting in a sense,” she says. “Because you have these moments where you think, ‘I’m in a place, I’m experiencing a location.’ You comprehend intellectually that it’s not real or that it’s at best a representation, but you still have this feeling in your brain and you’ll still dream about being in that place.”

Fraser teaches courses on topics including urban geography and virtual worlds and has written papers exploring topics like “mapping in the digital age” and “the virtual spectacle of the end of the city.” She says she started researching video game cities in part because, despite their influence and reach, they’re an underexplored space in academia. “I’m a geographer, and geographers are obsessed with cities,” she explains. “So much of geography is thinking about: How do we imagine cities? How do we navigate cities? How do we build cities? How do we map cities? And video games have all of that, but they’re not taken that seriously as an academic interest.”

Like much of the world, she’s been looking forward to GTA VI for years, particularly because of Rockstar’s on-the-ground approach to research. Before development on the game began, developers from the studio traveled to Florida to get an accurate picture. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me, the starting point for the game was the setting, rather than the story or characters. “We just went around to feel it out,” he said. “Go to the Everglades, go to the Keys, go to the city, as many places as we can, and start thinking about what aspects of the place we want to incorporate.”

While there are plenty of open-world games, many of the most successful — from Elden Ring to The Witcher — are sent in fantastical spaces. GTA stands apart in how its various settings look and feel true to the real world. And Fraser believes that this is one of the key reasons the series has such universal appeal. “You know immediately how to function in a city,” she explains. “You know there’s going to be law enforcement, there are going to be city blocks, there are going to be pedestrians, cars, and buses. It’s this really interesting environment that gives you a lot of possibilities to get a player more immersed in your world, because they already know a lot about a city as a general concept.”

“You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time.”

Fraser describes GTA VI’s world as having “implied expansiveness.” It’s not a one-to-one re-creation of the real location. There are plenty of things missing; you don’t see schools or daycares, and parking spaces are relatively sparse. But the game gets enough details right to be recognizable. Fraser explains that as long as certain parts of the city look correct — the lighting, the coastline, the decoration of street corners, the major arterial roads — that’s enough to convince people that they’re in something resembling Miami.

“You can’t hold a whole city in your mind at one time,” she says. “Instead it’s these highlights. What [Rockstar] do very successfully in the game is those snapshots. They’ve got far more content that is recognizable as Florida or Miami than they’ve been able to fit into previous games. So it’s a much more overwhelming sense of being in that place.” The “implied expansiveness” also comes in the form of dialogue, radio programs, and TV shows that suggest a much bigger world by discussing places and moments that exist outside of the game you can actually explore.

This level of verisimilitude — combined with the fact that players can explore the city from multiple perspectives, everything from walking to flying a plane — has led to an experience that Fraser likens to virtual tourism, which can result in all kinds of different playstyles. “Some tourists are going to blow a lot of money on taxis and get to wherever they’re going as fast as they can,” she explains, “and some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place.” Similarly, there are certain players who will just experience the story and play through the main missions, and others who will get lost in side activities like bird watching.

“Some people just like sitting on a bus or a train and getting to know a place”

What’s also notable about GTA VI is how its relationship-focused premise is motivating some players to experience the world in a much less violent way. And that includes how they move through the city. Some people are driving more carefully to avoid killing civilians, while others are exploring spaces while both characters hang out together. “In the first few games, you’re this empty vessel. You’re a criminal, you’re doing criminal things,” says Fraser. “Whereas with GTA VI your motivation and the way you think about your character is really important.”

Now that the game is out and millions of players are venturing through Vice City, Fraser is hoping to use it to research the ways that real and virtual worlds intersect when it comes to how we navigate cities. GTA VI offers a lot of choice in this regard; you can still steal a Lambo and speed through the streets, but you can also hop on a train, put on some headphones, and listen to a podcast while getting where you need to be. “Because this world is so fully furnished, and you have so many options, you might start to import your own real-world practices into the game,” she says.

But at this point, what has struck her most is the attention to detail that separates the universe of GTA VI from its contemporaries. “You can’t just generate a generic city and stick icons in, which is what a lot of games do,” she explains. “You aren’t going to get a sense of a real place if you do it that way.”

#10247. 9to5Google’s Best of 2026

We reviewed dozens of products in 2026, and the one through line across all of them was cost. Because of RAMageddon, everything was more expensive, and it became somewhat easier to separate the products that were good because they were cheap from the ones that were good at any price.

This year was a lot of things, but it was primarily a reminder that the best products are created through careful iteration. Only one product on this list, the XREAL Aura, represents an emerging class. The rest, from the Fitbit Air to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, showcase years of work in optimizing for design, weight, battery life, and performance. Some take more risks than others, but to us they all represent the very best of their respective categories.

Price: $99.99/$129.99 (special editions)Black Friday deal: Save $30 on the Google Fitbit Air Champagne Gold & Obsidian Bundle. Ends 12/02.Release date: May 26, 2026

A screenless Google device outside of a smart speaker wasn’t something I thought I needed. Yet the Fitbit Air has become one of my favorite products to come out of Mountain View in years. Fitness tracking is something I want happening quietly in the background, not another reason to check a screen.

That’s what the Air gets right. It isn’t trying to reinvent fitness tracking; it packages it in a comfortable, lightweight band that stays out of the way. Health tracking data isn’t locked behind a paywall, and there’s no display demanding attention throughout the day.

Smart rings and full-featured watches have their place, but this slim wearable strikes a particularly appealing balance. It gives me useful information when I want it without becoming another device to manage. It’s comfortable, inexpensive, and easy to live with—and sometimes that’s exactly what makes a product great.

— Damien Wilde, Daniel Bader & Andrew Romero

Price: $2,499Black Friday price: $1,899Release date: November 1, 2026

I’m primarily a TV person, especially when it comes to gaming. But after spending time with XGIMI’s Horizon 30 Pro, I’ve been enjoying a very different setup. I loved the older Horizon Pro 4K and used it until this arrived; the 30 Pro feels like a substantial leap forward.

VRR support has made it possible to play my Steam Machine on a roughly 200-inch image in the bedroom, while the built-in speakers do an impressive job of filling the room. Going from Forza Horizon 5 at 120fps to Blue Planet on BBC iPlayer is effortless thanks to Google TV.

The swiveling base is more useful than it might sound. I can position the projector in the corner of the room and let XGIMI’s keystone correction handle the rest. It’s an expensive upgrade, but for a home cinema setup that doubles as a giant gaming display, it’s a beast.

I still wish the Steam Controller cost less. Beyond that, though, I have very little to complain about: this is the best controller I’ve used in years. It’s comfortable, gives Windows users a way to control their PC, and brings together some of the best ideas from my beloved Steam Deck.

Steam Input is the real selling point. The depth of customization makes this controller feel at home on a PC in a way few alternatives do. I haven’t connected with a new controller this quickly in a long time.

That doesn’t mean everyone needs one. Most people would be well served by an 8BitDo controller—or even a Stadia controller converted to Bluetooth. But if you play on PC and want the premium option, this is my pick.

Price: $1,899.99Black Friday price: $1,549.99Release date: August 7, 2026

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 is my favorite foldable of 2026. I’ve been enthralled with its design since reviewing it in July, and it won’t be leaving my daily rotation anytime soon.

The short, compact outer screen is refreshing to use, but it’s the inner display that changed the way I think about foldables. Its proportions feel more flexible than the square-shaped displays that have become so common across the category. Samsung’s motivations for adopting this form factor may be obvious, but the result works—and that’s what matters when I’m using it every day.

— Ben Schoon, Daniel Bader & Andrew Romero

Price: Ear (3): $179 / Ear (3a): $99Black Friday price: Ear (3): $94 / Ear (3a): $69Release date: Ear (3): Sept 18, 2025 / Ear (3a): July 7, 2026

Ear (3a) earns the nod here, but this is really a celebration of Nothing’s entire audio lineup. Its clean sound profiles, thoughtful designs, and compatibility with Android and the other devices I use have kept me listening all year.

Ear (3) remains my primary pair of earbuds, while Ear (3a) gets plenty of use when pocket space is at a premium. Ear (open) and Nothing Headphone (1) Pro round out the rest of my listening needs.

I still stand by calling Ear (3a) simply ‘the best earbuds.’ More broadly, Nothing has built an audio lineup worth paying attention to, especially when end-of-year discounts make it easier to try.

Price: ~$1,999Release date: April 21, 2026 (China) / Nov 2026 (Global)

If there’s one phone from 2026 I wish I could return to, it’s the Oppo Find X9 Ultra. ColorOS has quietly become one of the best Android experiences by getting the small details right, and the Ultra’s camera hardware and shooting experience remain standouts—even next to Oppo’s newer Find X10 Pro Max.

This is one of those increasingly rare smartphones that feels unwilling to compromise. I’ll be thinking about it until there’s a proper successor, and the prospect of not getting one in 2027 is disappointing.

I wish Oppo had sold this phone officially in the US. Importing comes with real complications, but the Find X9 Ultra is one of the few phones good enough to make me consider it.

Price: ~$1,720Release date: March 13, 2026

It’s been a remarkable year for foldables, but the Honor Magic V6 is my favorite of the bunch. Its combination of durability, battery life, and camera quality finally made me stop thinking about going back to a conventional slab phone.

The cameras are a big part of that. I used to rely entirely on my Panasonic GH5 for work photos; now I often reach for the Magic V6 instead. Its large 1/2-inch telephoto sensor helps it deliver the kind of dependable results I want when I need to capture something quickly.

It’s also held up to far more punishment than I’d normally put a foldable through. After a mud torture test and a trip through the dishwasher, I’m still using it months later. Battery life has been another major strength.

Honor’s software still has rough edges, but the improvements are substantial, and the seven-year update promise matters. The remaining problem is availability: I’d love to see Honor make its phones officially accessible across North America.

Android XR has had an awkward start, but the XREAL Aura feels like the kind of product the platform needed from the beginning. It puts a fresh idea into a form factor that’s easier to imagine wearing than a bulky headset.

Think of it as smart glasses that behave more like a VR headset. Open the app drawer with a pinch—or use the tethered compute puck—and your chosen app appears as a floating window you can move around. It’s like having a tablet suspended wherever you need it.

That makes remote work and entertainment feel surprisingly natural, especially when the glasses weigh less than a fifth of many VR headsets. There are compromises: hand gestures can be finicky, and while Bluetooth game controllers work, there isn’t a Meta Quest-style motion controller available for immersive gaming.

Even so, Aura makes a compelling case for Android XR. It’s an appealing option for people interested in immersive entertainment who don’t want the weight and bulk of a conventional VR headset.

DroidDeck has changed the way I think about gaming on Android. It isn’t the first project to bring PC games to a phone, but it feels like one of the most capable. The pitch is straightforward, even if the technology isn’t: run Steam on your Android device.

Rather than emulating an entire PC in the traditional sense, DroidDeck brings together translation layers using projects such as FEX and Proton. The technical details are complicated, but the practical result is that your phone can run games it wasn’t originally designed to understand.

Performance across my devices has been impressive—good enough that I’ve seen games run better than on my Steam Deck. The project is also free, community-driven, and highly customizable. The trade-off is that support for brand-new hardware can take time.

If you’ve been on the fence about mobile gaming, pairing DroidDeck with a controller such as my favorite, the GameSir G8 Galileo, is a great way to see how far it’s come.

Price: $179.99 / $219.99 (special editions)Release date: October 27, 2026

The Fitbit Air is a good fitness tracker and, to my eye, an attractive bracelet. But years of wearing watches have trained me to expect the time on my wrist. Even toward the end of my time with the Air, I kept glancing down for a clock that wasn’t there.

The Fitbit Edge fixes that central complaint. Its always-on display reduces battery life to roughly two or three days, but that’s a trade-off I’m happy to make. The software’s Pixel Watch-inspired look also helps it feel like part of a more cohesive lineup. For me, a small screen makes a meaningful difference.

Price: $29.99Release date: November 11, 2026

We waited so long for a first-party Google tracker that the Find My Device network had time to become Find Hub. The Pixel Tag makes the wait worthwhile with a more integrated experience: everything is managed in the Find Hub app, rather than spread across separate software.

‘Notify when left behind’ was overdue, and ‘Ring this phone’ has worked well for me. These are practical features, but they’re also reminders of how much first-party hardware can do to improve the software around it.

I also like the pill-shaped design. Google didn’t simply copy the AirTag; it made something that feels at home in the Pixel family. It’s a small thing, but it’s pleasant to hold—and surprisingly satisfying to fidget with.

Price: $349.99Black Friday price: $314.99Release date: July 6, 2026

A dock needs to do more than look good, but Keychron’s Thunderbolt 5 dock makes a strong first impression on a desk. Its machined aluminum case fits neatly into my setup, and the usefulness goes well beyond the finish.

I switched between devices more often this year. Moving my work from a Windows PC to the Mac mini M6 left the PC on gaming duty, while the Googlebook launch gave me another computer to plug into the same monitors and workstation.

The Keychron dock makes those changes simple: I connect the USB-C input cable and let it handle the display and data connections. Its own power supply, four USB-A ports, three USB-C ports, SD card reader, and wired Ethernet connection give me the flexibility I need. It might be the most useful addition I’ve made to my desk all year.

I don’t think I’ll stop talking about the Boox Picco anytime soon. It’s a wonderfully simple little e-reader with a straightforward operating system and battery life that stretches across days or weeks, depending on use.

You can attach it magnetically to the back of your phone or slip it into almost any pocket. But the bigger benefit is how easy it makes picking up a book, whether I’m out of the house or just moving from one room to another.

At around $100, it’s an appealingly focused device. In a year when so much attention has gone to retro gadgets and handhelds, the Picco captures a similar pleasure: a small piece of technology that does one thing well.

Price: $499.99Black Friday price: $399.99Release date: October 14, 2026

If one gadget came out of nowhere to steal the show for me in 2026, it was the Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. Amazon rebooted its tablet lineup, dropped the Fire branding, and embraced a much more familiar version of Android. Install a third-party launcher to remove the permanent Alexa search bar, and it feels like a regular mid-range Android tablet—with full Play Store support, no sideloading required.

The hardware is where it really wins me over. The base configuration pairs 8GB of RAM with 128GB of storage, which is more than enough for browsing, movies, YouTube, and casual games. But the display is the standout: this is a much better LCD than I expect from a tablet under $1,000, and the nanomatte finish looks and feels fantastic.

I’m as surprised as anyone that Amazon finally figured out its tablet lineup. A little help from the person behind Microsoft’s Surface line seems to have gone a long way. At this price—and especially on sale—I struggle to recommend anything else, including Apple’s base iPad. It’s that good.

Price: $99Black Friday price: $84Release date: July 21, 2026

I have always been a reader, but in my effort to spend less time on my phone this year, I did my utmost to return to e-paper displays for most long-form reading.

The XTEINK X4 Pro is a tiny 4-inch touch-capable e-paper display with a backlight and plenty of battery life. Its magnets help the device stick to the back of most phones (though it’s a bit tall for some smaller devices like the Pixel 11 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro), and it supports custom firmware through the Crosspoint project.

While it occasionally feels cramped to read on, the sheer number of formatting and font options makes it easy to adjust the reading experience to suit your tastes. And because it supports KOReader, reading progress syncs with most other devices, including Kobo e-readers and supported phone apps.

What were your favorite products of 2026? Let us know in the comments.

#10246. What Is BIO Tagging and How to Use It for Document AI Training Data

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

If you've worked with named entity recognition (NER) in text, you've probably seen BIO tagging before. It's the standard way to mark where entities start, continue, and end inside a sequence of tokens. What you might not know is that the same tagging scheme has become the backbone of document AI -- the field where machine learning models extract structured data from invoices, receipts, contracts, and other business documents.

This guide explains how BIO tagging works, why it matters for document understanding, and how to build BIO-tagged training data that actually produces accurate models. We'll walk through the tagging logic, show real examples on financial documents, cover common mistakes that silently hurt model performance, and look at tools that speed up the annotation process.

BIO stands for Beginning, Inside, Outside. It's a labeling scheme that tells a model which tokens belong to an entity, which tokens continue that entity, and which tokens are just background noise.

● B (Beginning) -- the first token of a named entity

● I (Inside) -- any token that continues the same entity

● O (Outside) -- any token that doesn't belong to any entity

Take a simple line from an invoice: "Invoice #INV-2024-0891". If you're labeling invoice numbers, the BIO tags look like this:

Token          Label ─────          ───── Invoice        O #              O INV-2024-0891  B-invoice_number

Now consider a multi-word entity like a vendor name: "Acme Corporation Ltd". All three words are part of the same entity, so the tagging becomes:

Token          Label ─────          ───── Acme           B-vendor_name Corporation    I-vendor_name Ltd            I-vendor_name

The B prefix marks where the entity starts. The I prefix marks every following token that belongs to the same entity. Everything else gets O. This three-label structure is simple, but it gives models enough information to learn entity boundaries precisely -- even when two entities of the same type appear next to each other.

Traditional NER works on plain text -- a flat sequence of words. Document AI is harder because pages have two dimensions. A word's meaning depends not just on what comes before and after it in reading order, but also on where it sits on the page. The number "$4,250.00" could be an invoice total, a line item price, or a tax amount depending on its position relative to headers and columns.

Models like LayoutLMv3, LiLT, and BROS solve this by combining text tokens with their bounding box coordinates. Each token gets three inputs: the word itself, its position on the page (x, y, width, height), and its BIO label during training. The model learns to associate spatial patterns with entity types.

BIO tagging fits this architecture perfectly because it operates at the token level. Every word on the page gets exactly one label, and the model learns from thousands of these labeled tokens which spatial and textual patterns correspond to which fields.

If you're coming from a background in natural language processing in Python, the concept is identical -- BIO tagging works the same way whether your tokens come from a sentence or a document page. The difference is that document AI adds positional data to each token.

BIO isn't the only tagging scheme. You'll encounter several variants:

● BIO (IOB2) -- B marks the first token, I marks continuation tokens, O marks non-entities. The most widely used scheme.

● BIOES -- adds E (End) for the last token of a multi-word entity and S (Single) for single-token entities. More explicit boundary marking.

● BILOU -- adds L (Last) and U (Unit). Functionally identical to BIOES with different letters.

● IOB1 -- the original scheme where B is only used when two entities of the same type are adjacent. Rarely used today.

For document AI, standard BIO (IOB2) is the safest choice. Here's why:

● LayoutLMv3 and most pre-trained document models expect BIO format out of the box

● The FUNSD and CORD benchmark datasets use BIO, so your data format matches the academic baselines

● BIOES adds more label types, which means you need more training data to learn each one reliably

● Converting from BIO to BIOES is trivial if you later need it, but the reverse can lose information

Unless your model architecture specifically requires BIOES or BILOU, stick with BIO.

Before you tag a single token, you need a clear label taxonomy -- the list of entity types your model will learn to recognize. A poorly designed taxonomy creates confusion during annotation and cascades into model errors.

Ask yourself: what fields does the downstream system need? For invoice processing, a typical taxonomy looks like this:

vendor_name vendor_address invoice_number invoice_date due_date line_item_description line_item_quantity line_item_price subtotal tax total payment_method currency

**Rule 1 -- One label per semantic meaning. **Don't reuse amount for both line item prices and the invoice total. A model that learns "amount" means two different things depending on context will confuse them on novel layouts.

**Rule 2 -- Use hierarchical names. **Once your taxonomy exceeds 10 labels, flat names start colliding. line_item_price is better than price because it's self-documenting and prevents collisions with total_price.

**Rule 3 -- Include a catch-all label. **Call it other or O. Text that doesn't belong to any entity still needs a label for token classification. Without negative examples, the model can't learn what isn't a field.

**Rule 4 -- Match your model architecture. **Token classification models like LayoutLMv3 work best with fine-grained, word-level labels. Generative models like Donut output structured text, so they work with coarser labels. Choose your model first, then design labels to match.

Here's the practical workflow for turning raw PDF documents into BIO-tagged training data ready for model training.

Your model needs both the text and its coordinates on the page. For digitally generated PDFs, extract the text layer directly:

import pdfplumber def extract_words(pdf_path):     words = []     with pdfplumber.open(pdf_path) as pdf:         for page in pdf.pages:             for word in page.extract_words():                 words.append({                     'text': word['text'],                     'bbox': [word['x0'], word['top'],                              word['x1'], word['bottom']],                     'page': page.page_number                 })     return words

For scanned documents, you'll need OCR. Tesseract is the standard open-source option:

import pytesseract from pdf2image import convert_from_path def ocr_pdf(pdf_path, dpi=300):     images = convert_from_path(pdf_path, dpi=dpi)     all_words = []     for i, img in enumerate(images):         data = pytesseract.image_to_data(             img, output_type=pytesseract.Output.DICT         )         for j in range(len(data['text'])):             if data['text'][j].strip():                 all_words.append({                     'text': data['text'][j],                     'bbox': [data['left'][j], data['top'][j],                              data['left'][j] + data['width'][j],                              data['top'][j] + data['height'][j]],                     'page': i + 1                 })     return all_words

Models expect coordinates normalized to a 0--1000 range. This makes the model resolution-independent -- a word at the top-left corner is at (0, 0) whether the page is 72 DPI or 300 DPI.

def normalize_bbox(bbox, page_width, page_height):     return [         int(1000 bbox[0] / page_width), *        int(1000 *bbox[1] / page_height),         int(1000 bbox[2] / page_width), *        int(1000 *bbox[3] / page_height)     ]

If you've worked with bounding box annotation for document AI, you'll recognize this normalization step -- it's the same coordinate transformation used across all document understanding models.

This is the annotation step. For each word in the document, assign the appropriate BIO label based on what field it represents. Here's what a fully labeled invoice line looks like:

words = [     {'text': 'Invoice',      'label': 'O'},     {'text': 'Date:',        'label': 'O'},     {'text': 'March',        'label': 'B-invoice_date'},     {'text': '15,',          'label': 'I-invoice_date'},     {'text': '2024',         'label': 'I-invoice_date'},     {'text': 'Total:',       'label': 'O'},     {'text': '$4,250.00',    'label': 'B-total'},     {'text': 'Acme',         'label': 'B-vendor_name'},     {'text': 'Corporation',  'label': 'I-vendor_name'}, ]

Notice that "March 15, 2024" is a single entity spanning three tokens. The first token gets B-invoice_date, and the following tokens get I-invoice_date. The model learns that these tokens form one continuous entity.

LayoutLMv3 expects training data in a specific JSON structure. Each document becomes one training example with parallel arrays for words, bounding boxes, and labels:

{   "id": "invoice_001",   "words": ["Invoice", "Date:", "March", "15,", "2024",              "Total:", "$4,250.00", "Acme", "Corporation"],   "bboxes": [[84, 42, 145, 58], [84, 62, 120, 78],              [130, 62, 172, 78], [175, 62, 195, 78],              [198, 62, 230, 78], [84, 320, 125, 336],              [130, 320, 210, 336], [84, 22, 125, 38],              [130, 22, 210, 38]],   "labels": ["O", "O", "B-invoice_date", "I-invoice_date",              "I-invoice_date", "O", "B-total",              "B-vendor_name", "I-vendor_name"] }

If you're working with large volumes of documents, this guide on building JSON training datasets from PDFs covers how to automate much of this conversion pipeline.

Manually labeling every word on every page is slow. A single invoice might have 200-400 tokens, and you need hundreds of labeled documents for a usable model. Here are three approaches to speed things up.

Many financial fields follow predictable patterns. Dates, currency amounts, and invoice numbers can be pre-labeled with regex before a human annotator reviews them:

import re PATTERNS = {     'invoice_date': [         r'\b\d{1,2}[/-]\d{1,2}[/-]\d{2,4}\b',         r'\b(?:Jan|Feb|Mar|Apr|May|Jun|Jul|Aug|Sep|Oct|Nov|Dec)\w*\s+\d{1,2},?\s+\d{4}\b'     ],     'total': [         r'$[\d,]+.\d{2}\b'     ],     'invoice_number': [         r'\b(?:INV|inv)[- ]?\d{4,}\b'     ] } def pre_label(words):     for word in words:         word['label'] = 'O'  # default         for label, patterns in PATTERNS.items():             for pattern in patterns:                 if re.match(pattern, word['text']):                     word['label'] = f'B-{label}'                     break     return words

This won't catch everything -- vendor names, addresses, and line item descriptions need human judgment. But it can pre-fill 30-40% of the labels on a typical invoice, turning the annotator's job from labeling to reviewing.

Train a preliminary model on your first 50 labeled documents, then use it to predict labels on new documents. The annotator reviews and corrects the predictions instead of labeling from scratch. As the model improves, corrections become rarer and annotation speed increases.

The key is selecting documents where the model is least confident for the next round of human review. This focuses annotator time where it has the most impact on model accuracy.

If you're working with standard financial documents and want to skip the manual pipeline entirely, platforms like AI Asset Management can auto-generate structured labels from raw PDFs -- typically returning results in under 30 seconds per document. The annotator's role shifts from labeling to quality review, which is significantly faster than tagging every token by hand.

These are the errors that show up most often when teams start building document AI training data. Each one silently degrades model performance.

If "Acme Corporation" is labeled as one entity on page 1 but "Acme" and "Corporation" are labeled as separate entities on page 5, the model receives contradictory training signals. Pick a convention and enforce it across your entire dataset. For vendor names, include the full legal name ("Acme Corporation Ltd") every time.

A common beginner mistake is labeling every token of a multi-word entity with B instead of using B for the first token and I for the rest. "March 15, 2024" should be B-date, I-date, I-date -- not B-date, B-date, B-date. The B-B-B pattern tells the model these are three separate entities, which is wrong.

The word "Total:" is a header, not a value. Only the actual value ($4,250.00) should be tagged as B-total. Labeling "Total:" as part of the entity teaches the model to include headers in its extractions, which corrupts downstream processing.

Some OCR engines split punctuation into separate tokens. "$4,250.00" might become ["$", "4,250", ".", "00"]. If you label only "4,250" and skip the dollar sign and cents, the model learns incomplete extraction patterns. Make sure every token in the entity is covered by B or I tags.

If 95% of your tokens are labeled O and only 0.5% are B-invoice_number, the model will learn that predicting O is almost always correct. This is the class imbalance problem. It's normal for O to dominate, but watch for entity types that appear in fewer than 1% of tokens -- those need more training examples or the model won't learn them reliably.

Before you start training, run these checks on your labeled data. Catching errors here is cheaper than debugging a confused model later.

An I-vendor_name tag should never appear without a preceding B-vendor_name. If it does, either the B tag was missed or the entity boundaries are wrong.

def validate_bio_sequences(labels):     errors = []     for i, label in enumerate(labels):         if label.startswith('I-'):             entity_type = label[2:]             if i == 0:                 errors.append(f'I-{entity_type} at position 0 with no preceding B tag')             else:                 prev = labels[i - 1]                 if prev != f'B-{entity_type}' and prev != f'I-{entity_type}':                     errors.append(f'I-{entity_type} at position {i} follows {prev}')     return errors

Count how many times each label appears across your dataset. Flag any entity type that appears in fewer than 1% of total labels -- it likely needs more training examples.

from collections import Counter def check_distribution(all_labels):     counts = Counter(all_labels)     total = sum(counts.values())     for label, count in counts.most_common():         pct = 100 count / total *        flag = ' ** RARE **' if pct < 1.0 and label != 'O' else ''         print(f'  {label}: {count} ({pct:.1f}%){flag}')

Coordinates should fall within the page dimensions, and no bounding box should have zero or negative width or height:

def validate_bboxes(words, page_w=1000, page_h=1000):     issues = []     for w in words:         x0, y0, x1, y1 = w['bbox']         if x1 <= x0 or y1 <= y0:             issues.append(f"Zero/negative size: {w['text']}")         if x0 < 0 or y0 < 0 or x1 > page_w or y1 > page_h:             issues.append(f"Out of bounds: {w['text']}")     return issues

This depends on your document diversity and label count, but here are practical benchmarks based on fine-tuning LayoutLMv3 from a pre-trained checkpoint:

Single layout (e.g., one vendor's invoices)

These numbers assume fine-tuning from a pre-trained checkpoint, not training from scratch. Starting with a checkpoint like LayoutLMv3-base gives you document layout understanding for free -- your BIO-tagged data just teaches it which fields to extract from your specific document types.

Start small. Label 50 documents, train a model, check the error patterns, fix your taxonomy if needed, then scale up. Labeling 1,000 documents with a flawed taxonomy wastes more time than labeling 50 documents twice.

Once your data is tagged and validated, the training pipeline is straightforward. Here's the outline using Hugging Face Transformers:

from transformers import (     LayoutLMv3ForTokenClassification,     LayoutLMv3Processor,     TrainingArguments,     Trainer ) \

model = LayoutLMv3ForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(     'microsoft/layoutlmv3-base',     num_labels=len(label_list)  # your BIO labels ) \

args = TrainingArguments(     output_dir='./results',     num_train_epochs=30,     per_device_train_batch_size=4,     learning_rate=5e-5,     evaluation_strategy='epoch',     save_strategy='epoch',     load_best_model_at_end=True ) \

trainer = Trainer(     model=model,     args=args,     train_dataset=train_data,     eval_dataset=val_data ) trainer.train()

The key hyperparameters to tune are learning rate (start with 5e-5), batch size (4 or 8 depending on GPU memory), and number of epochs (30 is a good starting point for small datasets). Use an 80/10/10 train/validation/test split, and make sure document types are distributed across all three splits.

● BIO tagging assigns B (beginning), I (inside), or O (outside) to every token. It's the standard labeling scheme for token classification in document AI.

● Pair BIO labels with normalized bounding box coordinates so models learn both textual and spatial patterns.

● Design your label taxonomy before you start annotating. One label per semantic meaning, hierarchical names, and a catch-all O label.

● Validate early. Check BIO sequence integrity, label distribution, and bounding box coordinates before training.

● Start with 50-100 labeled documents, train a model, check errors, and scale up. Quality matters more than quantity.

● Use pre-labeling (regex or model-based) to speed up annotation. Manual labeling from scratch doesn't scale.

The annotation step is the foundation of every document AI pipeline. The model you train is only as good as the BIO labels you feed it. Take the time to build a clean taxonomy, label consistently, and validate before training -- it saves debugging time later and produces models that actually work in production.

Workers at Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games won’t unionize, after the vote for a formal recognition agreement failed, with only 25 percent of votes in favor of unionization. The Independent Workers Union of Great Britain (IWGB) said that Rockstar workers in the union will continue organizing even without formal recognition.

Voting ran from November 12th through 26th, covering the launch of GTA VI. If successful, the vote would have established a formal framework for collective negotiation with the studio over pay, overtime, bonuses, leave, and pensions, along with a right to consultation over future changes including AI implementation and layoffs. Without it, Rockstar won’t have an obligation to meet union representatives, though workers and union members can still lobby for change informally.

“For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn’t a sign to retreat, it’s a sign to double down on what we stand for,” IWGB said in a statement sent to The Verge. “Hundreds of our coworkers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We’re ready to put in the effort to make that happen.”

When Rockstar fired 31 IWGB members last year, the union accused it of “the most blatant and ruthless act of union busting in the history of the games industry.” That case has gone to a UK employment tribunal, with a judgment still pending.

“We are extraordinarily proud of our team, the culture we’ve built together and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” Rockstar head of publishing Jennifer Kolbe told Bloomberg News. “This result reflects our team’s strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong. As we look ahead, we’re excited to build on all we’ve accomplished together.”

#10243. One-Shot Any Web App with Gradio's gr.HTML

Gradio 6 quietly shipped a very powerful feature: gr.HTML now supports custom templates, scoped CSS, and JavaScript interactivity. Which means you can build pretty much any web component — and Claude (or any other frontier LLM) can generate the whole thing in one shot: frontend, backend, and state management, all in a single Python file.

We tested this by building different types of apps. Each one is a single Python file, no build step, deployable to Hugging Face Spaces in seconds.

Pomodoro Timer: A focus timer where a pixel-art tree grows as you work. Starts as a seed, sprouts branches, grows leaves. Complete a session and the tree joins your forest. Session tracking, theme switching, break modes — all interactive, all in one file.

The tree animation alone would normally require a separate React component. Here it's just CSS keyframes in css_template and state updates in js_on_load.

GitHub Contribution Heatmap: Click any cell to toggle contributions. Multiple color themes. Pattern generators (streaks, seasonal, random). Live stats that update as you edit.

Kanban Board: Full drag-and-drop between columns. Inline editing (double-click any card). Search feature that can filter in real-time. Collapsible columns.

Drag-and-drop usually means pulling in a library. Here it's native HTML5 drag events wired up in js_on_load, with state synced back to Python via trigger('change').

Spin-to-Win Wheel: Smooth CSS animation, rotation state that persists across re-renders. Preset configurations for yes/no decisions, restaurant picking, team selection. You can also add custom spinning segments on the fly.

This is where gr.HTML gets really interesting for ML work: you can build specialized components that can handle your exact output format, then use them like any built-in Gradio component.

Detection Viewer: A custom viewer for object detection, instance segmentation, and pose estimation results. Renders bounding boxes, segmentation masks, keypoints, and skeleton connections — all in a reusable gr.HTML subclass that plugs directly into your model pipeline.

The community's built some creative components with gr.HTML too:

3D Camera Control for Image Editing: A full Three.js viewport inside a Gradio app! Drag handles to control azimuth, elevation, and distance. Your uploaded image appears in the 3D scene, and the camera parameters feed directly into Qwen's latest image editing model. These kinds of interactive 3D controls would normally require a separate frontend — with Gradio it's just one gr.HTML subclass🔥

Real-time Speech Transcription: Live transcription with Mistral's Voxtral model. The transcript display is a custom gr.HTML component with animated status badges, a live WPM counter, and styled output that updates as you speak. Real-time UI feedback without using React!

Every gr.HTML component takes three templates:

${value} injects Python state. props.value updates it from JavaScript. trigger('change') syncs back to Python. That's the whole API.

For reusable components, subclass gr.HTML:

Now Heatmap() works like gr.Image() or gr.Slider() — use it in Blocks, wire up event handlers, whatever you need.

When you ask your LLM to build a custom component, single-file output is everything. No "now create the styles file" or "wire this into your build config." Just one Python file that runs immediately.

The feedback loop becomes: describe what you want → get code → gradio app.py → see it working → describe what to fix → repeat. Each cycle takes seconds with Gradio's reload mode.

Deploy to Spaces with gradio deploy or share a temporary link with demo.launch(share=True). Within a few seconds from an idea to a live app.

Gradio ships with 32 interactive components, but sometimes your perfect AI web app needs something special. That's where gr.HTML comes in.

If you’ve got an idea, try building it with gr.HTML: describe what you want to your LLM, generate the code, run it. You might be surprised what you can ship in 5 minutes.

#10241. Motorola Signature 27 hands-on: Pure elegance on display

It’s hard to believe we finally got a proper premium phone from Motorola again, and it feels a bit like the return of the Moto X.

Motorola’s slow regeneration in North America from a mostly budget device-minded company to one offering the most expensive non-folding flagship phone might become the thing of legend. That’s not to say the company hasn’t shown true greatness in the past — the Moto X, Moto Z, and Razr lines are proof of that — but it’s always shied away from pulling out all the stops until the Motorola Signature 27 arrived.

Freshly unboxed and sitting in my hands, the textile-clad Capulet Olive Motorola Signature 27 colorway has impressed me in every way, shape, and form over the past 24 hours. It’s a much longer period of time than I usually get with hands-on opportunities and, yet, the newness of the experience has yet to wear off.

Part and parcel to that experience is the design. For whatever reason, this is the year Motorola seems to have truly figured out what makes a phone nice to hold. The textile back, ribbed metal frame, rounded corners, and curved edges on the front and back of the phone are purely blissful to hold. It’s a reminder that a phone can be as good looking as it feels instead of being a flat, boring, off-balance slab like too many phones are now.

The weight also surprised me. On paper this sits right in the middle of all the Ultra/Pro Max-named phones, yet it feels lighter for some intangible reason. The camera hump makes it slightly top-heavy, and it’s almost as wobble-free as a Pixel (there’s just one off-center camera hump).

The new 120Hz LTPO tandem OLED display is as top-notch as you’re going to get. I had all of maybe 2 hours of direct sunlight yesterday to test it with, and boy does it ever get bright. The rest of the time, I’ve been either inside or out in overcast weather, all of which it looked brilliant in. And it uses a combination of DC dimming above 20% brightness, and 2160Hz PWM dimming below 20% brightness, making it super comfortable for me.

Motorola’s software has evolved again with this release, and the verdict is still out on whether or not this is actually better than the company’s Android 16 designs. The build of Android 17 that ships with this phone utilizes some major design changes we’ve only seen on a few random low-end Motorola phones, and I’m not sure I care for the gentle gradients on the quick toggle icons and some other system UI elements. It feels like a weirdly cheap effect that clashes with Material Design’s flatter motif.

Despite that, this is the most Pixelly (is that a word?) a Motorola phone has ever felt. Features like Rambler, Sign to Text, and Create My Widget are here and work impeccably well. Gemini Intelligence is also on the way, and while there’s no specific ETA for that at the moment, it’s exciting to know that the most advanced Android features — which are currently only available on a very small number of devices — are coming to this phone.

With the additional $200 bonus, that leaves the cost at a whopping $1060

This may also be the fastest phone I’ve used to date. Everything is unbelievably snappy. Tap an icon and the thing opens instantly. Animations are zippy, and the new lock screen and customization options feel cohesive. Plus, all the favorite Moto actions and gestures are still here, which I greatly appreciate.

I’ve got some lofty expectations for this camera hardware, too, and it’s because Motorola is talking up such a big game. DXOMark’s camera review rated it the 2nd-best smartphone camera in the world, just under the Huawei Pura 80 Ultra and above the iPhone 18 Pro. Some people don’t take much stock in DXOMark, but it’s still worth noting that they’ve praised the heck out of the camera and Motorola is also pushing this as a winner in a way they’ve never done before.

The hype for the Motorola Signature 27 certainly seems to be realized, and now only time will truly tell if it can live up to the lofty expectations Motorola’s $1,599 price has set for it. If nothing, it’s certainly off to a good start and has made an excellent first impression.

#10240. Grand Theft Auto VI is a different kind of GTA — so it needed a different kind of ending

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

GTA VI producer Rob Nelson explains Rockstar’s approach to letting players explore Vice City after the main story.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In most Grand Theft Auto games, and most open-world games for that matter, the world is left open for you to explore once the credits roll. It could be Los Santos or a twisted take on Manhattan, but the idea is that the main story is just one part of the experience. After that’s done, there are usually still places you haven’t explored or side missions you left lingering. But Grand Theft Auto VI doesn’t work quite the same way. Because of its storyline, which involves a couple trying to get out of the criminal life for good, that kind of ending didn’t really fit.

“In this one it didn’t make sense,” Rob Nelson, producer on GTA VI and co-studio head at developer Rockstar North, told me ahead of the game’s launch. “Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”

This story contains light spoilers for the ending of Grand Theft Auto VI, along with a key plot point from chapter 1.

To be clear, you can still play GTA VI after the main storyline wraps up. But in order for that to happen, you have to zip back in time to a moment before a pivotal decision — I won’t spoil it for you — that alters the lives of main characters Jason and Lucia, along with their young son Tomás, who they’re attempting to get custody of. Nelson says the team tried “all sorts of things” but soon realized that “in no way did it make sense” to have the game end like a traditional GTA experience.

“Their story needed to end and have some kind of conclusion.”

“You go back and have this open time again where you have the best single-player safehouse you’ve ever had in a GTA, with a garage full of supercars, a helipad, a gym, and all of the stuff you could ever want,” he says of the solution the studio landed on. “And you can spend as long as you want there. But you don’t have Tommy. So the characters don’t have the one thing that they wanted at the start. There’s the tension where you have to spend some extra time grinding to make some more money without knowing what it’s going to get you, and it plays out differently if you get that money.”

One advantage of this structure is that it lets you try out different endings. GTA VI’s story can wrap up in multiple ways based on a variety of factors: how much money you have saved up, what kind of criminal you were throughout the game, and some key decisions you’re forced to make in the final moments. The new postgame structure creates an opportunity to see some of the alternate ways the story can go. “There’s a large number of potential outcomes based on how you played it,” Nelson says.

#10239. IBM and UC Berkeley Diagnose Why Enterprise Agents Fail Using IT-Bench and MAST

Ayhan Sebin Saurabh Jha Rohan Arora Daby Sow Mert Cemri Melissa Pan Ion Stoica

ITBench HF Space ITBench HF Dataset MAST HF Dataset ITBench Github MAST Github

IBM Research and UC Berkeley collaborated to study how agentic LLM systems break in real-world IT automation, for tasks involving incident triage, logs/metrics queries, and Kubernetes actions in long-horizon tool loops.

Benchmarks typically reduce performance to a single number, telling you whether an agent failed but never why. To solve this black-box problem, we applied MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy), an emerging practice for diagnosing agentic reliability ). By leveraging MAST to analyze ITBench—the industry benchmark for SRE, Security, and FinOps automation—we turned raw execution traces into structured failure signatures, revealing exactly what broke and how to fix it. We annotated 310 ITBench SRE traces across three distinct model classes: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B.

Takeaways from our analysis when building agents:

If you’re building agents for enterprise IT workflows, this is the kind of evaluation you want: not just “did it pass?”, but “what broke, where, and what intervention is most leverageable?”

Benchmarks like ITBench are becoming the standard for measuring agentic performance in high-stakes IT automation tasks. In ITBench, agents act as Site Reliability Engineers (SREs) or Security Analysts tasked with diagnosing Kubernetes outages, patching vulnerabilities, or managing cloud costs in production environments.

This benchmarks use success rate as a main metric to evaluate agents. However, this metric is insufficient for engineering robust systems. Knowing that an agentic system achieves a 14% success rate on ITBench tells us that it failed, but not why: Did it fail because it forgot the context? Because it hallucinated a command? Or because it simply did not terminate?

Without a comprehensive approach to diagnose these failures, developers are left guessing, often resorting to blind prompting tweaks that solve one problem only to create another.

As a new standard to analyze the failure modes of complex agentic systems, we developed MAST (Multi-Agent System Failure Taxonomy). MAST brings more insights and open up the opaque evaluation of these benchmarks. Derived from a rigorous analysis of over 1,600 traces across seven different frameworks, MAST provides a standardized taxonomy for agent failures.

MAST converts unstructured execution logs into structured "failure vectors" based on 14 distinct patterns across three key categories:

We stress-test the idea of using MAST to make agent evaluations actionable and gain insights on the failure modes by applying it to ITBench, a popular evaluation suite for IT automation tasks across SRE, Security/Compliance, and FinOps.

We annotated 310 ITBench SRE execution traces produced by an SRE agent built with Codex in realistic environments. These traces capture natural language interactions between agents and their tools across three models representing different capability tiers: Gemini-3-Flash, Kimi-K2, and GPT-OSS-120B. This lets us look past simple success metrics and investigate the distinct failure signatures driving these results. For this we use the recall scores, as the models by design only output a maximum of 3-5 outputs and SREs prefer the recall scores over F-1 score.

Below, we detail the findings from this diagnostic analysis.

When we examine the failed traces, a clear hierarchy of complexity becomes apparent across the three models. This is measured by the number of distinct failure modes observed per failed run.

This disparity in failure mode density reveals a fundamental difference in how these systems break down. Gemini-3-Flash exhibits a surgical failure profile. Even in unsuccessful runs, it maintains high internal coherence and typically fails due to a single isolated failure, such as an incorrect verification step. These failures are precise and far easier to diagnose.

On the opposite end of the spectrum, GPT-OSS-120B suffers from cascading collapse. In these traces, we observe that errors tend to compound over time. A small reasoning mismatch early in the process often leads to a deviation from the task specification, which in turn triggers a total derailment of the agent. Kimi-K2 represents the middle ground, where failures are more frequent and complex than the frontier model but do not reach the systemic instability seen in the 120B open weights model.

The significance of this finding is that a higher success rate is often accompanied by isolated failure. Systems that fail with fewer simultaneous problems are far more predictable and simpler to improve through targeted engineering interventions.

Perhaps the most critical insight from MAST is distinguishing between failures that the system can tolerate versus those that are fatal to success of the downstream task. By comparing the distribution of failure modes in Successful Traces vs. Failed Traces, we can classify them into three categories.

Across all three models, certain failure modes appear frequently even in runs that ultimately succeed. These are often structural frictions rather than terminal bugs.

This separation is where MAST proves its value. It allows us to ignore the bening failures like repetition that often occurs in troubleshooting, and focus instead on fatal failures that killed a run.

Certain behaviors strongly separate success from failure. When these modes appear, the probability of a successful outcome drops precipitously. The most prominent example is FM-3.3 (Incorrect Verification). This mode shows a 52 percent increase in failed Gemini-3-Flash traces compared to its successful ones. Other prominent failure modes are 1.5 (Unaware of Termination Conditions) and 2.6 (Reasoning Action Mismatch).

If these happen, the run is likely dead; guiding practitioners to develop robust context management strategies across agents in the system and multiple turns of interactions.

Gemini-3-Flash is highly efficient, but its primary bottleneck is its tendency to assume success without rigorous proof. Its failure signature is dominated by a massive delta in verification errors. It often identifies the correct signals but terminates before cross-referencing them against the ground truth. To fix this, developers should implement an external verification gate. By requiring tool-based evidence like a cleared alert or a healthy metric threshold before allowing the agent to exit, we can mitigate this model’s inherent overconfidence.

While termination confusion (FM-3.1 and FM-1.5) is the prevalent failure mode for Kimi-K2, its failed trajectories are defined by a pervasive Action-Reasoning Mismatch (FM-2.6), which is present in a staggering 92% of its failures.

Kimi-K2 is a good example of an overthinking model, its reasoning chains are often too long but can fail at execution.

GPT-OSS-120B exhibits the most unstable failure signature of the cohort. This model exhibits an average of 5.3 distinct failure modes per failed trace, indicating a fundamental inability to maintain internal state.

In summary, MAST lets you split failure modes into two buckets:

These are failures which are not fatal and from which the system can recover to successfully complete the task.

These are failures from which the system typically cannot recover.

This is the “richer understanding” piece: two models can have the same success rate on a small slice, yet fail for entirely different reasons—requiring different fixes.

MAST is a tool that inspects the agentic system traces to identify fine-grain failure types that support system development and debugging. In this blog, we show that by applying MAST to ITBench, we move from generic observations ("Open models struggle") to a concrete engineering roadmap that help improving the performance of agentic systems relying on thse models, e.g.:

Develop and run interactive code notebooks with JupyterLab
