#10236. What to get right before you ship webhooks

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, and Cursor are all sending webhooks now, and all four built them on Standard Webhooks, the open spec written by Svix. Downloads of the spec's npm package went from 1.7 million a month in September 2025 to 220 million a month currently.

This may be boring to hear for the nth time, but the reason is agents. An individual person checks on a running job a few times. An agent told to watch for changes checks every resource, every minute, for as long as it runs, and almost every one of those requests comes back with nothing new. An agent that starts a job, polls until it finishes, and then starts the next one spends most of its time waiting: six steps with 15 seconds of polling each add 90 seconds, even when every operation is fast. Polling more often adds load, and polling less often adds delay, so there's not really a sweet spot.

An event-driven API gets rid of that trade-off. It tells consumers when something changed or finished, so they stop asking. That matters most for work that runs for minutes or hours, like batch inference, fine-tuning, and video generation, and many APIs still don't offer it. Of the 57 AI APIs with long-running jobs that Svix reviewed for its State of Webhooks 2027 report, 19 make you poll for the result.

Webhooks are how most APIs push those events, and you can get a v1 out pretty fast. Making it dependable is an infrastructure problem, which is a class of problem that requires more time by default. Before you ship webhooks, you need an append-only event log behind every delivery, a fixed event format, signed payloads, retries with backoff, event IDs receivers can deduplicate on, per-endpoint isolation, and delivery logs your customers can read. If you skip one of these things, a customer is just going to bring it up later.

Each section below covers one of them with adaptable code, and Standard Webhooks works with existing verification libraries in most languages.

If the request handler that changes the data also sends the webhook, a crash between the commit and the HTTP call loses the event, and nothing records that it should have gone out. A customer whose endpoint was down for longer than your retry window has no way to find out what they missed.

Both problems go away if you write each event to an append-only table, scoped per customer, in the same transaction as the change. Webhooks are delivered from that table, and the same table backs an HTTP endpoint customers can read from a cursor. Svix calls this design POKE (Publish Once, Kickoff Everywhere). Build the log first: a consumer who misses a webhook needs somewhere to resume from.

Every code path that changes state calls one helper inside its own transaction:

Pass the helper the transaction handle. An insert through the connection pool commits separately, so you can end up with the event and no change, or the change and no event.

The advisory lock prevents a subtler bug. Postgres assigns sequence values at insert time, but rows only become visible at commit. With two concurrent writers, a reader can see ID 102, store it as its cursor, and then never see ID 101 when the slower transaction commits. Holding a per-customer lock until commit makes each customer's events visible in ID order.

Reading the log is one indexed range query. The endpoint returns a cursor even when there are no new events, so a client can always store it and ask again later:

authenticate stands in for the middleware that already protects your API and sets req.customerId. That scoping stops one customer from reading another's events. A customer who was offline for a week asks for events after their last cursor and gets everything they missed, in order. Publish your retention period, since it limits how far back that works. The same log can also serve synthetic created events for existing records when a new integration needs to load its initial state.

Customers write handlers against your payloads, so you'll be supporting every field you ship.

Give each event an id, type, timestamp, and data. Use the log row's ID as the event ID so webhooks and the pull endpoint agree. Name types as a resource plus a past-tense action, like invoice.paid, and publish a catalog with an example payload for each type.

Emit an event for each state change a consumer would otherwise poll for. Deletions are the ones teams forget most. Long-running jobs need completion and failure events, such as export.completed and export.failed.

Adding a field is safe. Removing or renaming one breaks handlers, so ship a new type such as invoice.paid.v2 and keep sending the old one until customers have moved over.

Anyone who finds a customer's webhook URL can POST a fake invoice.paid to it. A signature lets the receiver confirm the request came from you, wasn't modified in transit, and isn't an old request being replayed.

Standard Webhooks signs the string id.timestamp.body with HMAC-SHA256, using a separate secret for each endpoint. Including the timestamp is what lets receivers reject old requests. Generate secrets with "whsec_" + crypto.randomBytes(24).toString("base64").

Send the result in three headers. The ID comes from the log and stays the same on every retry. The timestamp is the time of the current attempt, so each retry gets a new signature.

Receivers need the matching check, so put it in your docs:

The function takes the raw body because frameworks that parse JSON and serialize it again change the bytes, and the signature stops matching. It compares with crypto.timingSafeEqual, since === returns faster on an early mismatch and leaks timing information. It rejects requests more than five minutes old to block replays. The signature header is a space-separated list so that during a secret rotation you can send one signature per secret and the receiver accepts either.

That code shows how the scheme works. In production, use a Standard Webhooks library on both ends. It implements the same algorithm:

Receiving endpoints go down during deploys and outages, and they return errors when they're rate limited. If you only try once, each of those is a lost webhook.

Count any non-2xx response as a failure, redirects included. Following a redirect to an arbitrary host is a security problem in its own right. Count slow responses as failures too. The code below gives up after 15 seconds. Publish whatever limit you pick, because customer handlers have to respond within it.

These delays match the schedule Svix runs in production: eight attempts over a little more than 27 hours. The early retries cover restarts. The later ones give someone time to notice an outage and fix it. After each failure, pass the number of attempts so far to nextAttemptAt, and when it returns null, mark the delivery as failed. The event is still in the log, so once the customer fixes their server they can replay it or read it from the pull endpoint.

Store attempt state in a table next to the log. Timers in process memory disappear when the process restarts, and you don't need a message broker to avoid that.

Decide what happens to endpoints that never come back. Svix disables an endpoint after five days of continuous failure and emits an event so the sender can tell the customer. Pick your own threshold, notify the customer when you disable their endpoint, and let them turn it back on.

Retries mean some events arrive twice. Usually the receiver processed the event but timed out before you saw its response, so you sent it again. Senders accept this at-least-once behavior because the alternative is dropping events, and receivers handle the duplicates.

Receivers deduplicate on webhook-id, which doesn't change between retries. The insert that stores the event can also be the duplicate check:

webhook_inbox needs a text primary key id and a jsonb column payload. The handler verifies the signature, stores the event, and returns 204. A background worker processes the inbox, so the handler responds well within the sender's timeout. express.raw gives the route the unparsed body that verification needs.

Put this pattern in your docs with a note about ordering. Events in the log have a fixed order, but webhook deliveries don't always arrive in it. A retried invoice.created can land after invoice.paid. Receivers should keep whichever event has the newer updated_at, or read the pull endpoint when they need strict ordering.

With a shared worker pool, one customer's hanging endpoint can tie up every worker for the full timeout while other customers' events wait. Limit concurrent deliveries per endpoint, and slow down delivery to endpoints that keep failing.

Customer-supplied URLs are also an attack surface. Someone can register http://169.254.169.254/ or an internal hostname and get your servers to call your cloud metadata service or private network. This is server-side request forgery (SSRF). Resolve the hostname before connecting, reject private and loopback addresses, and don't follow redirects. The delivery code sets redirect: "manual" for this reason.

Without a self-serve view, every "did you send it?" question goes to an engineer who has to search logs.

Give customers a page to add and remove endpoints, choose event types, and rotate secrets. For each message, show every attempt with its timestamp, status code, and response body. The response body usually contains the customer's own error message. Add buttons to replay a failed message and to send a test event.

Expose the same operations in your API. Creating an endpoint and choosing its event types should take one authenticated request, because scripts and AI agents now set up a lot of integrations and can't click through a dashboard.

This is the biggest item here because it needs a UI, and it's the one teams most often leave out of the first release.

You can build all of this yourself, and many teams have. It comes down to the fact that it's cheap to manage delivery for 99% of your webhooks, but it's nontrivial to guarantee it for 100% of them. This is also ignoring the UX side such as offering the customer portal for your customers to manage their webhooks in.

Svix, which sponsored this article, handles webhook delivery. You keep the event log and decide what goes in it. A small relay reads new rows and passes each one to Svix:

Svix also hosts the debugging portal. This call returns a single-use link where the customer can manage endpoints, read delivery logs, and replay messages:

The free tier includes 50,000 messages a month and doesn't require a credit card.

#10235. This gaming mouse should be a Logitech-killer, but it has one big flaw

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Posts from this topic will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿

Keychron’s G6 HE uses magnetic switches like Logitech’s Superstrike mice, but the clicks are all off.﻿

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

When Keychron announced its $90 G6 HE gaming mouse, I immediately thought, “Cool! A cheaper alternative to the pricey $180 Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike.” Logitech’s innovation with the Superstrike is using magnetic Hall effect switches for a user-adjustable mouse click depth, with haptic vibrations mimicking the tactile click feel. The Keychron G6 HE, as its name indicates, also uses Hall effect switches for that same kind of customization. But something felt immediately off as I began testing it.

The mouse’s shape and design are very reminiscent of Logitech G Pro models, with more colorful flair. The magnetic switches are there and easily customizable (through a browser-based app, no less). But the clicks? The clicks are all wrong.

The left and right mouse buttons on the G6 HE use Keychron’s MagOptic switches, which are both magnetic Hall effect and optical. They click just like any standard mouse, regardless of where you set the actuation point. There are no fancy haptics on the Keychron. If you set the buttons to a shallow hair-trigger depth, you’ll register a press before you actually feel or hear any click. Set the depth for a very heavy press, and the mouse clicks before it actually registers. That… kind of defeats the purpose here.

There’s not much point in tuning the actuation depth of the G6 HE’s buttons if the click feel doesn’t match it. I suppose it’s still nice to have a hair-trigger-like setting for taking faster single shots in an FPS, but not feeling anything when you shoot is weird. And it gets frustrating when using the G6 HE as a regular mouse for productivity — like you’re getting phantom clicks as you mouse around your computer. At least I can feel my accidental clicks when using a Logitech Superstrike with the action set too high, and I know I’m to blame for leaving the mouse on my try-hard settings.

I reached out to Keychron for the reasoning behind the G6 HE’s magnetic-but-not-haptic setup, and cofounder Fab Chan said, “There are two reasons for this design. First, many users still prefer the feel of a traditional click over haptics. Second, a haptic motor adds weight, and for this model we prioritized a lighter design. That said, we’re planning a model with haptic feedback. It will be slightly heavier than the G6 HE, and we’ll share more details soon.”

The G6 HE is a lightweight mouse. It’s only 49g with its battery, or 40g in wired mode with the battery removed. The Logitech X2 Superstrike is 60g, and the newer X3 Superstrike is 59g — each still pretty light. If you ignore all the Hall effect stuff and just use the G6 HE as a regular mouse, it has some things going for it over the Superstrikes. In addition to its lighter build and much lower price, it feels a tiny bit comfier in my hand, thanks to its side walls that curve slightly inward at the bottom.

One of its best features is hot-swappable batteries. From my time testing Angry Miao’s AM Infinity Mouse, I know that once you can pop out a magnetic battery pack and quickly swap it, you never want to go back to plugging in your mouse to charge. You can also get the G6 HE in black with a standard built-in rechargeable battery for $15 less, but I don’t think that’s enough savings to forgo the convenience of hot-swap batteries.

The G6 HE’s charging base doubles as the wireless receiver, and of course it’s lit up with customizable RGB lighting. It has four programmable buttons for on-the-fly changes to things like DPI, lighting, mouse profiles, or just about anything else you want to program. The browser-based Keychron Launcher software is robust and makes tinkering with the G6 HE or its base very easy. And for some reason, the receiver / charging base is designed like a vacuum tube, which is fun, but it means you’re unscrewing its clear housing to access the battery — a little tedious.

I can’t shake my disappointment with the G6 HE’s lackadaisical magnetic switch implementation. Keychron seems proud of the fancy MagOptic Switch it put into the G6 HE, even going so far as to call it “next gen,” but this mouse seems a jack of all trades and master of none. The G6 HE is cheaper than most other mice with hot-swap batteries — which can still make it worthwhile if you don’t care about all the Hall effect stuff — but that is its lone saving grace.

We’ll have to wait and see if Keychron’s follow-up model with haptics can properly compete with the Superstrike mice and their hallmark feature. I’m excited to see where Hall effect tech goes in mice, and how more companies can evolve it, but the G6 HE is a half-measure.

Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

#10232. China’s AI hardware push is moving beyond GPUs to the PCBs underneath them — Beijing races to corner the market on copper foil and micro-drill bits as board complexity explodes

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Much of the attention on China's AI hardware industry has been focused on the country’s drive to develop domestic GPUs, including Huawei's Ascend processors, as U.S. export restrictions make it harder to buy advanced chips in the region. But making an AI server involves far more than securing its processors. The printed circuit boards (PCBs) connecting chips, memory, and networking equipment are becoming harder to manufacture, and Chinese companies are racing to supply the materials and equipment they require.

More than 20 Chinese PCB manufacturers announced major expansion plans in the first half of 2026. Three recent reports from HSBC and J.P. Morgan suggest the shortages could extend to products as unglamorous as drill bits and copper foil. Having a plentiful and regular supply of those components in the manufacturing process is important because the tiny drill bit used to make the circuit boards inside AI servers could be worn out after drilling fewer than 200 holes, according to HSBC, compared with around 2,000 holes for older materials.

It’s all part of a manufacturing process which stresses every part of the supply and manufacturing chain, beyond obvious components.

PCBs are built by layering copper and insulating material together, then drilling holes through them to connect their circuits. But the complexity of those boards is increasing as AI servers are designed to handle more data, including more layers than those seen in ordinary computers. HSBC estimates that a notebook PCB has four to eight layers, compared with more than 20 for Nvidia's H100 generation of GPUs.

But that’s just the beginning of the process. Analysts at the bank forecast that a backplane in Nvidia’s Rubin Ultra systems could contain 78 layers. Nor is the Rubin Ultra an outlier in that process: the bank also forecasts a 36% annual rise in the number of holes required per board between 2025 and 2028. The holes themselves are becoming more challenging to drill. According to a report by Taiwanese brokerage KGI Securities, the ratio between the depth of the hole and its diameter has increased from around 20:1 to 30:1 or 40:1. That requires pushing an extremely thin drill bit deeper into increasingly tough materials without bending or breaking it, or damaging the delicate circuitry, which can easily happen in such a sophisticated manufacturing process.

As well as the number of layers which have to be drilled through increasing in number, the materials involved are also adding complexity to the equation. New grades of copper-clad laminate — the glass-fibre-and-resin material onto which copper is bonded — are becoming trickier for the tiny tungsten-carbide tools previously used in the process to cut. “AI PCBs are denser with thicker layers, requiring more holes drilled per PCB,” writes Helen Fang, head of Asia Pacific industrials research at HSBC. The increasingly common use of harder laminates is resulting in the bits being consumed more quickly.

That’s good news for those making drill bits: HSBC forecasts global demand growing 55% a year in the coming three years. And as with many parts of the AI revolution, the voracious appetite of the sector means that supplies can’t keep up. Even with manufacturers increasing production, the bank forecasts a 24% supply shortfall in PCB drill bits in 2027.

That could push the world towards Chinese suppliers, right as the west is trying to wean itself off a dependency on the country for rare earths and other elements necessary to make GPUs. Guangdong Dtech, based in China, is the world’s largest PCB drill bit maker by volume. Around three in every 10 drill bits made in 2025 come from the company, with its monthly capacity potentially climbing from 160 million bits in June to more than 235 million by year-end. Japanese and Taiwanese manufacturers are still dominant at the premium end of the market, according to consultancy Frost & Sullivan, though Chinese manufacturers are trying to close that gap.

In its 2026 interim results, Dtech reported that it had begun mass-producing drill bits with aspect ratios exceeding 40:1, while developing techniques for producing bits exceeding 60:1. Its newer diamond-coated tools for particularly tough M9+ board materials have also entered small-scale use.

It’s not just in drill bits that China has a chokehold. Another Chinese manufacturer, Defu Technology, has historically been a key supplier of copper foil for lithium-ion batteries, but is increasingly changing its manufacturing processes to try and capitalise on the AI boom. “AI server PCB/CCL upgrades require smoother HVLP copper foil to reduce high-speed signal loss,” writes Avery Chan, a JP Morgan analyst.

HVLP stands for hyper-very-low-profile copper foil, and its manufacturers must make the surface smooth enough to minimise signal loss while making sure it can still stick to the insulating material it is attached to.

The business has historically been dominated by suppliers outside mainland China, with Japan’s Mitsui Kinzoku and Furukawa Electric, and Taiwan’s Co-Tech, holding more than 60% of global HVLP supply in 2025. Defu is trying to break in to disrupt that, with the firm shipping around 700 tonnes of HVLP foil in September, including more than 180 tonnes of HVLP4. JP Morgan’s Chan forecasts a shortage of qualified HVLP4 supply of around 700 tonnes a month in 2026, rising to 1,200 tonnes in 2027. Defu plans to add 50,000 tonnes of annual high-end PCB foil capacity over 2027 and 2028. But all the foil it creates will have to get past stringent testing.

Even before finished chips reach a server, they must be tested using specialist probe cards and sockets, which themselves rely on sophisticated PCBs of a type not found in a server but just used to check whether the chips work. “PCB is becoming the bottleneck and the value-add in probe cards,” wrote JP Morgan analyst Jerry Tsai.

Because of that, China is focusing attention there, too. In September, its Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and National Development and Reform Commission published a five-year plan calling for advances in high-frequency, high-speed and densely layered PCBs, alongside copper-clad laminates, low-profile copper foil and specialist manufacturing equipment.

But China won’t see the benefits of building new factories immediately. Producing the most sophisticated PCBs requires experience, specialist equipment and the ability to manufacture complex designs consistently at scale. Tsai warned that “the learning curve is measured in years, rather than quarters.”

While deals on consoles and key PC components are in short supply during Black Friday (or simply not good enough to warrant covering), there are numerous fantastic discounts on video games, accessories, and monitors to make up for it. We thought it’d be useful to display all of the deals we think are worth your attention on one page instead of sprinkled here and there in our coverage.

Below, you’ll find the very best discounts we’ve found for PlayStation, Xbox, Nintendo Switch 2, and PC players to shop. You can filter the table below to display exactly the type of products you’re looking for.

Both the white and midnight black versions of the DualSense Edge are discounted. Refurbished versions (with the same warranty as new controllers) are another $25 off.

The Nintendo Switch 2 features a 7.9-inch LCD display, magnetically attached Joy-Con 2 controllers, backward compatibility with most original Switch games, and exclusive titles like Donkey Kong Bananza and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Read our review.

The P9 is great if you need more storage for your Nintendo Switch 2. The microSD Express card offers sequential read speeds of up to 800MB/s, but only gadgets with a microSD Express card slot can take full advantage of the highest speeds. That includes certain cameras, tablets, and drones with a microSD USH-I slot.

Donkey Kong Bananza is one of the Switch 2’s first exclusive must-have titles. Its destructible environment allows you to smash your way through each of its 17 levels, and the paths you make will remain intact unless you specifically choose to reset the world. Your companion Pauline’s singing allows you to transform into animals that have abilities that allow you to reach previously inaccessible parts of levels. Read our review.

The Pro 3 features swappable ABXY face buttons and joystick caps, providing players with a highly customizable experience. It also features new L4 and R4 macro buttons between the triggers and its USB-C charging port, along with more durable and power efficient TMR joysticks.

Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive is the best way to relive what is arguably the best Zelda game of all time. The revamped visuals look gorgeous, and while the game’s improved controls might annoy some purists who still cling to the heyday of ’98, we reckon most folks won’t bat an eye.

Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition includes both the base game and the Shadow of the Erdtree expansion, along with new customization options.

The Fractal Scape gaming headset has a sleek, refined design, with a 2.4GHz low-latency connection and excellent sound for gaming or music.

The Meta Quest 3S is a battery-powered standalone VR headset that has the same chipset as the pricier Quest 3, but with the same lenses and screen resolution as the Quest 2. In addition to being able to play many games from the Meta Store, it can also be connected to a gaming PC to play VR games like Half-Life Alyx. Read our review.

The Nex Playground is a motion-controlled console that connects to your TV and uses a built-in camera and AI to track your movements as you play. Designed for ages five and up, it comes with games like Fruit Ninja and Whac-a-Mole. You can download more games, including titles featuring popular characters like Elmo, with a paid Play Pass subscription.

The World of Warcraft Celebration Pass cuts the price of a 12-month subscription during Black Friday, offering access to modern WoW, WoW: Forever, and WoW: Classic at a discounted rate.

The Witcher 3 lets you explore the war-torn Northern Kingdoms as Geralt of Rivia while preparing to face the mysterious Wild Hunt. The recent remaster adds improved visuals, smoother combat, and better movement, cementing the game’s status as one of the best RPGs of all time.

Clicking the Superstrike feels like using a regular gaming mouse, which is impressive considering there are no mechanical switches inside. Instead, it uses haptics to emulate the effect (to great effect).

One of the most affordable Tandem RGB Stripe OLEDs is even cheaper during Black Friday. The AW3226Q monitor has a 165Hz refresh rate, G-Sync compatibility, better-looking text rendering than most other OLED monitors, and unbeatable contrast.

Make this the year that the gamer in your life has an OLED TV to play their console games on. Despite being affordable, the B6E doesn’t skimp on features.

A gift for the gamer who already has all the gear they need (and who loves to read about gaming when they’re not gaming). The site focuses on well-researched deep dives and oral histories on classic video games.

The 1440p 240Hz refresh rate screen is sleek, but pretty basic for the price. It stands out, though, thanks to its DualSense-charging cradle that extends from its bottom. This is the first discount.

If you’re seeking out a prettier DualSense, the Chroma controllers are just a few bucks more than the standard color schemes.

No game has delivered more thrills per minute (TPM) this year than Star Wars Galactic Racer. Podracing is back and better than ever with this game’s stellar sense of speed, and it has a surprisingly memorable cast of characters.

Everyone knows gift cards aren’t the best gift, but with such steep discounts happening on Nintendo eShop credit, you can save a lot on a Switch 2, or games and accessories, if you’re alright with jumping through a couple extra hoops.

Halo: Campaign Evolved lets you revisit the original Halo: Combat Evolved campaign with better graphics, updated controls, and improved sound. The well-crafted remake also adds three new missions starring Master Chief and Sgt. Johnson that take place before the main campaign. Read our review.

USB-C display glasses can make travel (or relaxing on the couch) more fun by putting a huge virtual screen in front of your face. Xreal’s One Pro are some of the best out there at displaying content from your phone, tablet, laptop, or portable handheld.

Nintendo’s latest Pokémon spinoff for the Switch 2 is part Pokémon, part Minecraft, and part Animal Crossing. Yet, despite borrowing gameplay mechanics from each, the cozy life sim is more than the sum of its expansive, building-centric parts. It’s breezy and warm-hearted, with enough secrets to keep you occupied for hours on end.

The MK.2 version of the standard Stream Deck comes with 15 programmable buttons, a swappable faceplate, and a detachable stand.

The latest entry in the long-running survival horror series returned in 2026, with two different styles of gameplay (tense first-person and guns-blazing third-person perspectives) via its dual protagonists. Read our review.

#10230. The Motorola Signature 27’s haptics finally feel more like a Pixel, and it’s about time

Motorola has been content with mid-grade haptics for years, but the Motorola Signature 27’s haptics rightfully upgrade the experience.

Two days ago, I unboxed the Motorola Signature 27 and talked about my experience a bit in my Motorola Signature 27 hands-on. It’s as gorgeous as the pictures make it look, and the texture on the back of my “Capulet Olive” green colorway is the stuff of dreams. But the thing that sealed the new ultra-high-quality design for me wasn’t the comfortable curved edges or the textile back: it was the haptic motors.

Now, don’t get me wrong. The Motorola Signature 27’s build and design are probably my favorite of the year. I’ll need to use it for just a bit longer to be 100% sure, but the pebble-like aesthetic of the curved front, back, and edges feels tangibly amazing to hold and use. It reminds me a bit of the Galaxy S3’s design, just without the nasty, slimy plastic back. It’s curved just enough to feel amazing, but not enough to be an annoyance like some waterfall display phones were in the past.

But a haptic motor is completely intangible to you as the reader. You can’t see it in pictures, and even if I describe it, you may not fully understand why it makes such a difference. If you’ve been using Google Pixel phones for a long time, you’ve probably forgotten how good a quality haptic motor can feel, but let me remind you for a moment just how important such an invisible thing can be to completing the experience.

Typing on the Signature 27 is pure bliss because of it. Tapping each key feels more like the press of a physical keyboard key. Unlocking the phone emits a satisfying light punch to my thumb, signalling a successful read. When I send a reply on X (Twitter), the button tap and subsequent animation feel like the message is being sent through the phone onto the web. It’s wonderful, and it’s one of the reasons people love the Pixel experience so much.

Unfortunately, the Motorola Signature 27’s haptic responses aren’t applied to as many parts of the UI as Pixel phones do, and that’s where the real miss comes in. Adjusting the brightness or volume doesn’t feel like a physically rotating vertical dial the way it does on Pixel, and I’d love to see Motorola add this in an update. But at least the upgraded haptic engine is a huge step in the right direction for Motorola and a good way to make the Signature 27 feel like a proper flagship phone.

llama.cpp is the fundamental building block for local inference, and transformers is the fundamental building block for definition of models and architectures, so we’ll work on making sure it’s as seamless as possible in the future (almost “single-click”) to ship new models in llama.cpp from the transformers library ‘source of truth’ for model definitions.

Additionally, we will improve packaging and user experience of ggml-based software. As we enter the phase in which local inference becomes a meaningful and competitive alternative to cloud inference, it is crucial to improve and simplify the way in which casual users deploy and access local models. We will work towards making llama.cpp ubiquitous and readily available everywhere.

Our shared goal is to provide the community with the building blocks to make open-source superintelligence accessible to the world over the coming years.

We will achieve this together with the growing Local AI community, as we continue to build the ultimate inference stack that runs as efficiently as possible on our devices.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Product teams keep asking engineers for the same feature: “Can users fix the reaction in this clip without reshooting it?” It lands on the backlog as “add expression editing,” and it hides a lot of decisions.

This guide compares the realistic integration options in 2026, sketches a pipeline architecture, models costs, includes a small runnable job helper, and covers the consent and audit logging you need before changing a real person’s face. Vendor details change quickly, so check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Information about features, pricing, APIs and policies in this article was checked on November 10, 2026 and may change. Check each vendor’s documentation before you build against it.

Performance transfer is great for animation, but someone has to record a new take for every change. If your promise is “fix the reaction in the footage you already have,” direct editing fits better.

DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, users upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid plans. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

For developers, SyncMonster publishes public API documentation for DRAMA. Here is what those docs state, as checked on November 10, 2026:

A few things to note honestly. The same generate endpoint also serves other SyncMonster features behind their own flags, so read the parameter table carefully. In the version we checked, the parameter table marks an audio input as required on generate, and the drama-only example includes one, so plan for that in your request builder. The emotion values exposed in the API are the four core emotions, and the extra app presets did not appear in the API docs. The docs describe polling only, with no webhooks mentioned, and they do not publish rate limits, an SDK, or a numeric maximum video duration (an error code exists for exceeding a duration limit).

Runway exposes Act-Two through its developer API as the character_performance endpoint. You send a character (image or video) and a driving performance video, and Act-Two transfers facial expression, and optionally body and hand motion, onto the character. Output is 24fps.

Runway’s API pricing guide lists Act-Two at 5 credits per second of output, with credits priced at $0.01 each, so $0.05 per second. Earlier documentation mentioned a 15-credit minimum per generation, and the current pricing page does not list one, so check for minimums before you budget short clips. The documentation also exposes an expression intensity setting to control how strongly the performance is applied.

The catch is the input requirement: every edit needs someone to act the new reaction. That suits character animation, but it is a heavy ask for a user who wants a slightly warmer smile in an interview clip. It also drives one character per generation.

LivePortrait is an open-source portrait animation framework from Kuaishou’s KwaiVGI group. It animates a source image or video using a driving video or a saved motion template, supports video-to-video portrait editing, and offers retargeting controls for eyes and lips.

The README sets up a Python 3.10 conda environment and expects Git and FFmpeg, with an NVIDIA GPU recommended. It also notes that Apple Silicon runs roughly 20x slower than an RTX 4090, and that Humans mode needs PYTORCH_ENABLE_MPS_FALLBACK=1 on a Mac. That matters if you were hoping to prototype on a MacBook and ship the same setup. A basic run adapted from the README looks like this:

Here -s is the source portrait (an image or video) and -d is the driving clip. Retargeting is exposed through additional options and the Gradio interface, so check the README for current names because they change between releases. Also read the repository’s license file before you plan any commercial use.

The Hugging Face Spaces demo is handy for experiments, but production means owning GPU provisioning, queueing, model updates and quality review. You still steer with a driving input rather than a “happier by 30%” control.

Rule of thumb: if expression editing is a feature rather than your product, buy. If you need on-prem processing or model-level changes, build on LivePortrait and budget for ops.

Whatever the backend, the pipeline has five stages.

Here is the shape of the worker loop. This is illustrative pseudocode only, not any vendor’s SDK or real endpoints:

The idempotency and backoff tips below are easy to get wrong, so here is a small vendor-neutral module. The key function hashes the input file together with the parameters, so a retry with the same input maps to the same job. The poller backs off exponentially up to a ceiling and gives up after a maximum wait. It uses only the Python standard library.

A short test confirms the behavior: the same input gives the same key regardless of parameter order, different parameters give a different key, and the poller returns once the state becomes done.

Credits are not a shared currency across vendors, so compare units first and money second.

For prototyping, the DRAMA web app has a free plan (60 credits, 1080p, up to 2 minutes of processing, 2 projects, watermarked output), which is enough to judge quality on your own sample footage before writing integration code. The docs we checked list API billing in credits but do not state a dollar price per API credit, so confirm that with SyncMonster before you finalize a pricing model. Do not assume web-app plan credits convert at the same rate as API credits.

Plan details are as listed by the vendor on November 10, 2026 and can change.

Changing a real person’s expression can change what viewers believe they felt, so treat this as a product requirement.

For a product feature that edits reactions in existing footage, the DRAMA API is the most direct hosted option among those compared here: face detection with thumbnails for selection, per-face edits, and emotion values you set in code, with no driving performance. Go in knowing its current limits: four emotion parameters in the API, polling instead of webhooks, and no published rate limits or SDK. Starting with the free plan on your own clips is a low-risk way to judge quality. Product details and API access for this AI expression changer are on SyncMonster’s site.

Choose the Runway API if your users want to animate characters from an acted performance. Choose LivePortrait if you need on-prem processing or model-level control and have the GPU and ops capacity. Leave Flawless DeepEditor to studio editorial teams, and Photoshop to still-image workflows.

Yes. DRAMA by SyncMonster has a hosted REST API for editing expressions in existing video using emotion values, and Runway offers Act-Two through its API for performance transfer. LivePortrait is open source and can be wrapped in your own service.

Yes, with a direct editing tool. The DRAMA API takes emotion values from 0 to 1 for happy, sad, excited and angry on a selected face. Runway Act-Two and LivePortrait both expect a driving performance or motion template.

Run face detection first, let the user pick a face, then send that face’s ID with the edit request. The DRAMA API returns a face ID and a thumbnail for each detected face for this purpose.

Per vendor docs as of November 10, 2026: the DRAMA API bills 0.5 credit per second for face detection and 1 credit per second for drama generation, while Runway’s Act-Two API bills 5 credits per second at $0.01 per credit. LivePortrait costs whatever your GPU time costs.

Yes, but its README notes Apple Silicon can be about 20x slower than an RTX 4090. An NVIDIA GPU is recommended for anything beyond experiments.

Not a public one. DeepEditor is an Avid Media Composer extension with access by application, aimed at film and TV editorial teams.

Log the requester, consent record, selected face, emotion and intensity, backend used, input and output hashes, credits used, and a timestamp, and keep the original file.

#10225. Mixture of Experts (MoEs) in Transformers

Over the past few years, scaling dense language models has driven most progress in LLMs. From early models like the original ULMFiT (~30M parameters) or GPT-2 (1.5B parameters, which at the time was considered "too dangerous to release" 🧌), and eventually to today’s hundred-billion–parameter systems, the recipe was simple:

More data + more parameters gives better performance.

Scaling laws reinforced this trend, but dense scaling has practical limits:

This is where Mixture of Experts (MoEs) enter the picture.

If you're already familiar with MoEs and want to jump straight into the engineering work done in transformers, you can head directly to Transformers and MoEs.

A Mixture of Experts model keeps the Transformer backbone, but replaces certain dense feed-forward layers with a set of experts. An “expert” is not a topic-specialized module (e.g., "math expert", "code expert"). It is simply a learnable sub-network. For each token, a router selects a small subset of experts to process it.

Different tokens activate different experts, based on their hidden representations.

Model capacity depends on total parameters, but inference speed depends on active parameters.

For example, take gpt-oss-20b. It has 21B total parameters, but uses 4 active experts per token, out of a total of 32 experts. Considering the shared components plus the active experts, this model uses ~3.6B active parameters per token. Running this model on an M3 Ultra Mac, which has a memory bandwidth of about 800 GB, we could estimate generation speed as ~ 800 / (3.6 * 2) in bfloat16, where each parameter takes 2 bytes. This yields about 111 tokens per second. The actual performance number we get is ~115 tok/s, which is very close to the back-of-the-envelope calculation.

This super fast speed confirms the model works approximately as a 3.6B parameter one, but it has the same capacity (or quality) as a 21B parameter model.

(Note: speed would be even faster if we used kernels for the native mxfp4 quantization the model uses).

Given a fixed training FLOP budget, MoEs often outperform dense counterparts.

This means faster iteration and better scaling efficiency.

Experts provide a structural boundary in the computation graph. Since different tokens engage different experts, we can parallelize across experts (we discuss this later in Expert Parallelism).

Recent major MoE releases of open models that happened in the past few weeks include Qwen 3.5, MiniMax M2, GLM-5, or Kimi K2.5.

The trend accelerated after the success of DeepSeek R1 in January 2025, building on earlier systems like DeepSeek V2. Another early MoE was Mixtral-8x7B, released in December 2023.

Closed labs use MoEs too. ChatGPT has long been rumored to use a sparse architecture, and the open gpt-oss models certainly do.

If you want to learn more about MoEs in general, we strongly suggest reading this blog and watching our recent YouTube video on routing.

Most tooling in the ecosystem, including model loading, device placement, quantization, and backend execution was originally designed for dense models. MoEs challenge these assumptions.

Making MoEs first-class citizens in transformers means redesigning parts of the loading pipeline, execution model, and distributed abstractions, not just adding new model classes. We’ll focus on how the transformers library has evolved to support sparse architectures across:

AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("model_id") downloads and loads model weights into a PyTorch model. For dense models, loading is relatively straightforward where each tensor in the checkpoint maps one-to-one to a parameter in the runtime module.

For MoEs, it’s more complicated. In most MoE checkpoints, each expert is serialized independently. If you peek inside the DeepSeek-V3 checkpoint index, you’ll see keys like:

Each expert has its own set of weight matrices, essentially 256 (0 to 255 total, taking DeepSeek-V3 as an example) small feed-forward networks saved side by side. At runtime, however, GPUs execute optimized kernels. Modern MoE kernels such as grouped GEMMs and fused MoE implementations are designed to process all experts in a single operation, not by looping over them one at a time.

To do that efficiently, they require expert weights to be packed into a single contiguous tensor.

Bridging this gap systematically is what the weight loading refactor enables.

With the introduction of a generic WeightConverter, the mental model shifted from:

A checkpoint already matches my runtime layout; loading is mostly a key-by-key copy.

A checkpoint is just a serialized source of tensors. Loading is a conversion pipeline that transforms them into the runtime layout we want.

The central abstraction introduced by this refactor is dynamic weight loading via a WeightConverter.

Primitive operations (chunk, concatenate, etc.) are composable. Two that are particularly useful for MoEs:

MergeModulelist merges a list of tensors into a single tensor. For example, you can compose MergeModulelist with Concatenate to stack the experts in a MoE and pack them into one tensor.

SplitModulelist splits a tensor back into a list of tensors. For example, you can split a stack of experts back into individual experts.

The refactor improves not just what conversions exist, but how they’re scheduled.

The loader scans checkpoint keys once, matches them against converter patterns, and groups tensors per converter. Once a key is identified as needed, it’s registered as a future and materialized via a thread pool. Conversion operations run only once their dependencies are ready. For example, MergeModulelist waits until all experts for a layer are loaded.

This avoids repeated scans and reduces memory peaks.

To evaluate the improvements introduced by the new weight-loading pipeline, we benchmarked the v4 vs v5 versions of transformers. The focus is on loading speed of large MoE models, which is often a bottleneck in training and inference.

HF_ENABLE_PARALLEL_LOADING: Enables parallel shard loading via threads.

HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD:Disables the new async pipeline (v5 escape hatch).

Model: Qwen/Qwen1.5-110B-Chat GPU: 1× A100 (80GB)

It’s the combination of Single-pass routing, Async materialization, and Conversion-aware scheduling which together avoid unnecessary materialization and memory peaks while enabling expert packing and projection fusion at load time.

With this refactor we can now create the runtime module structure first and then convert the weights into the structure. We can now optionally attach quantization within the conversion pipeline, making quantization part of the weight loading pipeline itself. This is crucial because quantizing “per expert” only makes sense once experts exist in a predictable packed layout.

This end to end pipeline was not possible earlier and now it comes to the users as an exposed API.

Once experts are packed into a single runtime tensor, another question arises:

How do you actually route through them efficiently?

In a Mixture of Experts model, each token is routed to different experts. This means the runtime must dispatch tokens to their selected expert weights, execute the projections efficiently, apply the routing weights and then collect and reorder the results.

This is what the Experts Backend system (introduced in PR #42697) addresses. The Experts Backend introduces a pluggable execution architecture that decouples expert computation from the model implementation. Instead of hardcoding one dispatch strategy inside each MoE model, the system allows expert layers to dynamically select a backend at runtime.

This is implemented via a decorator pattern:

The decorator wraps expert classes and dispatches computation to the selected backend automatically.

eager which loops over the selected experts and applies projections per expert. This is used for correctness reference and debugging.

batched_mm uses the torch.bmm API. This duplicate selected expert weights per token and performs a single batched GEMM. This backend is very well suited for small batch, GPU-heavy workloads where memory is available.

grouped_mm uses torch._grouped_mm API. Here we sort tokens by expert ID, group them, and then perform a single grouped GEMM. This backend shines with large batches or memory-constrained setups.

Mixture of Experts (MoE) models can have hundreds of billions of parameters (far more than what fits on a single GPU). Expert parallelism (EP) addresses this by distributing experts across multiple devices. Each device loads only its assigned subset of experts, computes for those experts and then participates in result aggregation. This approach scales models to far larger parameter counts without increasing computation cost because each token activates only a few experts.

Expert parallelism is enabled via enable_expert_parallel:

Where N evenly divides the total number of experts, and possibly matches the number of GPUs in your node.

When enable_expert_parallel=True, the model switches from the standard tensor-parallel (TP) plan to an expert-parallel (EP) plan with specialized sharding strategies.

GroupedGemmParallel: This splits the expert weights along the expert dimension (dim=0). Here each device loads only num_experts / num_devices.

RouterParallel: This remaps global expert indices to local indices, masks out experts not assigned to the current rank, ensures each device computes only with its local experts and uses an all-reduce to combine partial outputs across devices.

MoEs are excellent for scaling inference, but training them is significantly more complex.

MoEs have a Massive parameter count, the distributed expert communication is complicated, there are routing in-stabilities that need to be handled. To address this, we collaborated with Unsloth to enable significantly faster Mixture-of-Experts training:

We leverage the Expert Backend abstraction, standardize around PyTorch’s torch._grouped_mm API and use custom Triton grouped-GEMM + LoRA kernels. Unsloth builds on top of the Transformers (and TRL) optimizations to push performance further.

For full details, we recommend reading: Unsloth’s official guide

As sparse architectures continue to evolve, we want the transformers library to evolve with them. If you’re building with MoEs or experimenting with new sparse ideas, we’d love to hear from you. Let us know what abstractions, kernels, or workflows you’d like to see next in transformers.

The enable_expert_parallel flag hiding the complexity of GroupedGemmParallel + RouterParallel behind a single config is a great DX win — distributing experts across devices used to require a lot of custom plumbing.

#10221. Your Pose Model Gives You Coordinates, Not Meaning

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Pose detection in the browser is a solved problem. You can load a model, point it at a webcam, and get a skeleton tracking a human body in real time, on a laptop, with no server involved.

And then you have a skeleton that follows someone around the screen, which is a toy.

The gap between that toy and a feature someone would pay for is smaller than most developers expect, and it isn't made of machine learning. It's made of trigonometry you already know. This article builds a working bicep-curl rep counter to show exactly where that line falls — and more importantly, which side of it your bugs live on.

I'm using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker from Google AI Edge, which is Apache-2.0 licensed and runs entirely in the tab. Here's the whole setup:

Point that at a

Thirty-three points. Each one is a normalised coordinate — x and y run 0 to 1 across the frame, z is a relative depth estimate — plus a visibility score saying how confident the model is that it can actually see that joint.

That's the entire output. Coordinates and confidences.

The model has no concept of exercise. It doesn't know what an arm is for. It has never heard of a bicep curl. It reports where it thinks your joints are, thirty-odd times a second, and stops.

Everything that turns that into a product is yours, and it's ordinary code.

A bicep curl is a change in the angle at the elbow. The elbow angle is defined by three of those 33 points: shoulder, elbow, wrist. In MediaPipe's pose topology those are indices 11, 13 and 15 on the left side, 12, 14 and 16 on the right.

Getting the angle is two vectors and a dot product:

This is the same maths you'd use to point a game character in a direction. Nothing about it is machine learning, and that matters for a reason I'll come back to.

One thing to notice: I'm ignoring z entirely. The depth estimate is relative, not metric — it's good enough for working out which parts of a body are nearer the camera, and not good enough to measure anything. For a 2D elbow angle, using it adds noise and buys nothing.

Here's where almost everyone's first attempt breaks.

The naive version looks at the angle and counts whenever the arm is up:

Run that at 30 frames a second and one slow curl gives you about twenty reps. You haven't counted repetitions. You've counted frames in which the arm happened to be bent.

A rep isn't a state. It's a transition between states:

Fifteen lines, and that's the feature. The counter increments exactly once per cycle, on the edge, because the guard on phase makes every other frame in that cycle a no-op.

If you used a single threshold — say, 100 degrees — you'd get a counter that fires repeatedly whenever someone holds their arm near 100 degrees and the estimate jitters by a degree either side. Every tiny fluctuation across the line is a transition, and every transition is a rep.

Two widely separated thresholds give you hysteresis. Once the arm is "up," it has to travel all the way past 150 degrees before the counter will consider another rep. Noise of a few degrees can't produce a count because no amount of jitter near 55 crosses 150.

This is the same trick a thermostat uses to avoid switching the heating on and off every few seconds, and it's the single most useful pattern in this whole category of work. Any time you turn a continuous signal into discrete events, you want two thresholds, not one.

visibility is the field people skip, and skipping it is how you get phantom reps.

When a joint goes out of frame or gets occluded, the model still returns a coordinate for it. It is obliged to return 33 points. What it does is return a guess, with a low visibility score attached — and a guessed wrist position can swing wildly between frames, which looks exactly like a very fast curl.

Returning null and having update bail out means an occluded frame holds the current state rather than corrupting it. The arm stays "up" until the model can actually see it come down.

If you want to be stricter, smooth the angle over the last three or four frames with a rolling median before it reaches the state machine. A median rejects single-frame outliers in a way a mean doesn't.

Once you've written one of these, you start recognising the shape everywhere:

None of those require a different model. They're the same 33 coordinates with different geometry sitting on top, and the geometry is a few dozen lines each.

Here's why I keep insisting on the distinction between coordinates and meaning.

When my rep counter miscounts, I don't retrain anything. I don't collect a dataset, I don't label examples, I don't spin up a training job. I look at two things: my thresholds, and my state machine. One of them is wrong.

That's a normal bug in normal code, and you already know how to find it. You can log the angle. You can set a breakpoint on the transition. You can write a unit test that feeds a synthetic sequence of angles through update and asserts the count — no camera, no model, no fixtures:

The hard part of this problem — turning pixels into joint positions — was solved by a research team and shipped to you as a file you can download. The part that's left is the part you're already good at.

You are not blocked on machine learning knowledge. You were blocked on nobody telling you this was available.

I set delegate: 'GPU' above without comment, and it deserves one. MediaPipe Tasks lets you choose between a CPU path and a GPU path, and availability of the GPU path varies by browser, platform and graphics driver.

The practical consequence is that you have to test the CPU path, because for some meaningful share of your users it isn't a fallback — it's the only path they will ever take. If you develop on a machine where the GPU delegate works and never exercise the CPU one, you have shipped something you've never run.

That, and the question of how often you should run the model at all, is a bigger subject than this article. It's the next one.

#10220. PRX Part 3 — Training a Text-to-Image Model in 24h!

In the last two posts (Part 1 and Part 2), we explored a wide range of architectural and training tricks for diffusion models. We tried to evaluate each idea in isolation, measuring throughput, convergence speed, and final image quality, and tried to understand what actually moves the needle.

In this post, we want to answer a much more practical question:

What happens when we combine all the tricks that worked?

Instead of optimizing one dimension at a time, we’ll stack the most promising ingredients together and see how far we can push performance under a strict compute budget.

To make things concrete, we’re doing a 24-hour speedrun:

This is very far from the early diffusion days, where training competitive models could cost millions of dollars. The goal here is to demonstrate how much the field has evolved and how far careful engineering can take you in just a single day of training.

This speedrun is not just a fun experiment. It will likely serve as the foundation for our large-scale training recipe going forward.

Alongside the results, we’re also open-sourcing our code (Github link), which contains:

So you can reproduce, modify, and extend everything yourself.

Now let’s walk through what went into this 24h run.

We use the x-prediction formulation from Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise [Li and He, 2025]. As seen in Part 2, this enables training directly in pixel space and eliminates the need for a VAE altogether. We use a patch size of 32 and use a 256-dimensional bottleneck in the initial token projection layer. This design keeps the sequence length under control, making pixel-space training computationally manageable even at higher resolutions.

(512/32)2=256 (512 / 32)^2 = 256 (512/32)2=256

(1024/32)2=1024 (1024 / 32)^2 = 1024 (1024/32)2=1024

Instead of following the usual 256px → 512px → 1024px schedule, we start directly at 512px and then fine-tune at 1024px.

With controlled token counts and modern hardware, pixel-space training is no longer prohibitive. It is simply a cleaner and more direct formulation.

One very nice side effect of predicting x0x_0x0​ directly in pixel space is that we can reuse a whole toolbox from classical computer vision.

When your model outputs latents, perceptual supervision becomes awkward. You either have to decode back to pixels or define losses in a learned latent space that may or may not align with human perception. Once you predict pixels directly, everything becomes straightforward again. You can plug in perceptual losses exactly as they were originally designed.

We take inspiration from the paper PixelGen: Pixel Diffusion Beats Latent Diffusion with Perceptual Loss [Ma et al.], where the authors introduce additional perceptual objectives on top of the diffusion loss. They show that adding perceptual signals can noticeably improve convergence speed and final visual quality.

For this 24h run, we add two auxiliary losses:

The idea is simple: In addition to the standard flow matching objective, we encourage the predicted clean image to match the target image in a perceptual feature space. LPIPS captures low-level perceptual similarity, while DINO features provide a stronger semantic signal.

We keep the same overall idea as the paper, but we tweaked a few details. In our experiments, we empirically found that it worked better to:

These are small implementation details, but in our setting they consistently gave better results.

We used a weight of 0.1 for the LPIPS loss and 0.01 for the DINO perceptual loss, matching the values recommended in the original paper.

These losses are lightweight compared to the main transformer forward pass, and in our setup they add only a small overhead while providing a consistent quality boost.

To make each step cheaper, we use token routing with TREAD [Krause et al., 2025]), which randomly selects a fraction of tokens and lets them bypass a contiguous chunk of transformer blocks, then re-injects them later so nothing is dropped.

We picked TREAD over SPRINT (Park et al., 2025) mostly for simplicity, and because the extra complexity of SPRINT did not feel worth the fairly small additional compute savings in our setting (sequence length 64 vs. 128 with TREAD at 512px).

Following the TREAD recipe, we route 50% of the tokens from the 2nd block to the penultimate block of the transformer.

Routed models can look worse under vanilla CFG, especially when undertrained, so we implemented a simple self-guidance scheme inspired by Guiding Token-Sparse Diffusion Models (Krause et al., 2025), which guides using a dense vs. routed conditional prediction instead of relying on an unconditional branch.

We used REPA [Yu et al., 2024] for representation alignment.

For the teacher, we went with DINOv3 [Siméoni et al. 2025] since it gave the best quality improvements in our previous experiments.

Concretely, we apply the alignment loss once,at the 8th transformer block with a loss weight of 0.5.

Since we combine REPA with TREAD routing, we only compute the alignment loss on the non-routed tokens, meaning the tokens that actually go through the blocks where we apply the loss. This keeps the REPA signal consistent and avoids comparing features for tokens that skipped the computation path.

We used the Muon optimizer, using the FSDP implementation from muon_fsdp_2, since it showed a clear improvement over Adam in our previous runs.

Muon is only applied to 2D parameters (basically matrices). Everything else (biases, norms, embeddings, etc.) is optimized with Adam, which is why the config has two parameter groups.

We trained on three publicly available synthetic datasets:

The schedule is basically: go fast at 512, then sharpen at 1024:

We also keep an EMA of the weights for sampling and eval:

Below are the evaluation curves we tracked throughout the run and a few sample grids from the final checkpoint:

For a one day training run, this is already a pretty solid place to be. The model is not flawless yet (you can still spot some texture glitches, occasional weird anatomy, and it can get a bit shaky on very hard prompts), but it is clearly usable. Prompt following is strong, the overall aesthetic is consistent, and the 1024 stage mostly does what we want: sharpen details without breaking composition.

The key takeaway is that we're very close. The remaining issues look more like undertraining artifacts and limited data diversity than signs of a structural flaw in the recipe. The failure modes are consistent with what you’d expect from a model that simply hasn’t seen enough varied data yet. With more compute and broader coverage, this exact setup should continue improving in a fairly predictable way.

Zooming out, this speed run also highlights how far diffusion training has come. By combining pixel-space training, efficient routing, representation alignment, and lightweight perceptual guidance, you can now get a meaningful model in about a day on a budget that would have sounded unrealistic not that long ago.

This 24h run is just a starting point, not the finish line. Next, we will keep pushing the same recipe with a bit more scale and iterate on the dataset mix and captioning.

All the code and configs behind this speedrun, as well as the full experimental framework used throughout Part 1 and Part 2, are available in the PRX repository: https://github.com/Photoroom/PRX.

While we don’t redistribute the exact training datasets used in this run, the pipeline is fully configurable and designed to be easily adapted to your own data. You can plug in different datasets, tweak individual components (TREAD, REPA, perceptual losses, Muon, etc.), and run controlled experiments with minimal friction. Our goal is to make this a practical playground for fast diffusion research, and we hope the community will use it to explore, benchmark, and iterate on these techniques in their own setups.

If you made it this far, thank you for reading. We would also love to have you join our Discord community, where we share PRX progress and results, and discuss anything diffusion and text-to-image related.

Goodbye for now, and stay tuned for the next round of experiments! 🚀

This speedrun was inspired by several recent efforts exploring fast and low-cost training of diffusion models. If you're interested in speedrunning text-to-image models, we encourage you to check out the following works:

24 hours is very impressive, but looking at 32 H200 makes it make a bit more sense xD. Super cool that you used Muon! And, are you planning on releasing the re-captioned brivangl/midjourney-v6-llava?

Yeah, definitely not possible on consumer hardware… yet :D That’s also why we added the $1500 tag.

Regarding releasing the captions, we hadn’t really thought about that. If you think it would be valuable for the community, we can work on releasing them as well.

Hi, this article is very inspiring.I'd like to get your thoughts on the perceptual loss. During a research internship on (raw) image restoration - and trying to explore the perception/distortion tradeoff , I did a few attempts at VGG and Dino loss aswell. I always ended up with checkerboard patterns (no matter vgg or dino). If you look at the original paper from Johnson , it's full of these artifacts.Did you face any such issue or can share useful insights about that topic ?

I don’t think we really observed such artifacts, or at least not due to LPIPS. We did see something similar without LPIPS when using JIT on undertrained models, but I don’t think we observe them anymore. It might simply be because the model had not converged yet.One situation where we started to observe checkerboard patterns was during reward alignment with GRPO or SRPO on one of these models. In that case the artifacts were much more noticeable, but I don’t think they were related to LPIPS since we were not using it at the time.What type of model were you using?

#10218. Introducing Modular Diffusers - Composable Building Blocks for Diffusion Pipelines

Modular Diffusers introduces a new way to build diffusion pipelines by composing reusable blocks. Instead of writing entire pipelines from scratch, you can mix and match blocks to create workflows tailored to your needs! This complements the existing DiffusionPipeline class with a more flexible, composable alternative.

In this post, we'll walk through how Modular Diffusers works — from the familiar API to run a modular pipeline, to building fully custom blocks and composing them into your own workflow. We'll also show how it integrates with Mellon, a node-based visual workflow interface that you can use to wire Modular Diffusers blocks together.

Here is a simple example of how to run inference with FLUX.2 Klein 4B using pre-built blocks:

You get the same results as with a standard DiffusionPipeline, but the pipeline is very different under the hood: it's composed of flexible blocks — text encoding, image encoding, denoising, and decoding — that you can inspect directly:

Each block is self-contained with its own inputs and outputs. You can run any block independently as its own pipeline, or add, remove, and swap blocks freely — they dynamically recompose to work with whatever blocks remain. Use .init_pipeline() to convert blocks into a runnable pipeline, and .load_components() to load the model weights.

For more on block types, composition patterns, lazy loading, and memory management with ComponentsManager, check out the Modular Diffusers documentation.

Modular Diffusers really shines when creating your own blocks. A custom block is a Python class that defines its components, inputs, outputs, and computation logic — and once defined, you can plug it into any workflow.

Here's an example block that extracts depth maps from images using Depth Anything V2.

Let's use this block with Qwen's ControlNet workflow. Extract the ControlNet workflow and insert the depth block at the beginning:

Blocks in a sequence share data automatically: the depth block's control_image output flows to downstream blocks that need it, and its image input becomes a pipeline input since no earlier block provides it.

You can publish your custom block to the Hub so anyone can load it with trust_remote_code=True. We've created a template to get you started — check out the Building Custom Blocks guide for the full walkthrough.

The DepthProcessorBlock from this post is published at diffusers/depth-processor-custom-block — you can load and use it directly:

We've published a collection of ready-to-use custom blocks here.

ModularPipeline.from_pretrained works with any existing Diffusers repo out of the box, but Modular Diffusers also introduces a new kind of repo: the Modular Repository.

A modular repository is able to reference components from their original model repos. For example, diffusers/flux2-bnb-4bit-modular contains a quantized transformer and loads the remaining components from the original repo.

Modular repositories can also host custom pipeline blocks as Python code and visual UI configurations for tools like Mellon — all in one place.

The community has already started building complete pipelines with Modular Diffusers and publishing them on the Hub, with model weights and ready-to-run code.

Teams can build novel architectures, package them as blocks, and publish the entire pipeline on the Hub for anyone to use with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained.

Check out the full collection of community pipelines for more.

💡 Mellon is in early development and not ready for production use yet. Consider this a sneak peek of how the integration works!

Mellon is a node graph interface integrated with Modular Diffusers. If you're familiar with node-based tools like ComfyUI, you'll feel right at home — but there are some key differences:

This integration is possible because every block exposes the same properties (inputs, intermediate_outputs, expected_components). This consistent API means Mellon can automatically generate a node's UI from any block definition and compose blocks into higher-level nodes.

For example, diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular contains a pipeline definition, component references, and a mellon_pipeline_config.json — all in one repo. Load it in Python with ModularPipeline.from_pretrained("diffusers/FLUX.2-klein-4B-modular") or in Mellon to create either a single-node or multi-node workflow.

Here's a quick example. We add a Gemini prompt expansion node — hosted as a modular repo at diffusers/gemini-prompt-expander-mellon — to an existing text-to-image workflow:

Gemini expands your short prompt into a detailed description before generating the image. No code, no configuration — just a Hub repo id.

This is just one example. For a detailed walkthrough, check out the Mellon x Modular Diffusers guide. You can also check out this video!

Modular Diffusers brings the composability and flexibility the community has been asking for, without compromising the features that make Diffusers powerful. It's still early — we want your input to shape what comes next. Give it a try and tell us what works, what doesn't, and what's missing.

Thanks to Chun Te Lee for the thumbnail, and to Poli, Pedro, Lysandre, Linoy, Aritra, and Steven for their thoughtful reviews.

This is such a well written blog post! Thanks to the diffusers team for blessing us with this.
