#10190. A Practical Guide to Browser Developer Tools for Debugging and Improving Websites

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Building a website involves more than writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. Developers also need to test how their code behaves in different browsers, identify layout problems, investigate JavaScript errors, and understand why certain pages take longer to load.

Browser developer tools make these tasks easier. They provide a way to inspect the code currently running in a browser without constantly changing files or guessing what might be wrong.

Whether you're developing a new website or maintaining an existing application, learning to use these tools can improve your debugging workflow and help you write more reliable code.

Let's explore some useful browser development tools and how to apply them to everyday web development tasks.

Browser developer tools, commonly called DevTools, are built-in utilities available in modern browsers such as Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, and Safari.

They allow developers to examine a webpage's HTML structure, modify CSS properties, debug JavaScript, inspect network requests, and test responsive layouts.

You can usually open them by right-clicking a webpage and selecting Inspect. On Windows and Linux, the F12 key or Ctrl + Shift + I shortcut also opens DevTools in most browsers.

The following table highlights some commonly used features:

Understanding what each panel does makes it easier to select the right tool for a particular problem.

The Elements panel is one of the most frequently used features in browser DevTools.

It displays the Document Object Model (DOM), which represents the structure of the webpage currently loaded in the browser. Developers can select individual elements and examine the CSS rules affecting their appearance.

For example, imagine that a heading has more spacing than expected. Instead of immediately editing the stylesheet, inspect the heading and review its computed styles.

You might discover that the spacing comes from a margin inherited through another CSS rule or from a conflicting selector.

You can also experiment with CSS properties directly inside DevTools.

If the card appears too wide, you can temporarily change its width or padding in the Styles panel.

The browser immediately displays the result, allowing you to compare different values without repeatedly editing and saving your stylesheet.

However, these temporary changes do not automatically update your original CSS files. Once you've identified the correct solution, apply it to your project source code.

For more detailed CSS debugging techniques, developers can also read SitePoint's guide on CSS Debugging and Optimization: Browser-based Developer Tools.

JavaScript errors can prevent interactive features from working correctly. A navigation menu might stop opening, a form might fail to submit, or a button might not trigger the expected action.

The Console panel helps developers investigate these problems.

For example, consider the following JavaScript:

If the page does not contain an element with the ID submitButton, the selected value will be null. Calling addEventListener() on that value causes an error.

You can prevent this particular issue by checking whether the element exists:

The Console panel also allows developers to execute JavaScript expressions manually.

This returns the number of image elements currently present in the document.

You can use similar expressions to inspect elements, check values, and test small pieces of functionality.

Sometimes a JavaScript error is not immediately visible. A function may execute successfully but produce an unexpected result.

In such cases, the Sources panel in Chrome DevTools or the Debugger panel in Firefox can help.

A breakpoint pauses JavaScript execution at a specific line. Developers can then inspect variable values, examine the call stack, and execute the code step by step.

If the application displays an incorrect total, you can place a breakpoint inside calculateTotal().

When the function executes, the browser pauses and allows you to inspect the values of price, quantity, and total.

This is more useful than repeatedly adding console.log() statements throughout a large application.

Breakpoints are particularly helpful when debugging complex functions, asynchronous operations, and event handlers.

A webpage may contain several resources, including images, stylesheets, JavaScript files, fonts, and API requests.

If one of these resources fails to load, part of the website may stop working correctly.

The Network panel provides information about requests made by the browser.

It displays request URLs, HTTP status codes, response sizes, loading times, and other useful details.

For example, the following table explains some common HTTP responses developers may encounter:

Suppose an image is missing from a product page. Open the Network panel, reload the page, and filter the requests by images.

If the image returns a 404 response, check whether the file path is correct and whether the resource exists on the server.

The same process can help investigate failed API requests.

For example, if a frontend application requests product information from an API, the Network panel allows you to inspect the request method, response status, and returned data.

This helps developers distinguish between frontend problems and backend errors.

A website that looks correct on a desktop computer may not work properly on a smartphone.

Text can overflow, navigation menus can become difficult to use, and images may extend beyond their containers.

Browser DevTools include responsive design and device emulation features that allow developers to test different viewport sizes.

In Chrome, you can enable the device toolbar from the DevTools interface. Firefox provides a similar feature called Responsive Design Mode.

The desktop layout displays three columns, while smaller screens display one column.

You can test this behavior by changing the viewport width inside DevTools.

A useful responsive testing process includes:

Checking common mobile and tablet widths.

Testing both portrait and landscape orientations.

Checking whether navigation remains usable.

Verifying that buttons and links are easy to interact with.

Device emulation is useful during development, but it does not completely replace testing on physical devices.

A website can have correct HTML, CSS, and JavaScript but still provide a poor experience if it loads slowly or performs unnecessary work.

The Performance panel helps developers investigate browser activity over time.

It can record page interactions and provide information about scripting, rendering, painting, and other browser operations.

For example, a page might become unresponsive when a user opens a navigation menu. A performance recording can help identify whether a long-running JavaScript function is blocking the main thread.

Developers can also use tools such as Lighthouse to audit performance, accessibility, SEO, and other aspects of a webpage.

Instead of making random optimization changes, use the available measurements to identify the actual problem.

Some useful areas to investigate include:

Performance analysis should be repeated after making changes to determine whether the optimization actually improves the result.

These features are useful, but they can also introduce debugging challenges.

For example, an application might continue displaying outdated information because an old value remains stored in local storage.

The Application panel in Chrome DevTools allows developers to inspect and manage several types of browser storage.

If the application behaves unexpectedly because of stored data, inspecting local storage can help identify the problem.

Be careful when clearing storage because doing so may remove authentication sessions, saved preferences, or other application data.

Knowing individual DevTools features is useful, but developers benefit even more from using them in a consistent order.

The following workflow can make troubleshooting more efficient:

This process helps developers identify the cause of a problem before changing multiple parts of the application.

It also makes debugging easier when working with other developers because the issue can be reproduced and explained using specific observations.

Browser developer tools are essential for modern web development. They help developers inspect HTML and CSS, debug JavaScript, analyze network requests, test responsive layouts, and investigate performance issues.

The most effective approach is to select the appropriate tool for the problem instead of making changes based on assumptions.

Whether you're working on a small website or a complex web application, becoming familiar with DevTools can make your development workflow more efficient and help you build websites that are easier to maintain.

Rather than treating debugging as something that happens only after development, make it a regular part of your workflow. This allows you to identify problems earlier, verify your solutions, and deliver more reliable web experiences.

#10189. Android app developers will have to publicly post address, phone number in 2027

Following new regulations, Google Play will require Android app developers to publicly post a business address starting in 2027 and, while there are workarounds, it’s not going to be the easiest thing.

New Digital Services Act regulations in the EU and UK will require developers to share a phone number and address publicly. While this is only required in those regions, this information will be visible worldwide. Google does not allow PO boxes to be used for this requirement, meaning that many smaller developers will be left with limited options beyond posting their own personal address.

Exceptions to the rule include apps that are not published in the UK or Europe, or developers that qualify as “non-traders” which is essentially those making no money off of their apps.

Here’s how Google defines a “trader” in the context of Android apps:

The Verge notes that a “registered agent service” can be used as a business address for those who don’t have a physical office, and that Apple is allowing iOS developers to use a PO box if they prove the box is linked to a physical address.

Google will require Android app developers to confirm their trader status and their address by February 1, 2027. Account-wide status can be found in the Google Play Console via Manage account > Account details > About you, while status on a per-app basis can be handled via Monitor and improve > Policy and programs > App content.

#10188. A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences

User interactions with agents today are where computers were in the terminal era: capable, and answering almost everything in text. Users can ask an agent for anything by typing or talking, and what comes back is usually a wall of text, a poor way to compare three products or edit and approve a detailed plan.

Today, we're releasing A2UI 1.0, the first stable version of our open protocol for generative UI. It lets AI agents answer with interactive screens, such as a form to confirm or a chart. Developers can use it now with open-source renderer SDKs for the web, Android, and iOS and agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. Companies such as Atlassian, Alation, Bloomberg, and ByteDance are already building with it.

With A2UI, the agent describes what to show, and every app draws the UI with its own native components. The application receives A2UI messages and each app renders the content securely and at native speed. Users get the same low latency, high trust, and complete native fidelity whether they reach a company's agent in its own app or in a third-party AI assistant that hosts MCP apps, such as Gemini or Claude.

You wake up sick. Getting through the morning takes six apps: book a video visit, move your meetings, tell your team, turn on an out-of-office reply, ask your partner to do school pickup and order soup. Ask a text-only agent instead, and you get a numbered wall of text, then round after round of “which ones?”. A2UI won't handle your sick day, but it gives developers the framework to build an agent that can. That agent could answer with one view of all six apps. Changing your plan is a couple of taps instead of another round of messages, and nothing is sent until you confirm.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

The same agent output works on any screen. Ask an agent to “move dinner with Priya to Friday”, and it can answer with one view that lines up your calendar, open tables from a restaurant booking app and prices from a rideshare app, so the time that works for everyone is obvious. The developer builds that view once with A2UI, and it renders natively on your phone and on your laptop.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

In both examples, A2UI is the framework that simplifies building these experiences across platforms. Developers build the agent and choose the platforms it works with. A2UI gives them the protocol the agent uses to describe each view, a way to combine components from different apps in one view, and renderers that draw it natively on the web, Android, and iOS.

New to A2UI? Start with the A2UI Playground by CopilotKit or check out industry examples.

Atlassian is bringing A2UI to Jira, where teams can assign work items to AI agents. When an agent needs a follow-up from the team to finish a work item, such as a missing detail or a decision, it asks with an interactive card in the work item, and the team answers right there in Jira.

The Alation Intelligence Operating System (AIOS) builds its feeds using A2UI: metric cards, charts, and more. Each chart can show the SQL query and data behind it. Ask Claude for a feed about profitable products, and the feed renders in the conversation using A2UI to render metric cards, charts, and custom components. The same feed with the same information can be viewed directly inside Alation with a nearly identical layout.

ByteDance released an A2UI renderer for Lynx, its cross-platform framework, in June 2026. Lynx keeps streamed screens smooth and ships a default set of components built on its `lynx-ui` library. In the Lynx GenUI Playground, you can watch A2UI messages rendered natively, for example, as a two-day trip planner for Kyoto. Lynx supports A2UI 0.9 today and is adapting to 1.0 with the A2UI team.

Ask Gemini Notebook for a slide deck and it replies with a card that asks two things: presenter slides or a detailed deck, and which topics to focus on. A review card follows with the format, focus, and visual style, which you can edit before it generates the deck. The same cards guide Video Overviews on the web and on mobile.

Organizations can register their own agents that respond with A2UI. Gemini renders those responses using the components in its A2UI component gallery, and supports A2UI 0.9.1 today. The Google Cloud documentation covers registering an agent and hosting one on Cloud Run.

Several other Google teams, including some behind our largest products, are building features with A2UI.

Several other Google teams, including some behind our largest products, are building features with A2UI that haven’t launched yet. We’ll share more as they ship.

A2UI and MCP Apps work together. Alation already uses both to show its A2UI feeds in Claude. Our June post, A2UI + MCP Apps, covers three ways to combine them, and the A2UI in MCP Apps guide shows how to run A2UI screens inside an MCP App.

Jetpack Compose support for 1.0 is coming soon. Agents in Gemini Enterprise can already use A2UI, and we're working on upgrading Gemini Enterprise to A2UI 1.0. The A2UI roadmap covers the rest, from design-system primitives that render natively on every platform to official SDK support for decision models like Jev.

We’ve collaborated with partners who have built A2UI 1.0 demos across different industries to give you inspiration on how to adapt A2UI to your use cases. Explore what they’ve built:

#10187. Build a Domain-Specific Embedding Model in Under a Day

If you are building a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) system, you have likely hit this wall: Everything works… until it doesn’t. General-purpose embedding models are trained to understand the internet; not your contracts, manufacturing logs, proprietary chemical formulations or internal taxonomy. They capture broad semantic similarity, but they do not understand the fine-grained distinctions that matter in your domain. Fine-tuning an embedding model can improve the performance of your retrieval pipeline when off-the-shelf models fail to effectively capture domain-specific nuances. Despite how critical embeddings are to RAG performance, the process remains surprisingly fragmented, the skills required are specialized, and the time investment is daunting.

With a single GPU and less than a day of training time, you can transform a general-purpose embedding model into one that truly understands your domain, no manual labeling required. To help you hit the ground running, we are also releasing a ready-to-use synthetic training dataset generated from NVIDIA's public documentation using this exact pipeline. Using this data and the recipe, we saw over 10% improvement in both Recall@10 and NDCG@10. Atlassian applied this recipe to fine-tune on their JIRA dataset, increasing Recall@60 from 0.751 to 0.951, a 26% improvement - on a single GPU.

By the end of this post, you’ll know how to:📄 Generate training data from domain documents without labeled data🎯 Use hard negative mining for effective contrastive training🔗 Improve embedding quality with multi-hop queries⚙️ Fine-tune a bi-encoder embedding model📊 Evaluate whether fine-tuning improves retrieval🚀 Deploy the fine-tuned model in your pipeline

In this tutorial, we will finetune the base model Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 - a 1-billion-parameter embedding model that balances quality and inference cost. To get started, follow this setup guide.

Fine-tuning an embedding model requires thousands of (query, relevant document) pairs. Most use cases don’t have this data readily available. Creating it manually is expensive, slow, and often biased by the annotator’s personal interpretation of what’s “relevant.”Instead of labeling data by hand, you can use an LLM (nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b) to read your documents and automatically generate high-quality synthetic question–answer pairs.

Behind the scenes, this runs a four-stage synthetic data generation (SDG) pipeline powered by NeMo Data Designer:

The thermal design power (TDP) of the H100 GPU is 700W in SXM form factor. The cooling solution must maintain junction temperature below 83°C under sustained workloads. Liquid cooling is recommended for dense deployments exceeding 4 GPUs per node, as air cooling cannot dissipate sufficient heat in standard 2U chassis configurations.

Notice the difference: the first question is a simple factual lookup. The second requires multi-hop, causal reasoning. The pipeline generates both types, with configurable complexity levels (2–5) and hop counts (1–3). Each QA pair then undergoes quality evaluation, receiving sub-scores for relevance, accuracy, context support, and clarity, along with an overall score. Only pairs that meet the threshold are included in training.

If you train an embedding model with only positive pairs (query + correct document), it learns to distinguish obviously different documents but fails on the hard cases — passages that look relevant but are not the right answer. In a real retrieval system, these near-misses are exactly the documents that cause bad answers. Hard negative mining finds these confusing passages so the model can learn to tell them apart.

The above command runs three sub-steps automatically:

The generated QA pairs are split into training (80%) and test (20%) sets. The test set is formatted as a BEIR-compatible benchmark for standardized evaluation in Step 5.

Using the base embedding model, the pipeline:

The result: hard negatives are the most similar non-positive passages that still fall safely below the positive-score ceiling. They are passages the current model considers highly relevant but that are not the labeled answer.

Why this works: Training on easy negatives (completely unrelated passages) teaches the model nothing new. Training on hard negatives forces it to learn the subtle distinctions that matter in your domain. For example, in a medical corpus, a question about "metformin dosage for Type 2 diabetes" might have hard negatives about "metformin side effects" or "insulin dosage for Type 1 diabetes" — close but critically different. The 95% margin ceiling prevents the miner from selecting passages that are too close to the positive, which could actually be correct answers that simply weren't labeled during SDG.

Multi-hop questions reference multiple positive documents. For example, a question like "How does the thermal management system in Section 3.2 relate to the power constraints described in Section 5.1?" has two positive passages.

Unrolling creates one training example per (query, positive document) pair, so the contrastive loss sees each positive independently. A question with 2 positive documents becomes 2 training examples, each with the same hard negatives but a different positive.

The final output is a training-ready JSON file:

Standard embedding fine-tuning generates one question per passage and trains the model to match them. This works for simple factual lookups, but real users ask complex questions that span multiple documents or sections. If the model has only seen single-hop training data, it will struggle to retrieve all the relevant passages for these complex queries.

The SDG pipeline generates questions at 1 to 3 hops by default:

Each hop is tracked with its own context summary and segment IDs, so the training data preserves the full reasoning chain. After unrolling (Step 2c), each (question, relevant passage) pair becomes an independent training signal, teaching the model that all of these passages are relevant to the multi-hop query.

The fine-tuned model learns to retrieve contextually related documents, not just lexically similar ones.

The training uses a biencoder architecture with contrastive loss.

The temperature of 0.02 is deliberately aggressive, it produces a very sharp probability distribution. This works well because the hard negatives from Step 2 are high-quality: they are genuinely confusing passages that the model needs strong gradients to learn to distinguish.

If ckpt_every_steps is omitted from the config, checkpoint frequency is set automatically:

This means you can start with a small corpus (50–100 documents) for a quick proof-of-concept and scale up later without manually tuning checkpoint settings.

Did fine-tuning actually help? Let’s find out by running a standardized evaluation comparing the base model against the fine-tuned checkpoint on the held-out test set:

The evaluation uses the BEIR framework and computes four standard information retrieval metrics at k = 1, 5, 10, and 100:

A successful fine-tune typically results in a 10% improvement in nDCG@10 and Recall@10 within <1 day.

Results using Retrieval Synthetic NVDocs:

This recipe has been validated on real enterprise data by Atlassian. They applied this pipeline to fine-tune Llama-Nemotron-Embed-1B-v2 on a public Jira dataset using a single NVIDIA A100 80GB GPU, following the same stages described above

Recall@60 jumped from 0.751 to 0.951 — a 26.7% gain.The fine-tuned model retrieves the correct document within the top 60 results for 95.1% of queries, up from 75.1% with the base model. For a retrieval system underpinning Jira search, this directly translates into more relevant results for millions of users. Find more details in their blog post Advancing semantic search for millions of Rovo users.

A PyTorch checkpoint is great for evaluation but too slow for production. The final two stages convert the model and serve it behind an API.

This exports the fine-tuned checkpoint to ONNX (opset 17). Optionally, it compiles a TensorRT engine for maximum inference throughput, with configurable optimization profiles for batch size (1–64) and sequence length (3–256):

The exported model is deployed inside an NVIDIA NIM container — a production-ready inference microservice exposing an OpenAI-compatible /v1/embeddings endpoint:

Because NIM serves an OpenAI-compatible API, you can drop it into any existing RAG pipeline that uses the embeddings API format — no code changes needed.

The pipeline includes a NIM accuracy verification step that runs the same BEIR evaluation against the deployed endpoint:

This catches any accuracy loss from the ONNX/TensorRT conversion. Metrics that match within tolerance (0.03 for @1, 0.01 for @5+) are marked with a check; deviations beyond conversion noise are flagged.

The full embedding fine-tuning pipeline can be run in six commands, from raw documents to a deployed model.

Total: under a day, with most time being hands-off training. For a small corpus (~500 documents), the entire pipeline completes in about 2–3 hours.

The pipeline can run end-to-end, but each stage can also be executed independently depending on your starting point. For example, if you have raw documents, you can begin with synthetic data generation (SDG), while datasets that already include hard negatives can skip earlier steps and go directly to fine-tuning. Since every stage uses standard formats such as JSON, BEIR, and ONNX, it’s easy to integrate custom components or reuse intermediate outputs in other workflows. The recipe is also flexible in how it runs, supporting execution on a local machine, inside Docker containers, or on Slurm-based clusters.

If you have domain documents and some time in your hand, you can generate your first batch of synthetic training data today! The full pipeline - from documents to a deployed, domain-adapted embedding model - runs in under a day on a single GPU. You can start with our ready-made nvidia/Retrieval-Synthetic-NVDocs-v1 dataset to try the pipeline right away. Let us know what you build.Star the repos for Nemotron, NeMo Data Designer and NeMo Automodel if you find them useful.

Thank you Nvidia for this. Could you please make it possible, even if not the default, to call a "locally" / internally deployed LLM (OpenAI compatible endpoint) for the SDG phase ? The whole point of self-hosting a fine-tuned embedding model, appart from accurracy, is that the company's data never leave the premises. Thanks

Thanks for the feedback. We will add the support in the next release of the recipe.

The domain-specific evaluation and the thread's point about keeping sensitive data local are both important. Before choosing whether to fine-tune an embedding model, a useful control is a lexical baseline on the same held-out domain queries, including paraphrase-heavy and exact-identifier slices. We explored BM25 + semantic reranking here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). Our reranking experiment uses a hosted API, so it doesn't satisfy a strict no-data-leaves-premises requirement; we haven't compared it with this recipe.

#10183. A New Framework for Evaluating Voice Agents (EVA)

Conversational voice agents present a distinct evaluation challenge: they must simultaneously satisfy two objectives — accuracy (completing the user's task correctly and faithfully) and conversational experience (doing so naturally, concisely, and in a way appropriate for spoken interaction). These objectives are deeply intertwined: mishearing a confirmation code renders perfect LLM reasoning meaningless, a wall of options overwhelms a caller who can't skim spoken output, and delayed responses can pass every accuracy check while remaining unusable in practice. Existing frameworks treat these as separate concerns — evaluating task success or conversational dynamics, but not both.

We introduce EVA, an end-to-end evaluation framework for conversational voice agents that evaluates complete, multi-turn spoken conversations using a realistic bot-to-bot architecture. EVA produces two high-level scores, EVA-A (Accuracy) and EVA-X (Experience), and is designed to surface failures along each dimension. EVA is the first to jointly score task success and conversational experience. We release EVA with an initial airline dataset of 50 scenarios covering flight rebooking, cancellation handling, vouchers, and more — the first in a planned series of domains.

We also provide benchmark results for 20 cascade and audio-native systems, such as speech-to-speech (S2S) models and Large Audio Language Models (LALMs). Our biggest finding is that there is a consistent Accuracy-Experience tradeoff; agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa.

The field currently lacks a framework that evaluates the full quality of voice agent interactions, as most existing efforts assess individual components in isolation. For example, AudioBench, SD-Eval, VoxEval, Kimi-Audio-Evalkit, VoiceBench and VoxDialogue evaluate core speech understanding capabilities for Speech-to-Text (STT) — transcription, paralinguistics, acoustic cues — but remain confined to single-turn, non-interactive settings. On the other hand, EmergentTTS-Eval and SHEET assess perceived speech quality using subjective listening tests (e.g., Mean Opinion Score). Beyond speech perception, FD-Bench, Talking Turns, Full-Duplex-Bench provide deeper analyses of conversational dynamics — interruptions, backchanneling, turn-taking — yet evaluate these in isolation from task-oriented tool use, leaving the relationship between dialogue quality and agentic capability unexamined. More recent efforts, notably VoiceAgentBench and CAVA, take steps towards evaluating the agentic capabilities of commercial voice agent systems, including tool-calling and complex instruction-following. However, these voice-agentic capabilities are not evaluated within complete conversational workflows that voice agents must navigate in practice: from initial user request through multi-step tool orchestration to final task resolution.

The lack of frameworks that jointly capture accuracy and experience underscores the need for a framework that treats voice agent quality as an integrated whole. This means evaluating not only whether the task succeeded, but whether the agent communicated accurately, concisely, and naturally throughout, and surfacing how these dimensions trade off against one another in realistic deployment conditions.

End-to-end evaluation reveals interaction dynamics that are not apparent at the component level: whether the agent interrupts users during natural pauses in speech, whether it recovers smoothly when a user corrects a transcription error, or whether high latency disrupts the conversational flow enough to prompt users to repeat themselves or abandon the task entirely.

EVA simulates multi-turn spoken conversations over live audio in which the agent must invoke appropriate tools, adhere to task-specific policies, and reach a deterministically verifiable end state. EVA evaluates voice agents using a bot-to-bot audio architecture composed of five core components:

User Simulator — A conversational AI configured with a specific goal and persona that plays the role of a caller. It operates in audio using high-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) models, ensuring the evaluation captures representative speech-understanding challenges in natural-sounding conversational speech and realistic turn-taking dynamics.

Voice Agent — The voice agent being evaluated, built with Pipecat, an open-source Python framework for real-time voice applications. EVA supports both cascade architectures (STT → LLM → TTS) and audio-native models (S2S or LALM → TTS).

Tool Executor — The engine that provides deterministic, reproducible tool responses via custom Python functions. It dynamically queries and modifies a predefined per-scenario database.

Validators — A set of validation metrics that check that conversations are complete and that the user faithfully reproduced the intended behavior and speech, with no human annotation required. Any conversation that fails in this validation step is regenerated, ensuring that only valid, correctly executed conversations enter evaluation. This stands in contrast to approaches that rely on post-hoc human labeling to identify simulator errors.

Metrics Suite — A suite of metrics evaluates the voice agent using the conversation recording, transcript, and tool call logs.

Each test case (scenario) in our framework is an evaluation record, structured to make tests reproducible:

We release EVA with a synthetic airline dataset of 50 scenarios and 15 tools, spanning IRROPS rebooking, voluntary itinerary changes, cancellations, same-day standby, and compensation vouchers. Scenarios are designed to test temporal reasoning, policy-following, constraint satisfaction, and named-entity handling.

EVA evaluates voice agents across two fundamental dimensions, EVA-A for accuracy, and EVA-X for experience. EVA also includes a set of diagnostic metrics. Unlike the primary metrics, these are not used directly to compare or rank models — rather, they offer granular insight into why a model scores the way it does, helping identify and understand specific failure modes (e.g., ASR, speech synthesis, etc.). We report pass@k (the probability that at least one of k runs succeeds) and pass^k (the probability that all k runs succeed) across three trials per scenario (k = 3), capturing both peak performance and behavioral consistency.

EVA uses two evaluation methods: deterministic code-based metrics, which compute scores directly from structured data and are fast; and LLM-as-Judge metrics, which use Large Language Models (LLMs) to assess qualitative aspects of the conversation, or Large Audio Language Models (LALM) to evaluate speech directly. Each judge-based metric uses the model that performs best on a curated evaluation dataset for that specific metric.

Task completion alone is a necessary but insufficient measure of accuracy. An agent can reach the correct end state while fabricating a policy detail, misreading a confirmation code aloud, or hallucinating a flight number mid-conversation. These failures are invisible to a binary pass/fail check but directly harm users. EVA-A therefore measures three dimensions of accuracy:

Turn-taking timing matters, but it tells only part of the story. An agent can have perfect timing while overwhelming a caller with a wall of spoken options they cannot skim, or repeatedly asking for information already given. These failures degrade the experience without ever involving a mistimed response. EVA-X therefore measures three dimensions of experience:

We evaluated 20 systems — proprietary and open-source, cascade and audio-native — and find a consistent accuracy-experience tradeoff: agents that perform well on task completion tend to deliver worse user experiences, and vice versa — a tradeoff invisible to benchmarks that score only task completion. No single configuration dominates both axes, confirming that accuracy and experience must be measured jointly.

Additionally, we identified named entity transcription as a dominant failure mode. A single misheard character can cascade into an authentication failure and a full conversation breakdown. Also, multi-step workflows break agents in predictable ways. Rebooking a flight while preserving ancillary services — seats, baggage — is the dominant complexity breaker across all configurations. Finally, we observed that additional calibration is needed for real-world use cases. The gap between pass@3 and pass^3 is substantial across all configurations. Even agents that can complete a task often cannot do so consistently, which is critical for real-world success.

EVA is designed to provide rigorous, end-to-end evaluation of conversational voice agents, but several limitations are important to acknowledge, across the framework, data, and metrics dimensions:

Metrics — LLM-as-judge models carry inherent biases and may favor certain response styles independent of quality, with additional risk of systematic bias when the evaluated and judge models share a provider. While we validate our judges against labeled datasets and report accuracy measurements on our website, these alignment scores do not eliminate systematic bias entirely. Additionally, task completion is measured as binary, which does not capture partial credits and may understate the relative quality of systems that fail gracefully versus catastrophically.

Simulation — The current release covers 50 English-language scenarios in a single domain (airline); results may not generalize to other domains, languages, or accents. Also, the user simulator may not perfectly replicate real caller behavior (e.g., disfluencies, hesitations, emotions) or guarantee full policy adherence.

Framework — The user simulator relies on a single commercial provider whose voice characteristics may systematically favor certain ASR systems, and the bot-to-bot pipeline — including audio format conversions and real-time audio interfaces — may not fully represent production deployments. Also, full reproduction requires commercial API access, and latency measurements will vary across providers and infrastructure.

On the evaluation side, we plan to add prosodic quality assessment (pronunciation, rhythm, expressiveness) — currently an open problem after finding very low alignment between LALM-as-Judge and human judgments. We also plan robustness testing under noisy conditions, diverse accents, multilingual users, and varied speaker behaviors, alongside affect-aware evaluation of how agents respond to user distress. In terms of data, we are developing additional domain datasets — each with distinct policy structures, named entity profiles, and conversational dynamics — and more complex scenarios involving compound requests, multi-step follow-ups, and longer conversational memory. On the tooling front, we will release a results and error analysis application that automatically identifies errors per metric and model, surfaces representative examples for exploration, and generates structured summaries of each model’s strengths and weaknesses. Finally, we intend to expand the leaderboard continuously to provide an up-to-date assessment of voice agent capabilities across the field.

View more details about limitations and our upcoming roadmap here.

Core contributors include Tara Bogavelli, Gabrielle Gauthier Melançon, Katrina Stankiewicz, Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Hoang Nguyen, Raghav Mehndiratta, and Hari Subramani.

We also thank Lindsay Brin, Akshay Kalkunte, Joseph Marinier, Jishnu Nair, and Aman Tiwari for their careful data review and thoughtful contributions to the framework, and Fanny Riols, Anil Madamala, Sridhar Nemala, and Srinivas Sunkara for their management, leadership, and support throughout. We also extend our thanks to the PAVA and CLAE ServiceNow teams, whose prior work on evaluations and voice agents provided valuable inspiration for this project.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

A mobile app sends POST /orders. The server creates the order, but the response is lost when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 4G. The app sees a timeout and retries. Now the customer has two orders, and your support team has a refund to process.

Retrying is the right thing for a client to do. The problem is that POST is not idempotent: RFC 9110 defines GET, PUT and DELETE as idempotent methods, but not POST or PATCH. Repeating a POST can repeat its side effects.

An idempotency key fixes this. The client generates a unique key for each logical operation and sends it with every attempt. The server does the work once, stores the response against the key, and returns the stored response for any retry. The IETF HTTPAPI working group is standardizing this pattern as the Idempotency-Key HTTP header field, and this tutorial follows its recommendations.

We'll build it with Node.js, Express 5 and PostgreSQL. By the end you'll have a table that stores keys, a function that safely claims a key under concurrent requests, an Express route that replays stored responses, and a client that retries without creating duplicates.

The client's job is simple: generate a key, usually a UUID, and send the same key on every retry of the same operation. The draft defines the header value as a quoted string:

The server's job is harder, because every request falls into one of five cases:

To tell case 3 from case 4, the server stores a fingerprint of the request alongside the key. A matching fingerprint means a genuine retry; a different one means key reuse. Case 5 is the one most implementations get wrong, because it only shows up under concurrency. A database constraint handles it for us.

Create a project and install the two dependencies:

The key table records who sent the key, the request fingerprint, whether the work has finished, and the response to replay:

Two details matter here. The primary key includes client_id, so keys are scoped per client: two customers who happen to generate the same value can't see each other's responses. And locked_until lets the server recover a key whose request crashed halfway, which we'll use in Step 3.

The draft defines the header value as a structured field string, which means it arrives wrapped in double quotes. Many clients send it without quotes, so the parser below accepts both and limits the characters and length it will store:

The fingerprint has to be identical for identical requests, even if a client serializes the JSON body with its properties in a different order. Sorting object keys before hashing takes care of that. The hash uses SHA-256 from Node's built-in crypto module:

Including the method and path means a key reused on a different endpoint counts as a mismatch, not as a retry.

The tempting approach is to SELECT the key, and insert it if nothing comes back. Under concurrency that fails: two retries arriving a few milliseconds apart both see no row, and both do the work.

Instead, let the primary key decide. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING either inserts the row or does nothing, atomically, even across many application processes. The PostgreSQL INSERT documentation describes this behavior in detail. If the insert returns a row, this request owns the key. If not, we read the existing row and decide which case we're in:

The UPDATE in the last step is also atomic. If two retries find the same expired lock, only one of them matches the locked_until < now() condition and gets the key. If the row disappears between the two queries, for example because it was released after a failure, the function reports in_progress and the client simply retries.

Set LOCK_SECONDS comfortably above the slowest time your operation takes. If the lock expires while the original request is still running, a retry can take over and run the work a second time.

Once a request owns the key, it creates the order and marks the key as completed. Both writes happen in one transaction, so there is no moment where the order exists but the key still says in_progress, or the other way round. Note that a transaction in node-postgres has to use a single client checked out from the pool, as the node-postgres transaction documentation explains:

releaseKey runs when the work fails. Deleting the claim lets the client retry with the same key instead of waiting for the lock to expire. It only deletes rows that are still in progress, so a completed response is never thrown away.

The route validates the body first. A request with invalid input never touches the key table, so the client can fix the input and resend with the same key. Error responses use the application/problem+json format from RFC 9457, which the idempotency draft also uses in its examples:

The server side only works if the client keeps the key stable. The most common client bug is generating a new key inside the retry loop, which turns every retry into a new operation. Generate the key once per logical action, before the first attempt:

The catch branch is the reason idempotency keys exist. After a timeout, the client can't know whether the order was created. With a stable key, retrying is safe either way: if the first attempt succeeded, the retry returns the stored order; if it didn't, the retry creates it. The random jitter spreads retries out, so many clients recovering from the same outage don't all hit the server at once.

In a browser or mobile app, store the key with the pending action, for example in the form state or a local queue. If the user taps "Place order" again after an error, reuse it. Only generate a new key when the user starts a genuinely new action.

Keys can't live forever, or the table grows without limit. The draft leaves the retention period to the server but says it should be published in the API documentation, so clients know how long a retry stays safe. Twenty-four hours covers most retry scenarios. A scheduled job can delete older rows in batches:

Run it every few minutes from cron or your job scheduler until it deletes zero rows. Deleting in batches keeps each transaction short, and the created_at index from Step 1 keeps the inner query fast. A retry that arrives after its key has expired is treated as a new request, which is why the retention period belongs in your documentation.

Start the server with node server.js, then send the same request twice:

The second request lists the properties in a different order, and it's still recognized as a retry because of the canonical fingerprint. Both responses carry the same order ID, and the orders table contains one row.

Now change the quantity while keeping the key. The server answers 422, because the key now belongs to a different request:

To see the concurrent case, add await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 3000)); before completeKey in the route, restart the server, and fire two requests with a new key at the same time:

One request prints 201 and the other 409. Without the ON CONFLICT claim, both would have printed 201 and created two orders. Remove the delay when you're done.

This design guarantees that the database work in Step 4 happens once per key. Two situations need extra care:

Idempotency keys don't replace other safeguards either. A unique constraint on a natural business key, such as one payment per invoice, still catches duplicates that arrive with different keys, for example when a user submits the same form from two tabs.

With one table, an atomic claim and a transaction that stores the response next to the work, POST endpoints become safe to retry. Clients get a simple rule: generate one key per action, reuse it on every retry. The server takes care of the rest, including the concurrent retries that a SELECT-then-INSERT approach misses.

The same pattern works for PATCH endpoints and for webhooks you send to other systems. Start with the endpoints where a duplicate costs real money or confuses a customer, and publish your key format and retention period in the API documentation so client developers know what to send.

#10177. TRL v1.0: Post-Training Library Built to Move with the Field

We’re releasing TRL v1.0, and it marks a real shift in what TRL is. What started as a research codebase has become a dependable library people build on, with clearer expectations around stability. This isn't just a version bump. It reflects the reality that TRL now powers production systems, and embraces that responsibility.

TRL now implements more than 75 post-training methods. But coverage isn’t the goal by itself. What matters is making these methods easy to try, compare, and actually use in practice. The design of the library wasn’t decided upfront. It is the result of years of iteration — the first commit goes back more than six years — and it has been shaped by everything the field threw at it: new algorithms, new models, shifting paradigms. Over time, this pressure forced the codebase toward a very specific design. Parts of it might look unusual at first, but like in many evolutionary codebases, they exist for a reason.

TRL is built for a field that doesn’t sit still. So the question is not how to design the perfect abstraction. It is how to make stable software in a domain that keeps invalidating its own assumptions. This is what we tried to solve in TRL v1.0, and this post explains how.

Post-training has not evolved as a smooth refinement of one recipe. It has moved through successive centers of gravity, each changing not just the objective, but the shape of the stack.

PPO [Schulman et al., (2017); Ziegler et al., (2019)] made one architecture look canonical: a policy, a reference model, a learned reward model, sampled rollouts, and an RL loop.

Then DPO-style methods such as the original DPO [Rafailov et al., (2023)], ORPO [Hong et al., (2024)], and KTO [Ethayarajh et al., (2024)] cut through that stack: preference optimization could work without a separate reward model, value model, or any online RL. Components that had looked fundamental suddenly looked optional.

RLVR-style methods such as GRPO [Shao et al., (2024)] shifted the center again. On tasks like math, code, and tool use, rewards often come from verifiers or deterministic checks rather than learned reward models. Sampling and rollouts matter again, but the objects in the loop are no longer quite the ones PPO libraries were designed around.

The lesson is not just that methods change. The definition of the core keeps changing with them. Strong assumptions here have a short half-life. This is probably why no post-training library is really stable yet.

So what does it mean to build a library for a field that won't sit still? The answer is counterintuitive: don't try to capture the essence of what's stable today. Instead, design around what could change. Reward models illustrate why: they looked essential in PPO, became optional in DPO, and came back as verifiers in RLVR methods — structures that could be deterministic functions rather than learned models. Any abstraction built around their original form would have been obsolete twice over by now. The library survives by recognizing that strong assumptions have a short life, and by making that changeability central to how the codebase is organized.

This is the environment in which TRL is downloaded 3 million times a month, and in which major downstream projects treat it as stable infrastructure. The field keeps shifting the ground, and at the same time, those users need things not to break.

TRL didn’t make a deliberate decision to become a library. It found out it already was one. Projects like Unsloth and Axolotl — with thousands of users between them — had built directly on top of TRL’s trainers and APIs. A breaking change in TRL propagated instantly into their stacks. A renamed argument, a shifted default, a restructured output — any of these became someone else’s incident. The shift had already happened. v1.0 is the moment TRL acknowledged it explicitly.

The unusual thing about TRL’s stability model is not what it guarantees, it is what it tolerates alongside those guarantees. Stable and experimental coexist within the same package, with explicitly different contracts. The stable core follows semantic versioning. The experimental layer makes no such promises — it is where new methods land while they are still being evaluated, and where the API can move fast to keep up with the field.

This isn’t a compromise. It’s a response to a specific constraint: the field produces new methods faster than any of them can earn stability. Refusing to add immature methods would make TRL irrelevant within months. Adding them all to stable would break every downstream project every time an algorithm turned out not to work as expected.

Promotion from experimental to stable isn’t automatic. What matters is the ratio between maintenance cost and actual usage. Some methods earn their place because the community uses them heavily. Others become viable because we can make them cheap enough to maintain — and the design of the codebase is what makes that possible.

In practice, the stable surface includes trainers for SFT, DPO, Reward modeling, RLOO, and GRPO, along with their close variants. The experimental surface is broader and moves faster; for an up-to-date view, the best reference is the TRL documentation.

The breaking changes needed to reach v1.0 were distributed deliberately across the 0.x releases. Migration from the last 0.x version is minimal — see the migration guide.

In a domain where patterns keep changing, the temptation is to build flexible abstractions that can accommodate anything. Our answer was the opposite: limit abstractions to the strict minimum — while recognizing that this “minimum” is almost always overestimated.

In practice, this translates into a very local approach to code:

The goal is not to eliminate structure altogether — shared utilities still exist — but to avoid imposing abstractions where the domain itself is not yet stable. For instance, rather than defining a common base class for offline trainers, we prefer independent implementations when their future evolution is uncertain.

Judges are a good example of what happens when we don’t follow this principle. Early on, we introduced a Judge abstraction to unify the various ways of evaluating model outputs. It looked reasonable at the time. In practice, it was never really used — the abstraction didn’t match how people actually approached evaluation, and it added indirection without adding value. It still lives in the repo, mostly as legacy. In hindsight, shipping the concrete implementations without the unifying abstraction would have served users better.

This approach favors explicit and modifiable usage over rigid frameworks: less magic, but more control. It comes with an obvious cost: code duplication. While often seen as an anti-pattern, in this context it has proven not only acceptable, but effective. Contrary to intuition, it remains manageable in practice with a small but consistent discipline: keeping deltas between implementations minimal and avoiding unnecessary divergence. Like in the Transformers design philosophy, we accept duplication and local explicitness by design. The motivations largely coincide, with some nuance in focus.

This is easier to see than to describe. Compare RLOO and GRPO: large parts of their implementation are duplicated almost line for line. That is not accidental, and it is not dead weight. These methods are close enough that keeping their code paths aligned makes them easier to read, easier to evolve, and cheaper to maintain.

The goal of this comparison is not to argue that TRL should be judged as best on every axis. It should not. Some systems are built for maximum throughput (like PipelineRL), some are optimized for a narrower slice of the problem (like LLaMA-Factory), and some offer a more opinionated development experience in a specific environment (like Tinker). TRL occupies a different place in the ecosystem: it is a general-purpose post-training library that tries to keep the API and the code as simple as the domain allows, while combining broad method coverage, deep Hugging Face integration, a relatively low infrastructure burden, and an explicit stability contract.

Libraries like Unsloth and Axolotl are not included here because they build on top of TRL rather than sitting beside it in the comparison; in that sense, many of their users are also TRL users indirectly.

Some rows are factual (GitHub stars, Last release, Last commit), others are qualitative judgments (Semver stability).

Taken together, these comparisons point to a clear role for TRL: a general-purpose library designed to keep breadth, simplicity, integration, and stability in the same place. Its full downstream footprint is hard to measure, since most deployments are private and reverse dependencies are largely invisible, but the available signals already show that TRL operates at a distinctly different scale.

By now, the logic of v1.0 should be clear: it is not a claim that post-training has stabilized. On the contrary, it is an acknowledgment that the field will keep shifting, and that we're confident that the library has the right shape to absorb whatever comes next. The question is not what comes after v1.0, but what’s next for v1.0.

Today, GRPO in TRL is primarily used through a synchronous loop: generate rollouts, score them, then step the optimizer. That shape is simple and dependable, but it ties throughput to the slowest stage and leaves performance on the table at scale.

The fix is conceptually simple: generation and training don't need to be lock-stepped. We already have an early asynchronous GRPO design, and the next step is to harden it. The core idea is to decouple generation and training, letting generation run continuously on dedicated inference resources while training consumes a steady stream of scored trajectories, with buffering, backpressure, and clear policy-version accounting. This improves utilization and scales across GPUs and nodes. Other libraries already offer forms of asynchronous RL, but bringing it to TRL would make this style of training available through broader integrations, simpler APIs, and a much lower barrier to adoption.

The next candidates include KTO and newer distillation trainers such as SDFT, SDPO, and possibly GOLD or GKD. As discussed in Section 2, before moving them to stable, the goal is to minimize code differences across implementations and monitor sustained community interest relative to maintenance cost.

TRL supports large-scale training, including multi-node runs and larger models; the next step is to make this path significantly more robust and easier to operate in production. That includes stronger guarantees around distributed stability, clearer scaling defaults, and deeper support for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE), especially expert parallelism, where routing, load balancing, and memory behavior become critical.

Training is still too often driven by vibes. Loss curves go down, reward curves go up, a few samples look better than before, and people convince themselves the run is working. When it fails, they scroll through logs, compare runs by eye, and guess. That is already a weak interface for humans. For agents, it is worse: it is barely an interface at all.

One of the most important directions for TRL is to make training legible to software, not just to people. That means going beyond dashboards and raw metrics to produce explicit signals: is the policy improving, collapsing, over-optimizing the verifier, drifting off-distribution, or plateauing? The goal is for TRL to surface these patterns automatically, explain them clearly, and turn them into actions.

The plan is to embed heuristics directly into the training loop and emit structured, actionable warnings — the kind a beginner can act on immediately and an agent can parse:

Not just logging what happened — reasoning about what it means and what to do next. Useful for beginners who need guardrails, and for agents that need a training stack they can actually automate.

Post-training doesn't converge. It shifts, and the next shift is already coming.

v1.0 is not a claim that things have settled. It's an acknowledgment that they haven't yet, and a commitment that the library can be relied on anyway. Six years of evolving alongside the field — and alongside the hundreds of contributors who made it possible — shaped a design we're confident is ready for what comes next, whatever that turns out to be. The community and the downstream projects had already assumed that stability — v1.0 makes it real.

Migration from the last 0.x release is minimal, and the migration guide covers everything. If you're new, now is a good time to start.

#10176. Like clockwork, the Pixel 11 is a way better buy after a few months [Video]

Like clockwork, the first quarter of the Pixel 11 brings discounts, and this shines a light on the base model that needs to be explored.

By this point, you don’t need me to tell you that this is a familiar design. It’s turning into a comfortable pair of slippers at this point in time. Nothing is wrong, and nothing particularly stands out. A safe but samey design that is inoffensive.

I hoped that the maximum brightness bug would have been resolved by now with the screen. It creates a shadow around the edges of the display after a minute or so when in direct sunlight. Somewhat like blooming on a cheap LCD screen. It does diminish what is otherwise a great display.

The thickness has started to feel like a relic of the 2023 design that feels a little dated now. I have been using the Pixel 11 without a case most of the time, which mitigates it, but throw a case on and it’s a chunky boi. The added thickness would probably have been acceptable had the extra space been filled with more battery, but it feels like that boat has set sail a long time ago. A slimmer profile probably would have helped differentiate without deviating too much from last year’s phone.

After months of using the Pixel 11, the move of the NFC module to the top edge has been huge for me because my car uses an NFC terminal to lock and unlock when you’re without a set of car keys. With the Pixel 10, it worked but not quite as smoothly. It’s one of those inconsequential changes that makes a real-world difference.

Gemini Intelligence has been something I’ve started to rely on quite heavily. I love that I get a prompt to add an appointment to my calendar, and all of the important details have been taken care of, like the location, extra contact details, the works.

I’m not sure what the hold-up is for adding wider functionality. It’s actively hurting things, in my opinion. Google Messages is great, but some of the automation functions locked in there mean I haven’t been saving any time with Gemini’s prowess at doing the legwork of keeping my life up to date.

I’ve tried using Pause Point, but found it’s just easier to leave my phone face down rather than use an app to try and stop using my phone…maybe if we all did that, so many of the world’s ills wouldn’t be so pronounced. Just a thought.

The November Pixel Drop has also made some notable changes to the Pixel 11 experience that I can’t believe were held back since launch. If you waited and bought in the last few weeks with the substantial discounts kicking around, you objectively get a better phone today than at launch.

The improvements don’t overhaul things, just enhance or heighten the fluidity and experience above what was available in the months post-launch. More cohesive theming, little tweaks to the UI; it’s not reinventing the Pixel 11, just augmenting it in ways that would have been nice back in August.

I don’t really have much to complain about with the Pixel 11 lifespan even after months of charging. Yes, charging is still slow, but you only need to charge once per day. If we were talking about a phone with bad battery life and slow charging, I’d have more to complain about. However, it’s still solid and dependable.

The camera continues to impress without really improving drastically. I can’t help but feel that every couple of generations, the Pro camera setup should be passed on to the base Pixel, then we get a newer, improved system on that specific Pro model. It’d allow for quicker improvements and maybe, dare I say it, make the camera system cheaper as parts get reused. If anything, it would help Google’s supposed environmental pledges by preventing camera components from hitting landfill.

A lot of people will tell you the best camera is the one you have with you, and this hasn’t ever been a problem for a recent Pixel. I can count on one hand the frustrations I have felt with the Pixel 11 camera since it landed on my desk on launch day. I am happier than a year ago with the base Pixel 10 than the 11, which is to say this is a bigger leap or a return to form.

Having the ability to tune Camera Looks was something I have loved, but you might just fall into using one tuned look that fits your own personal style. There is an element of this that might change the perception of the Pixel 11 camera consistency versus its predecessors. What I mean is that while it does still excel at point-and-shoot, the fact that Looks are baked into the JPEG could be a problem. There are times when I’ve thought that an image might have been better using default settings.

That said, I have stuck to “Shadows” with Contrast set to -5, Highlights to -5, Shadows to -5.5, warmth to 0.5, and Grain to “Strong.” That is a recipe I’ll probably stick with for a long time to come. It’s still weird that we can do all this at the camera level with a Pixel. Whether “normies” even use the options or just stick to the out-of-the-box default settings is another discussion for another day.

At $699, the Pixel 11 becomes a decent buy for a lot of people. For others, the distinct lack of power is something that can’t ever be overcome. I would buy this for a relative because it’ll do everything they could ever want and more. For a friend who cares about having the cutting edge in their pocket? Probably not.

A lot of the problems over the past few years on Pixel phones have come from the price tag.

Even with the discounts in and around Black Friday, the fact that you can get a device like the Galaxy S25 Ultra that’ll have better specs and lots of valuable features for around the same price. The last few generations of the Pixel have been harder to recommend because of the drawbacks versus the cost and the competition.

I said a few months ago that there is a good phone under the price hikes, and that remains unchanged. However, there are better products from the year prior that won’t compromise and are even cheaper. In a silo, you’re getting a 7/10 product at a 3/10 price. Just how that changes depends on forthcoming updates. One saving grace is that no Pixel is ever quite the same months after it rolls off the production line. A few Pixel Drops, even more discounts, and maybe a true seal of approval might be easier.

To put it into context, this was never a $900 phone and arguably never should have been. That’s somewhat a failing on Google’s part in more ways than one. At least it’s down to a palatable price that should be the Pixel baseline.

#10175. How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

AI agents now read email, book travel and move money for the people who use them. Every tool call also pulls in text that someone else wrote, and whoever controls that text can try to steer the agent. OWASP calls this agent goal hijack and ranks it first in its Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026).

In September we announced Agent Anomaly Detection in Private Preview on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It reads your agents' traces and logs asynchronously, without adding latency, and flags sessions where an agent acts outside its intended boundaries. We tested this feature against benchmarks for this top risk of agent goal hijack.

Security tools tend to look good on tests their own team wrote, so we ran five non-Google-written, public agent-security benchmarks through Agent Anomaly Detection without changing anything. In four of them, the harmful instruction hides in data that a tool returns. In the fifth, the user asks for harm directly.

The model itself didn't follow about half of the harmful instructions it read. It refused three in four direct requests for harm, and ignored or failed at about 30% of the instructions hidden in tool output. Of the ones that were executed, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% for post-execution review. It raised false alarms on 2% to 16% of benign sessions, depending on the tools the agent uses. Poisoned memory is the clear gap: when instructions planted in the agent’s long-term memory made it act, Agent Anomaly Detection caught 4 of 18.

We ran each benchmark case through an agent built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) using gemini-2.5-flash, on the benchmark's simulated apps. The agent sent its traces and logs to Agent Anomaly Detection, as a customer's agent would. Then the benchmark's own Python check read the final state of the apps, such as whether money left the account, and labeled the session. Deterministic code decides the label, not a model, so an injected instruction can't mislead the grader, and Agent Anomaly Detection cannot cheat the benchmark. Each agent first ran at least 300 benign sessions, because Agent Anomaly Detection learns how each agent usually behaves.

We also recorded whether a tool returned the harmful instruction to the agent. In many cases, the agent never opens the email or file that holds it. So each harmful session ends one of three ways:

In AgentHarm, the user sends the request, so the agent always reads it.

The five benchmarks are AgentDojo (NeurIPS 2024), InjecAgent (ACL 2024 Findings), Agent Security Bench (ASB, ICLR 2025), AgentDyn (2026) and AgentHarm (ICLR 2025). ASB plants the instruction in the agent's long-term memory. In all, Agent Anomaly Detection scored 1,774 sessions.

Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 87% of the harmful instructions that the agent carried out, and raised a few false alarms on ordinary office work. It's strongest on goal hijack and tool misuse, and weakest on poisoned memory.

Each finding carries a threat category, and four of Agent Anomaly Detection’s five categories align with the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications. We graded each OWASP category on what this study showed, not on what Agent Anomaly Detection is designed to catch.

Public benchmarks concentrate on goal hijack and tool misuse, so our evidence is strongest there. We did not find public benchmarks with labeled agent traces for cascading failures or for identity and privilege abuse. Shared benchmarks for those categories would help the whole field.

By benchmark, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 85% of the carried-out harmful instructions on AgentDojo, 87% on InjecAgent, 99% on AgentDyn and 81% on AgentHarm. Over all harmful sessions, including the ones that the agent never read or resisted, it flagged 45% to 62%. In the 141 sessions where the agent never read the instruction, nothing happened, and it flagged just 1.

Results held across the apps. In 8 of the 11 apps, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged at least 95% of the carried-out harmful instructions. The lowest rate was in AgentDojo's Slack app, at 63%. Many of those instructions ask for one small action, such as a page visit, which looks like normal browsing.

Agent Anomaly Detection also flags many requests that the agent refuses. In AgentHarm, the agent refused most requests and carried out 108 of 412, and Agent Anomaly Detection still flagged 55% of the refused sessions, because the request sits in the user's own message, which it reads. When the agent didn't follow an instruction hidden in tool output, it flagged only 11% to 25%, because the instruction sits deep inside a tool result.

False alarms were rare on ordinary office work: on the three injection benchmarks, whose benign sessions are office tasks, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 2% to 4% of benign sessions. On AgentHarm it flagged 16%. Those benign tasks are twins of the harmful ones, so they post to social media, run terminal commands and download files. High-impact tools in normal use look more like misuse.

Agent Anomaly Detection did less well in five areas. It flagged only 11% to 25% of the instructions that the agent resisted, because a resisted instruction changes little in how the agent behaves. It missed more small actions, like single page visits, because they look like normal work. And it raised more false alarms for agents whose everyday work uses high-impact tools. If your agent is one of them, expect more findings at first, and triage them by severity and threat category.

The other two areas are new agents and poisoned memory. Some Agent Anomaly Detection methods need a few hundred sessions of history: on AgentDyn, it flagged 33% of carried-out harmful instructions when each agent had about 220 benign sessions, and 99% with 360. And it caught only 4 of the 18 sessions where poisoned memory made the agent act.

Protect your agents with defense in depth. Use controls that stop harmful actions before they run, and Agent Anomaly Detection to find what gets through.

We used one agent model and simulated apps, and the benchmarks' benign tasks are likely simpler than your production traffic, so your false-alarm rate can differ. Agent Anomaly Detection returned no result for about 6% of the sessions we sent; counting those as misses lowers the overall rates by 1 to 2 points.

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview. To request access, read the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

#10173. How SD Card Photo and Video Recovery Works: A Practical Guide With a JPEG Carving Example

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

For photographers, videographers and content creators, an SD card is more than a storage device. It holds the raw material behind a finished project: wedding photographs, travel footage, product demos and drone recordings that may be impossible to recreate. Data loss can happen at almost any stage of that workflow, from a folder deleted to make space to a card formatted before the footage was backed up.

This article explains why files on a card become unavailable, what to do in the first minutes, how recovery tools find data, and how to compare options. It includes a small Python example that recovers JPEG files from a disk image, so you can see the mechanism for yourself. It also compares free open-source tools with paid graphical ones, using criteria you can apply yourself. Recovery is never guaranteed, and tool features change, so confirm details against each vendor’s current documentation.

Recovery is not just a matter of finding a deleted filename. Several different problems can make files unavailable, and they call for different approaches.

These steps cannot guarantee recovery, but they reduce avoidable risk.

Most tools combine two methods, and understanding them helps you read scan results.

Carving has a cost. Because file system information is ignored, names and folder structure are usually lost, which is why scan results often show generic names. Fragmented files can also be recovered incomplete, since the tool assumes the pieces are stored one after another. Free tools build on these same ideas. Wondershare Recoverit V15, which also offers a free version for Windows and Mac, adds a graphical interface, while PhotoRec and ddrescue stay closer to the command line.

The script below is a teaching sketch, not a recovery product. It reads a raw disk image, finds JPEG start markers, and writes out the bytes up to the last end marker before the next start. That detail matters because a JPEG can contain an embedded thumbnail with its own markers, so stopping at the first end marker would cut a file short.

A short test builds two real JPEGs, hides them in random bytes, and checks that both are carved and open as valid images:

Use it on an image rather than the card itself. On Linux you can make one with a read-only copy, for example with the GNU ddrescue tool, which is designed to copy data from failing media. Then run the carver against the image and save the output to a different drive. Real tools handle many more formats, trim files using header information, and deal with video containers, so treat this as a way to understand the idea.

The right choice depends on the problem, your platform and how comfortable you are with the command line. The table summarizes what each project’s own documentation states.

The order of steps matters more than the choice of tool. A cautious workflow on Linux or macOS looks like this:

Graphical tools follow the same logic and mainly change step 3, with thumbnails, filters and search that make large result sets easier to browse. Whether that is worth paying for depends on how many files you need to sift through and how comfortable you are on the command line. When comparing any tool, ask:

Features such as search by capture time, folder or AI-based tagging depend on metadata surviving the loss, and they narrow results without proving a file is intact. Treat them as convenience, not verification.

Recovering a video file does not necessarily mean recovering a playable video. A recording interrupted during writing can lack the structural information a player needs, and other files may be damaged in ways that block playback.

The distinction matters. Recovery retrieves missing or inaccessible data, while repair tries to fix damage that affects a file’s usability. Some cases need one, the other or both. Repair has limits too: if essential video data was overwritten or never recorded, software cannot recreate the original footage in full. After any recovery or repair, play the file all the way through and compare it with what you expect.

For a quick check of a recovered clip, ffprobe can show whether the container is readable:

An error or a missing duration suggests the file needs repair or is incomplete.

Often yes, if nothing has overwritten them. Stop using the card immediately and scan it or an image of it.

Not before recovery. Formatting changes file system structures and may make recovery harder.

Recovery retrieves missing data. Repair fixes a file that exists but will not open or play correctly.

Not always. PhotoRec and TestDisk are free and open source, while paid tools add a graphical interface and extras such as previews, filtering and video repair.

On a different drive from the card. Saving to the same card can overwrite data you still want.

SD card data loss creates two related challenges: getting files back, and working out which recovered files are useful. Stopping use of the card, working on an image and understanding the difference between file system recovery, carving and repair put you in a better position, whichever tool you choose. Graphical tools aim to make large result sets easier to navigate, and free tools such as PhotoRec and TestDisk remain solid options. Try your chosen tool on a copy first, verify what you recover, and keep a backup so you do not need to do this again.
